p.seg: "On the Faults of Qin - Part I"
Duke Xiào of Qin held the strategic fortifications of Xiáo and Hán,
possessed the lands of Yōngzhōu,
and with his ministers steadfastly guarded them,
while eyeing the house of Zhōu.
He harbored the intention to roll up the world like a mat,
to bag the entire realm,
to envelop all within the four seas,
and to swallow up the eight wildernesses.
At that time,
Lord Shāng assisted him,
establishing laws and regulations internally,
promoting farming and weaving,
and preparing the tools of defense and attack;
externally, he practiced horizontal alliances to pit the feudal lords against each other.
Thereupon, the people of Qin effortlessly took the lands west of the Yellow River.
After Duke Xiào passed away,
Kings Huìwén, Wǔ, Zhāo, and Xiāng inherited the existing enterprise,
following the established strategy,
capturing Hànzhōng to the south,
seizing Bā and Shǔ to the west,
cutting off fertile lands to the east,
and acquiring strategic commanderies to the north.
The feudal lords were filled with fear,
forming alliances to plot how to weaken Qin.
They did not spare precious vessels, valuable treasures, or rich lands,
in order to attract the talented men of the world.
They formed vertical alliances and established ties,
uniting as one.
At this time,
Qí had Mèngcháng,
Zhào had Píngyuán,
Chǔ had Chūnshēn,
and Wèi had Xìnlíng:
these four lords,
all wise and sincere,
generous and benevolent,
respected the worthy and valued scholars.
They pledged vertical alliances to break the horizontal ones,
uniting the masses of Hán, Wèi, Yān, Zhào, Sòng, Wèi, and Zhōngshān.
Thus, the scholars of the six states, such as Nìng Yuè, Xú Shàng, Sū Qín, and Dù Hè, devised strategies for them,
while Qí Míng, Zhōu Zuì, Chén Zhěn, Shào Gǔ, Lóu Huǎn, Zhái Jǐng, Sū Lì, and Yuè Yì conveyed their intentions,
and Wú Qǐ, Sūn Bìn, Dài Tuó, Ní Liáng, Wáng Liào, Tián Jì, Lián Pō, and Zhào Shē commanded their troops.
They once relied on a territory ten times larger,
with a million-strong army,
advancing to the pass to attack Qin.
The Qin opened the gates and lured the enemy in,
but the armies of the nine states hesitated and fled, not daring to advance.
Qin did not spend a single arrow or lose a single arrowhead,
yet the feudal lords of the world were already exhausted.
Thereupon, the vertical alliance dissolved and the covenants broke,
as they competed to cede lands and bribe Qin.
Qin had surplus strength to exploit their weaknesses,
pursuing the fleeing and defeated,
leaving a million corpses,
with blood flowing enough to float shields,
taking advantage of the situation,
carving up the world,
dividing the mountains and rivers,
forcing strong states to submit,
and weak states to pay homage.
This continued through Kings Xiàowén and Zhuāngxiāng,
whose reigns were short,
and the state was without incident.
When it came to the First Emperor,
he built upon the achievements of the six preceding generations,
wielding a long whip to rule the world,
annexing the two Zhōu and extinguishing the feudal lords,
ascending to the supreme position to control the six directions,
brandishing clubs to whip the world,
his might shaking the four seas.
To the south, he seized the lands of the Bǎi Yuè,
establishing the commanderies of Guìlín and Xiàng,
the lords of the Bǎi Yuè bowed their heads and tied ropes around their necks,
entrusting their fate to low-ranking officials.
Then he sent Méng Tián to build the Great Wall in the north to guard the barriers,
pushing the Xiōngnú back over seven hundred lǐ,
so the barbarians dared not come south to pasture their horses,
and their warriors dared not bend their bows to seek revenge.
Then he abolished the ways of the former kings,
burned the writings of the hundred schools,
to stupefy the black-headed people.
He destroyed the famous cities,
killed the heroes,
collected all the weapons of the world and gathered them in Xiányáng,
melted down the spearheads and arrowheads,
and cast them into twelve metal statues,
to weaken the people of the world.
Then he trod Mount Huà as his wall,
used the Yellow River as his moat,
relying on the towering heights,
facing the unfathomable depths for security.
Excellent generals with strong crossbows guarded the strategic points,
trusted ministers and elite troops,
displayed sharp weapons to challenge any who approached.
The world was already settled,
and the First Emperor's heart
believed that the defenses within the passes were secure,
a thousand lǐ of impregnable walls,
an imperial enterprise for ten thousand generations of his descendants.
After the First Emperor passed away,
his remaining might still shook distant customs.
Yet Chén Shè was a son of broken jars and rope-hinged doors,
a man of the common masses,
a conscripted laborer,
whose ability did not reach that of an average person,
who possessed neither the virtue of Zhòngní or Mò Dí,
nor the wealth of Táo Zhū or Yī Dùn.
Treading among the ranks,
he rose from the fields,
leading weary and worn-out soldiers,
commanding a few hundred men,
turned to attack Qin.
They cut trees to make weapons,
raised poles as banners,
the world gathered like clouds and responded,
carrying provisions and following like shadows,
the heroes east of the mountains rose together and destroyed the Qin clan.
Now, the world was not small or weak;
the lands of Yōngzhōu and the fortifications of Xiáo and Hán
remained as they were.
Chén Shè's position
was not more exalted than the lords of Qí, Chǔ, Yān, Zhào, Hán, Wèi, Sòng, Wèi, or Zhōngshān;
his hoes and wooden spears
were not sharper than hooks, halberds, or long lances;
his conscripted multitude
was not superior to the armies of the nine states;
the strategies of deep planning and distant vision, the ways of marching and employing troops,
did not match those of the earlier scholars.
Yet success and failure changed places,
accomplishments turned opposite,
why is this?
If we were to compare the states east of the mountains with Chén Shè in length and size,
weighing their authority and strength,
they could not be mentioned in the same breath.
Yet Qin, with its small territory,
achieved the power of ten thousand chariots,
ordering the eight provinces and making its peers pay homage,
for over a hundred years.
Then it made the six directions its home,
and Xiáo and Hán its palace.
One man's rebellion caused the seven temples to collapse,
and he died at the hands of others,
becoming the laughingstock of the world,
why is this?
Because they did not practice benevolence and righteousness,
and the circumstances of offense and defense had changed.
"On the Faults of Qin - Part II"
Qin extinguished the sacrifices of Zhōu,
unified the lands within the seas,
annexed the feudal lords,
faced south and called himself emperor,
nourishing the scholars of the world with the wealth of the four seas,
elegantly turning them toward the wind,
why was this so?
It is said:
For a long time in recent antiquity, there had been no true king.
The house of Zhōu was lowly and weak,
the five hegemons had already perished,
orders were not carried out throughout the world,
thus the feudal lords relied on their strength,
the strong bullied the weak,
the many oppressed the few,
warfare did not cease,
and the scholars and people were exhausted and worn out.
Now Qin faced south and ruled the world,
this meant there was a Son of Heaven above.
Thus, the common people hoped to secure their lives,
all humbly looking up to the ruler.
At this time,
consolidating authority and securing achievements,
the root of safety and danger lay in this.
The King of Qín harbored a greedy and base heart,
acted upon his own self-assertive wisdom,
distrusted his meritorious officials,
did not befriend the scholars and common people,
abolished the way of the true king and established his private affections,
burned the writings and enforced harsh punishments,
valued deceit and force over benevolence and righteousness,
making cruelty the beginning for all under heaven.
Now, those who engage in annexation exalt deceit and force,
while those who secure stability value顺应权威,
judging from this,
the methods of seizing and maintaining power are different.
Although Qín had moved beyond the Warring States to rule the empire,
its ways did not change,
its governance did not reform,
this is why it obtained what it did.
Isolated and possessing it alone,
thus its downfall could be awaited standing up.
Had the King of Qín considered the affairs of past ages,
and emulated the paths of Yīn and Zhōu,
to regulate his governance,
even if later there were wanton and arrogant rulers,
there still would not have been the peril of collapse.
Therefore, the three dynastic founders established the empire,
their fame and titles illustrious and admirable,
their achievements enduring.
Now that the Second Emperor of Qín has ascended,
all under heaven crane their necks to witness its fall.
For the cold find benefit in short coarse garments and the hungry find sweetness in chaff and husks,
the world is in uproar,
which is the asset for a new ruler.
This means that toiling people are easily won by benevolence.
If the Second Emperor had the conduct of an average ruler,
and employed the loyal and worthy,
with ruler and ministers united in heart, concerned about the troubles within the seas,
dressed in plain white to rectify the errors of the former emperor,
divided lands and distributed people to enfeoff the descendants of meritorious officials,
established states and set up rulers to show courtesy to the empire,
emptied the prisons and spared punishments and executions,
abolished the confiscation of families and other corrupt crimes,
allowing each to return to their hometowns,
opened the granaries,
distributed wealth and coins,
to relieve the orphaned, solitary, poor, and distressed scholars,
lightened taxes and reduced corvée,
to aid the urgent needs of the hundred surnames,
simplified laws and reduced penalties to maintain the aftermath,
enabling all under heaven to reform themselves,
change their conduct and cultivate virtue,
each cautious of their own person,
fulfilling the hopes of the myriad people,
and with abundant virtue, bring rest to the empire.
Then within the four seas,
all would joyfully find peace and happiness in their places,
fearing only change,
even if there were cunning and harmful people,
none would have the heart to turn against their superiors,
thus treacherous ministers would have no means to disguise their cunning,
and the evils of violence and rebellion would cease.
The Second Emperor did not follow this method,
but compounded it with unprincipled rule,
destroyed the ancestral temples,
and initiated changes with the people,
constructed the Ēpáng Palace,
multiplied punishments and severe executions,
governance by officials became harsh and deep,
rewards and punishments were inappropriate,
tax collections knew no bounds,
the empire was full of troubles,
officials could not maintain order,
the common people were destitute, yet the ruler did not relieve them.
Thereafter, deceit and falsehood arose together,
and superiors and inferiors evaded each other,
those burdened with crimes were numerous,
punishments and executions lined the roads,
and the empire suffered from it.
From the local gentry down to the masses,
each harbored a sense of personal danger,
personally experiencing the reality of hardship and poverty,
all uneasy in their positions,
thus easily moved to action.
Therefore, Chén Shè did not need the worthiness of Tāng or Wǔ,
nor rely on the dignity of a duke or marquis,
yet raising his arm in the great marsh, the empire responded,
because his people were in peril.
Thus, the former kings,
seeing the changes from beginning to end,
understood the causes of survival and downfall,
therefore governed with the Way,
focusing solely on bringing peace to them.
Even if there were ministers who acted rebelliously below,
they would certainly lack the aid of responsive support.
Hence it is said, "Those at peace can be led to righteousness,
while those in peril are easily led to wrongdoing,"
this refers to this.
Noble as the Son of Heaven,
rich in possessing the four seas,
yet ending up executed,
is due to failure in correction.
This is the fault of the Second Emperor.
Qín annexed the feudal lords with over thirty provinces east of the mountains,
guarded the ferries and passes,
relied on steep strongholds,
repaired armor and weapons to defend them.
Yet Chén Shè led a scattered crowd of several hundred,
raised his arms and shouted loudly,
without using the weapons of bows or halberds,
but with hoes, mallets, and wooden clubs,
eating wherever they found houses,
roamed freely across the empire.
The Qín people, relying on their strongholds, did not defend,
passes and bridges were not closed,
long halberds did not thrust,
strong crossbows did not shoot.
Chǔ and Pèi advanced deep,
fought at Hóngmén,
without even the difficulty of a fence.
Then the region east of the mountains was greatly disturbed,
feudal lords rose together,
heroes and leaders established themselves.
Qín sent Zhāng Hán to lead troops eastward on campaign,
Zhāng Hán used his three armies to bargain for terms abroad,
plotting against his superiors.
The lack of trust among the ministers,
can be seen here.
Zǐ Yīng ascended but remained unawakened,
had Zǐ Yīng possessed the capability of an average ruler,
and merely had moderate assistance,
even if the east of the mountains were in chaos,
the land of Sān Qín could have been fully preserved,
and the sacrifices at the ancestral temples should not have ended.
The land of Qín, surrounded by mountains and girded by rivers, was considered secure,
a state of fourfold strongholds.
From Duke Mù onwards,
up to the King of Qín,
over twenty rulers,
often stood as the strongest among the feudal lords.
Was this because they were all worthy generation after generation?
It was their strategic position that made it so.
Moreover, the empire once united in heart and effort to attack Qín.
In that era,
the wise and intelligent stood together,
excellent generals led their troops,
worthy ministers conveyed their strategies,
yet they were hindered by the obstacles and could not advance,
Qín then invited them in to fight by opening its passes,
millions of troops fled in defeat and thus crumbled; those hindered by obstacles and unable to advance,
was it due to lack of courage, strength, or wisdom?
The terrain was unfavorable,
the circumstances were inconvenient.
Though Qín had small towns,
it attacked and annexed large cities,
guarded the perilous passes and stationed armies,
built high ramparts and avoided battle,
closed the passes and held the narrows,
bearing halberds to defend them.
The feudal lords arose from commoners,
gathered for profit,
not possessing the conduct of an uncrowned king.
Their alliances were not close,
their people were not attached,
in name they sought to destroy Qín,
but in reality, they sought gain from it.
They saw that Qín's defenses were difficult to assault,
and would surely retreat and form battle lines.
Qín could have pacified the land and rested the people,
awaiting their exhaustion,
taking advantage of their dispersal to attack the weary,
to command the feudal lords,
without worry of not achieving their ambition within the seas.
Noble as the Son of Heaven,
rich in possessing the four seas,
yet ending up captured,
his method of rescuing failure was wrong.
The King of Qín was self-satisfied and did not seek counsel,
thus persisting in error without change.
The Second Emperor inherited this,
following without alteration,
and through cruelty aggravated the calamities.
Zǐyīng stood isolated without kin,
endangered and weak without support.
These three rulers' delusion,
unawakened throughout their lives,
led to their downfall—
was it not fitting?
At that time,
the age was not without men of deep strategy and foresight who understood transformation,
yet the reason they dared not exhaust loyalty to rectify faults
was Qín's customs of numerous taboos and prohibitions.
Before loyal words even left their mouths, their bodies were already destroyed.
Thus causing the scholars of the realm
to strain their ears listening,
stand with feet rooted in fear,
and shut their mouths without speaking.
Therefore, the three rulers lost the Way,
and loyal ministers did not remonstrate, wise men did not strategize.
When the realm was already in chaos,
treacherous ministers did not report upward—
is this not tragic!
The former kings knew that obstruction harms the state,
so they established dukes, ministers, officials, and scholars
to embellish laws and institute punishments,
and the realm was well-governed.
In its strength,
it prohibited violence and punished rebellion, and the world submitted;
in its weakness,
the Five Hegemons campaigned and the feudal lords followed;
in its decline,
it defended internally and attached externally, yet the altars of state survived.
Thus when Qín was prosperous,
complex laws and harsh punishments made the world tremble;
when it declined,
the common people resented and looked elsewhere, and within the seas there was rebellion.
Therefore, the Zhōu kings' sequence attained the Way,
and lasted over a thousand years without end.
Qín failed in both root and branch,
thus it could not endure long.
From this perspective,
the threads of safety and danger are far apart.
A common saying goes:
"Not forgetting past affairs
provides a teacher for future affairs."
Thus the noble person governing a state,
observes antiquity above,
tests it in the present age,
compares it with human affairs,
examines the principles of prosperity and decline,
scrutinizes what is appropriate in power and influence,
removes and follows with order,
responds to the times with change,
thus enduring long spans of time while the altars of state remain secure.
"Ancestral Heads"
Now perhaps a blood brother plots to become Eastern Emperor,
a nephew of the emperor strikes westward,
and now Wú is again reported.
The Son of Heaven is in the prime of life,
his conduct of righteousness without fault,
his virtuous grace increasingly bestowed,
yet still it is like this—
how much more so with the greatest feudal lords
whose power is ten times this?
Why then is the realm somewhat peaceful?
The kings of the great states are young in the embrace,
while the tutors and chancellors appointed by Hàn still hold their affairs.
After several years,
when the feudal lords' kings have mostly come of age,
their vigor at its peak,
the tutors appointed by Hàn return home and refuse to stay,
the chancellors appointed by Hàn claim illness and are granted dismissal,
they themselves place their private men from assistant commandants upward throughout,
like this,
how different is it from the actions of Huáinán and Jìběi!
At that time to then desire peace and order,
even Yáo and Shùn could not achieve it.
Your servant therefore says:
The time is nearly past,
if Your Majesty does not plan early,
doubts will arise in years to come about what is not desired.
Huángdì said:
"At midday one must sun-dry,
grasping a knife one must cut."
Now to follow this way and preserve complete safety
is very easy;
if unwilling to act early,
later one will destroy kin and behead them,
how different is this from Qín's final age?
Moreover, to say Heaven grants authority not very extraordinary yet repeatedly controls people—
how can this be obtained?
With the position of Son of Heaven,
using the power of Son of Heaven,
riding the present time,
aided by Heaven,
still fearing to turn danger into safety,
and chaos into order—
if we suppose Your Majesty were in Qí Huán's place,
would you not assemble the feudal lords and rectify the realm?
Reaching this point, Your Majesty is greatly mistaken;
the time is nearly lost,
my heart secretly leaps, fearing it is already difficult to leave this spring,
Heaven tilts, time tilts, strength tilts,
able to gaze intently yet unwilling to act, thus losing the time—
is this not wasteful?
One could have perfected the realm and been praised,
but instead created this record.
I secretly ache deeply for Your Majesty,
may Your Majesty above deign to briefly consider this.
"Counting Peace"
Your servant privately considers the situation:
one thing deserving deep pain and regret,
two that may cause flowing tears,
six that may provoke long sighs,
as for others that defy reason and harm the Way,
they are difficult to exhaustively list.
Those presenting words all say:
"The realm is already at peace."
Your servant alone says:
"Not at peace."
Some say:
"The realm is already ordered."
Your servant alone says:
"Not ordered."
I fear opposing wishes and incurring death penalty,
even so,
truly it is not peaceful,
truly it is not ordered,
thus I dare not consider my own safety,
dare I not risk death to inform you?
Those who say the realm is peaceful and ordered
are either extremely foolish and ignorant,
or certainly flatterers;
none are those who truly know the substance of order and chaos.
To place fire under a pile of kindling and sleep atop it,
the fire not yet reached burning,
and thus call it safe—
this is stealing safety;
the current situation
how does it differ from this!
Root and branch are inverted,
head and tail broken apart,
the state's systems in disarray,
without proper order—
how can it be called ordered!
Why does Your Majesty not issue one order, in the span of a few days,
to let your servant thoroughly enumerate before you,
thus presenting strategies for peace and order,
for Your Majesty to try and choose among—
what great harm is there?
Which is more urgent: the pleasure of archery and hunting, or the critical matters of safety and peril?
I have heard that
from Yǔ onward, five hundred years passed before Tāng arose;
from Tāng onward, over five hundred years passed before King Wǔ of Zhōu arose.
Thus, the emergence of sage kings
largely follows a cycle of five hundred years.
Since King Wǔ of Zhōu, more than five hundred years have passed;
is it any wonder that a sage king has not appeared?
As for Qín Shǐhuáng,
he seemed to be one but ultimately was not,
ending in disgrace.
Now, the world is gathered under Your Majesty.
I observe your magnanimity and profound wisdom,
and I privately say:
Thus, to manage disordered affairs,
grasp precarious situations,
if there is a worthy today,
sufficiently enlightened and perceptive,
and the celestial order is also aligned,
Heaven ought to invite Your Majesty to undertake it.
Yet it has not happened;
whom else must we wait for?
If governing requires toiling intellect and worry,
hardships to the body,
and lacking the joys of galloping and bell-and-drum music,
it would be better not to do it.
But the joy can be the same as now,
augmented by constant peace,
with no troubles in any direction,
as the feudal lords adhere closely and follow the Way,
devotedly loyal and trusting the sovereign.
As the sovereign does not suspect his ministers,
with no clan punishments,
no movement of weapons or armor,
the people long preserve their lives.
As virtue reaches the farthest,
the nearby Xiōngnú,
and the distant four wildernesses,
wherever human footprints can reach,
all turn toward your influence and admire your righteousness,
gladly becoming your subjects.
As the world is wealthy and abundant,
with surplus resources and wealth,
people have enough food for ten years.
As the people are inherently simple and honest,
obedient and happy to follow orders.
As official duties are very minimal,
lawsuits and theft can be made rare.
Once the great principles are attained,
the world follows orderly rule,
the atmosphere within the seas,
clear and harmonious, all well-managed,
then all living things flourish abundantly.
Yànzǐ said:
"Only by governing in accord with the spirits can one increase longevity."
Fàzǐ said:
"At the pinnacle of perfect governance,
no father buries his son,
no elder brother buries his younger brother,
no burials of infants on the roads,
each ends their life in natural order."
The method of grain consumption,
certainly ensures a full hundred years,
then Your Majesty's lifespan lightly reaches a century.
In ancient times, the Five Emperors all lived over a hundred years.
Trusting in these words,
thus the king becomes an enlightened emperor,
his ministers become enlightened aides,
the beauty of their reputation,
endures endlessly.
The "Book of Rites" says: ancestors are honored for their achievements, and patriarchs for their virtue.
Initiating the conquest of the world is an achievement;
initiating the governance of the world is virtue.
Thus, viewing the completed temple,
becoming the Great Ancestor of the world,
succeeding the Great Founder with the world,
Hàn endures eternally.
Thus, the lowly do not doubt the noble,
the humble do not surpass the esteemed,
the distinctions between noble and humble, esteemed and lowly,
clear as black and white,
then the masses under heaven are not confused or dazzled.
Thus, the principles are rooted in heaven and earth,
governance and laws rely on the four seasons,
later generations have no upheavals,
no changes to constants,
following the path to long endurance.
I privately believe that establishing a long-lasting stable situation,
fostering enduring governance,
to continue the ancestral temple,
and serve the six family relations,
is the highest filial piety;
to rule the world,
govern all living beings,
with spirits and people all content,
the state altars long enjoyed,
is the highest benevolence;
establishing classics and setting forth principles,
balancing priorities perfectly,
so that they can serve as a model for ten thousand generations,
even if later there are foolish, immature, or unworthy successors,
they can still inherit the enterprise and remain secure,
is the highest wisdom.
Longevity matching the Five Emperors,
favor extending far and wide,
what loss is there for Your Majesty?
With Your Majesty's intelligence and perception,
if those with some knowledge of governance are allowed to assist humbly,
achieving this governance is not difficult.
Why does Your Majesty not try it once,
and when the details can be plainly presented before you,
I hope you will not neglect it.
I have carefully studied heaven and earth,
verified it with ancient times,
and examined current affairs,
pondering this day and night until thoroughly familiar,
sighing alone in sorrow and indignation,
not daring to neglect it at any time.
Even if Yǔ or Shùn were reborn,
and planning for Your Majesty,
how could they change this?
There is a method to achieve it,
certainly perfectly safe and harmless.
I dare to stake my life on it;
Your Majesty, please try summoning knowledgeable ministers to deliberate on it.
If anyone can show it is inconvenient for the Son of Heaven or不利 for the world,
I request death.
"On the Harm of Feudal States"
Establishing a state must carefully assess the situation of mutual suspicion,
where the lower levels repeatedly suffer calamities,
the upper levels repeatedly face distress,
famines and disasters frequently occur,
and strange events will surely arise.
Where disaster strikes,
how can it be predicted in advance?
Thus, it is utterly unfit to secure the sovereign,
unfit to preserve the great ministers,
and utterly unfit to fully protect beloved sons.
Once they are appointed as feudal lords,
and become subordinates,
yet enriching their power,
increasing their authority,
causing them to have arrogant hearts and resist obedience,
how is it different from sharpening Mòyé swords and giving them to an archer?
Inviting disaster upon oneself is certain.
Loving them should mean letting them savor fine grains and meats,
enjoy the sounds of metal and stone instruments,
with numerous subjects and people,
vast lands,
sufficient to support and guard their persons;
yet with authority insufficient to gamble on luck,
power insufficient to commit rebellion,
thus having no arrogant heart,
no wicked deeds,
respecting laws and fearing orders,
obeying necessarily and compliantly,
living long in peace and joy,
without the disaster of mutual suspicion between high and low;
preserving the great ministers,
fully protecting beloved sons,
what is more precise than this?
Moreover, with feudal states and regulations,
their power is not solely reduced;
the rule: if one has a son, the state goes to the son,
if without a son, establish a share to await one,
once a son is born, establish him,
the person themselves being the son,
what fault can there be?
In reality, there is no loss, and the state is preserved without peril,
descendants generation after generation supporting Hàn,
all like Chángshā,
can endure long,
as they say, giving life to the dead and putting flesh on white bones,
why favor this more?
"On Strengthening Feudal States"
Tracing past events,
generally the strong rebelled first.
Huáiyīn, King of Chǔ, being the strongest,
thus rebelled first;
Hán Xìn, King of Hán, relying on the Hú,
then rebelled again;
Guàn Gāo, relying on Zhào's resources,
then rebelled again;
Chén Xī having elite and strong troops,
then rebelled again;
Péng Yuè using Liáng,
then rebelled again;
Qíng Bù using Huáinán,
then rebelled again;
Lú Wǎn's state in the north being the weakest,
thus rebelled last.
Chángshā had only twenty-five thousand households,
its strength insufficient to commit treason,
thus with little merit it remained most intact,
with weak influence it was most loyal,
when flesh and bone were preserved,
Chángshā was without incident,
not because its nature differed from others,
but its situation made it so.
Had Fán, Lì, Jiàng, Guàn been enfeoffed with several tens of cities,
even now their remnants might have perished;
had Hán Xìn, Qíng Bù, Péng Yuè and their peers been ranked as marquises and settled,
they might have survived to this day.
Then the grand strategy for the realm can be known.
To make all kings loyal and submissive,
none is better than making them like the King of Chángshā;
to prevent ministers from being minced into pickles,
none is better than making them like Fán, Lì, Jiàng, Guàn;
to ensure the realm's stability and the Son of Heaven's peace,
none is better than establishing many feudal lords and reducing their power.
With less power, they are easily guided by righteousness,
with smaller states, they harbor no wicked intentions.
If they contend with your ministers,
or consume each other like flesh and bone,
even if the realm is in danger, it is harmless,
then nothing is better than following the present course without change.
Looking at the past,
those with the largest states
rebelled first.
《The Great Capitals》
Formerly, King Líng of Chǔ asked Fàn Wúyǔ, saying:
"I wish to greatly fortify the cities of Chén, Cài, Yè, and Bùláng,
assigning a thousand chariots to each,
which should be enough to confront Jìn,
plus the strength of Chǔ itself,
will the feudal lords not come to pay homage!"
Fàn Wúyǔ said:
"It cannot be done.
I have heard that great capitals suspect the state,
great ministers suspect the ruler,
these are mediums of chaos.
Capitals suspecting leads to mutual strife,
ministers suspecting leads to competing orders,
these are profound calamities.
Now greatly fortifying Chén, Cài, Yè, and Bùláng,
if not fully manned,
is insufficient to awe Jìn;
if filled with resources,
and staffed with highly salaried ministers,
this is neglecting the root and emphasizing the branch.
I have heard, 'If the tail is too large, it cannot be wagged;
if the branch is too big, it will break.'
Does this not serve the intention to display authority over the feudal lords?
Yet what will ultimately become a great trouble for Chǔ
must be these four cities."
King Líng did not listen,
indeed fortified Chén, Cài, Yè, and Bùláng,
filled them with war chariots,
and staffed them with great ministers.
That year,
the feudal lords did come to pay homage.
After several years,
Chén, Cài, Yè, and Bùláng,
some supporting the young master Qìjí, started internal troubles,
Chǔ fell into chaos,
and the king eventually died at the well of the Taro Officer Shǒu Hài in Gànxī.
To plan in such a way,
is it not grievous!
Alas!
The root slender, the branch large,
relaxation must reach the heart.
Oh times, oh times,
what is lamentable is this.
The situation of the realm,
is like suffering from a great swelling,
a shin as large as a waist,
a finger as thick as a thigh.
I have heard, 'If the tail is too large, it cannot be wagged;
if the branch is too big, it will break.'
It is a malignant disease,
normally one cannot bend or stretch,
if one or two fingers twitch,
the body is surely distressed.
If not treated now,
it will become an incurable illness,
later even with a Biǎn Què,
nothing can be done.
Alas!
If the branches and offshoots are too large,
relaxation must reach the heart,
this is why I secretly worry for Your Majesty.
The ailment is not just swelling,
but also afflicted with twisted feet,
the son of King Yuán,
is the emperor's cousin;
the current king,
is the cousin's son.
The son of King Huì,
is the emperor's nephew;
the current king,
is the nephew's son.
Close relatives may have no fiefs to secure the realm,
distant ones may monopolize great power to oppress the Son of Heaven.
Therefore I say it is not just the ailment of swelling,
but also afflicted with twisted feet.
What can make one weep bitterly,
is this very ailment.
《Equalizing Uniformity》
The palace guards of the feudal lords,
weaving shoes and squatting like barbarians,
are governed by the laws of the emperor's residing palace;
the court attendants and receptionists receiving petitions and handling reports,
are granted authority according to the methods for serving the emperor;
if they serve the feudal lords with dishonesty or lack of impartiality,
they are punished under the laws for serving the emperor.
It is said that the use of Hàn laws uniformly
means serving the feudal lords is akin to serving the emperor,
thus elevating the feudal lords to equal the supreme.
Then, between the Son of Heaven and the feudal lords,
and between ministers and subordinates,
should the distinction be so blurred and equal?
The chancellor of the Son of Heaven,
titled as chéngxiàng,
bears a gold seal;
the chancellor of a feudal lord,
also titled as chéngxiàng,
bears a gold seal,
with no difference in honor,
and a rank above two thousand dàn.
The high ministers of the Son of Heaven hold a rank of two thousand dàn,
while those of the feudal lords also hold two thousand dàn,
making the ministers identical.
The ruler elevates ministers to honor them,
but if ministers are already equal,
how can the laws not be uniform?
The guard and charioteer of the Son of Heaven,
titled as tàipú,
holds a silver seal and a rank of two thousand dàn;
the charioteer of a feudal lord,
also titled as tàipú,
holds a silver seal and a rank of two thousand dàn;
thus the charioteers are equal.
If the charioteers are equal,
how can the chariot decorations not be uniform?
The mother of the Son of Heaven,
is titled Tàihòu;
the mother of a feudal lord,
is also titled Tàihòu;
the consort of the Son of Heaven,
is titled Hòu;
the consort of a feudal lord,
is also titled Hòu.
Then, what do the feudal lords lack, and what does the Son of Heaven gain?
If the wives are already the same,
how can the husbands differ?
The palace gate of the Son of Heaven is called Sīmǎ,
and unauthorized entry is punished as chéngdàn;
the palace gate of a feudal lord is also called Sīmǎ,
and unauthorized entry is punished as chéngdàn;
the hall gates are both called diànmén,
and the crime of unauthorized entry is also punishable by public execution.
The palace wall gates and guards share the same names,
their strictness is of the same level,
and the crimes are already equal.
The decrees of the Son of Heaven are called lìng,
such as Lìng Jiǎ and Lìng Yǐ;
the decrees of feudal lords are also called lìng,
such as Lìng Yí and Lìng Yán.
The humble address for the Son of Heaven is Bìxià,
and for feudal lords, it is also Bìxià;
the carriage of the Son of Heaven is called shèngyú,
and that of feudal lords is also called shèngyú,
making the carriages equal.
Clothing and textiles, in order and quality, are woven with warp and weft;
if craftsmanship is skillful and desires arise,
they only encroach upon superiors and surpass rulers in rank.
Then, where does the so-called ruler reside,
and where do the ministers stand?
Human nature does not differ in face and eyes,
appearances are of the same kind;
the distinction between noble and base
is not rooted in heaven and manifested in form.
What is used to distinguish noble from base and clarify honor and humility
are rank, power, clothing, and decrees.
If chaos persists unceasingly,
disorderly and without order,
while innate nature is the same,
human affairs lack distinction.
Then, the so-called ministers and rulers
have no means of oversight or principles of honor and humility;
they are only differentiated by facial features.
One must be familiar with their appearances
to recognize them,
then those distant have no model to follow,
the masses have nothing to expect,
so how can subordinates not doubt their superiors?
If ruler and minister share the same ethics,
and different ranks wear the same attire,
how can the superior not be confused by subordinates?
Confucius said:
"Those who lead the people should not vary in clothing,
maintain consistency in demeanor,
to unify the people,
then the virtue of the people will be one."
The Book of Songs says:
"Those metropolitan gentlemen,
in fox-fur robes and yellow skirts,
return to Zhōu,
are the hope of the myriad people."
Confucius said:
"The superior should be recognizable at a glance,
the subordinate should be categorizable and identifiable;
then the ruler will not doubt his ministers,
and ministers will not be confused about their ruler.
But if this is not practiced,
with boundaries blurred and no limits,
this is indeed something to deeply sigh over."
"Doubt in Attire"
Doubt in clothing leads to contention for precedence;
doubt in generous favors leads to contention for rewards;
doubt in power leads to contention for strength;
unlimited ranks lead to contention for honor.
Those people, when close, hope for favor;
when in doubt, they form factions and contend.
Therefore, if ranks are clearly defined,
subordinates will not have doubts;
if power is supremely unique,
ministers will have no ambitious desires.
Thus, the Son of Heaven, regarding his subordinates,
adds five ranks or more
to designate them as ministers;
ministers, regarding their subordinates,
add five ranks or more
to designate them as servants;
servants also observe the rites of ministers.

Yet they call themselves servants and dare not call themselves ministers, to honor the Son of Heaven and avoid suspicion. The way of regulating attire is to give the most suitable and harmonious to the people,
and offer the most beautiful and divine to the emperor.
Unique garments and patterns
are used to rank superiors and inferiors and differentiate noble from base.
Thus, if status differs,
then titles differ,
then power differs,
then circumstances differ,
then banners and insignia differ,
then auspicious signs differ,
then ritual honors differ,
then ranks and stipends differ,
then hats and shoes differ,
then clothing and sashes differ,
then rings and pendants differ,
then carriages and horses differ,
then wives and concubines differ,
then generous favors differ,
then palaces and rooms differ,
then beds and mats differ,
then utensils differ,
then food and drink differ,
then sacrifices differ,
then death and mourning differ.
Thus, the high have all these items elevated,
the low have all these items lowered;
those above others use these items to oversee,
those below others use these items to serve;
promotion advances these items,
demotion reduces these items;
the noble have abundance throughout,
the base have humility throughout;
noble and base have grades,
attire and position have levels;
once levels are established,
each stays within their bounds,
people follow their measures;
unauthorized demotion leads to reprimand,
usurpation of superiors leads to punishment;
laws are established to practice this,
officials are appointed to govern this.
Thus, the world sees their attire and knows noble from base,
observes their insignia and knows their power;
it settles people's minds,
fixes their gaze clearly;
thus, even with many, the world is not confused,
and even from afar, the world recognizes reverence.
Are humility and honor already clear?
Are superior and inferior already distinguished?
Then human relations are ordered.
Thus, between ruler and ministers,
it is like the sun and the stars;
ministers cannot nearly doubt the ruler,
the base cannot encroach upon the noble;
if subordinates do not trespass ranks, the superior's position is honored;
if ministers do not overstep levels, the ruler's position is secure;
strictly upholding order prevents chaos from arising.
"Increasing Territories"
If Your Majesty does not establish a governance that ensures security for a thousand generations,
and considers the current situation,
how could it last beyond one succession?
The feudal lords are already acting wantonly without restraint;
as for their interactions,
they merely form alliances through horizontal and vertical pacts to draw close.
The laws and decrees of Hàn cannot be enforced,
yet they still stand tall and submit to the strong.
Now, compared to the major feudal lords, Huáiyáng
is like a small mole on the face—
how could it suffice to defend against Chǔ?
And what Your Majesty relies on as a protective barrier
is merely Dài and Huáiyáng.
Dài borders the powerful Xiōngnú to the north,
as is evident;
the Crown Prince also relies solely on these two states.
What Huáiyáng possesses now
is just enough to bait the large states.
Currently, control lies with Your Majesty;
governing the state and appointing your sons
merely serves as bait for the large states—
how can this be called skillful?
The actions of a ruler differ from those of commoners.
Commoners
adorn minor virtues,
compete in small acts of integrity,
to establish themselves in their villages and communities;
a ruler, however,
ensures the stability of the realm and the firmness of the altars of state.
Thus, Huángdì
was the elder brother of Yándì.
When Yándì acted without virtue,
Huángdì attacked him in the wilderness of Zhuōlù,
where blood flowed enough to float pestles,
executed Yándì, and annexed his territory,
and only then did the realm achieve order.
Emperor Gāo divided the realm to enfeoff his meritorious officials as kings.
Rebels arose like the bristles of a hedgehog;
Emperor Gāo deemed this unacceptable,
so he eliminated the unrighteous feudal lords and emptied their states.
Choosing an auspicious day,
he established his sons outside the Shàngdōng Gate of Luòyáng,
and once all his sons were enfeoffed as kings,
the realm was then secured.
Therefore, great men
are not enticed by minor integrity,
nor constrained by small deeds;
thus, they establish great convenience to achieve grand accomplishments.
Now, some distant territories in Huáinán span several thousand lǐ,
crossing two feudal states to be administered as counties under Hàn.
The officials and people who travel to Cháng'ān for corvée labor
exhaust themselves to make up for it;
their clothes wear out midway,
and their expenses for money and other needs correspond to this.
The hardship of being under Hàn’s rule and desiring a king,
their suffering is extreme;
those who wish to have a settled end are akin to having a good intention,
and those who flee to the feudal lords along the way are likely not few.
This is ultimately not a sustainable way to govern the land.
Why does Your Majesty not expedite the situation,
and have others guard the commanderies—
how could that compare to appointing your sons?
In my humble plan,
I wish Your Majesty would allocate the lands of Huáinán to augment Huáiyáng;
if Liáng later faces troubles,
cede two or three border cities from Huáiyáng’s north to Dōngjùn,
to strengthen Liáng;
if there are no future troubles,
Dài could be moved and its capital established at Suīyáng.
With Liáng extending from Xīnxī northward to the river,
and Huáiyáng encompassing Chén southward to the river,
then any major feudal lords with rebellious intentions
will be too terrified to plot.
What we rely on now
are only the two states of Dài and Huáiyáng,
and the Crown Prince also depends on them.
According to my plan,
Liáng would be sufficient to defend against Qí and Zhào,
and Huáiyáng enough to restrain Wú and Chǔ;
then Your Majesty could rest on your pillow with ease,
free from worries east of the mountains.
I privately believe this benefits two generations.
If Huáinán remains long administered under Hàn,
it will only empower treacherous individuals.
I implore Your Majesty to give this slight consideration.
Reflect.
I risk death to present this.
I, Yì, dare to risk death, wishing to prostrate and elaborate on the measures;
the strategies I, Yì, propose for governance and security—
if Your Majesty would grant a brief moment
to listen and test them in practice,
there would be no harm or detriment.
A dim ruler seeks wisdom,
consulting his ministers without initiating matters himself;
thus, a minister can fully express his loyal folly.
I beseech Your Majesty to consider and favor this.
Now, Your Majesty grants accumulated wealth to unexpected individuals;
if this does not lead to revenge like Zǐxū or Báigōng in broad daylight,
then one might suspect a resurgence of Jīng Kē rising between pillars—
how is such a strategy safe or expedient?
This is what is called lending weapons to a brigand and wings to a tiger;
I beg Your Majesty to give slight thought and deliberate on it.
《On Power and Weight》
When feudal lords have power enough to act autonomously,
and strength enough to commit treason,
even if they wear a maiden’s cap,
do not say they dare not.
If their power is insufficient for autonomy,
and strength inadequate for treason,
even if a Xià Yù is alive,
with enmity and grudges,
it still causes no harm.
Yet the reason the realm is tranquil today
is merely because the feudal lords are all still young;
in a few years hence,
when they all come of age,
Your Majesty will witness it.
Will it not be bitter?
To have the power to act and not do so,
hoarding chaos and nurturing calamity,
sitting high with folded hands yet worrying—
the disorder will grow severe and rampant,
which can be called neither wise nor benevolent.
Now, Qín, acting against its own interests,
pondered day and night,
toiling with heart and strength,
in peril of survival,
to eliminate the threat of the six states;
yet now Your Majesty, with power to control the realm,
commanding with a nod as you wish,
still speaks of the calamity of the six states—
it is hard to call this wise.
If one remains constantly inattentive,
only inviting disaster,
without control over the situation,
as the seeds of chaos grow daily,
gazing upon it without settling it—
after ten thousand years,
passing it to an aged mother and a weak son,
so that even Cáo and Bó cannot control it—
can this be called benevolent?
《The Five Excellences》
The situation within the realm is like the body commanding the arms,
and the arms commanding the fingers,
all submitting without exception.
The rulers of the feudal states,
dare to take their own lives but dare not harbor rebellious intentions,
knowing they would surely be minced into pickled meat.
They dare not have disloyal hearts,
but converge and advance together to submit to the Son of Heaven.
Under Heaven, there is no power that can rely on luck,
no deeds that stir up calamity and summon chaos.
Even among the common people,
they all know peace,
so all under Heaven recognize Your Majesty's brilliance.
Divide the land and establish the system,
making Qí into several states,
Zhào and Chǔ into several states.
The regulations being thus properly arranged,
then the descendants of Qí Dàohuì Wáng,
have their princely fiefs fully and correctly allocated.
The descendants of Zhào Yōu Wáng and Chǔ Yuán Wáng,
also each in order receive their ancestors' allotted lands.
Yān, Wú, Huáinán, and other states are all treated likewise.
For those with extensive lands but few descendants,
establish them as states,
leave them vacant and set aside,
waiting for their descendants to be born,
then appoint them to rule.
Lands of the feudal lords that were significantly reduced and incorporated into Hàn,
by moving their marquisates or enfeoffing their descendants there,
are thus compensated in full.
Hence, not an inch of land,
nor a single person,
does the Son of Heaven profit from,
truly aiming only to secure governance.
Thus all under Heaven recognize Your Majesty's integrity.
Once the land system is fixed,
no imperial clansman worries about not becoming a king.
After the system is established,
those below have no rebellious hearts,
those above have no punitive intentions.
Superiors and subordinates are joyful and close,
feudal lords submit and adhere,
so all under Heaven recognize Your Majesty's benevolence.
Once the land system is fixed,
then the imperial way is restored to clarity and ministers' hearts to rectitude.
Laws are established but not violated,
commands are issued but not opposed.
Plots like Guàn Gāo and Lì Jī do not arise,
schemes like Jī Qí and Qǐ Zhāng do not sprout.
Common folk incline toward goodness,
great ministers offer obedience,
all achieved by the ruler's actions.
Thus all under Heaven recognize Your Majesty's righteousness.
Once the land system is fixed,
even placing an infant atop the realm brings stability.
Setting up a posthumous heir,
facing court in ceremonial robes,
yet the realm does not fall into chaos.
The state remains long at peace,
the ancestral temple long honored,
handed down to later generations,
with no end in sight.
Thus, great order prevailed at the time,
and later ages praise the sagehood.
One move brings five virtues,
so why does Your Majesty hesitate and long refrain from achieving these five virtues?
《System Not Fixed》
Yán Dì
was the brother of Huáng Dì sharing the same parents,
each holding half of the realm.
Huáng Dì practiced the Way, but Yán Dì would not listen,
so they battled in the wilderness of Zhuōlù,
until blood flowed enough to float pestles.
Without a proper land system,
even Huáng Dì faced hardships.
With Gāo Huángdì's brilliance, sagacity, might, and martial prowess,
after pacifying the realm,
and ascending the Son of Heaven's throne,
yet ministers rebelled nearly a dozen times.
With the emperor's power, he toiled personally in the midst of troops,
repeatedly in turmoil, almost losing the realm several times.
Huáiyīn Hóu, Hán Wáng Xìn, Chén Xī, Péng Yuè, Qíng Bù, and Lú Wǎn,
all were meritorious officials,
once beloved and trusted.
The beloved turned into enemies,
the trusted became rebels.
Is it not strange?
Had the land system been established early,
would such changes have occurred?
Since Your Majesty's accession,
Jìběi rebelled once,
Huáinán committed treason,
now Wú is reported,
all being minor instances.
The greater feudal lords remain calm without cause,
not because the realm has a method of solid security,
but merely relying on their youth and the limited circumstances.
Moreover, those of different surnames who relied on strength to act,
Hàn was fortunate to defeat them,
yet did not change the causes.
Those of the same surname follow in their footsteps,
flesh and blood turning against each other,
already showing signs,
the situation is bound to repeat.
The return of calamity,
none know where it will shift.
Continuing like this, where will it end?
Even a wise emperor could not secure peace,
how much less later generations!
Butcher Tán could dismember twelve oxen in one morning,
with his sharp blade unblunted,
because where he pushed and struck,
where he cut and carved,
all followed the natural lines.
But when it came to the hip and thigh bones,
he used either a hatchet or an axe.
Benevolence, righteousness, kindness, and generosity,
these are the ruler's sharp blade;
authority, power, laws, and institutions,
these are the ruler's hatchet and axe.
When the situation is settled,
and power is sufficient,
then apply benevolence, righteousness, kindness, and generosity to moisten it,
so virtue spreads and the realm admires.
Now the feudal kings are all like hip and thigh bones.
To set aside the control of hatchet and axe,
and try to handle them with a sharp blade,
I fear the blade will either break or chip.
Why not use it on Huáinán and Jìběi?
The situation made it impossible.
《Examining Subtleties》
Good cannot be called small and without benefit,
evil cannot be called small and without harm.
Not that a small good alone can benefit the realm,
nor a small evil alone can disrupt the state.
But if one takes beginnings lightly and scorns subtleties,
the course will surely lead to great chaos.
Therefore, those who govern the people must be cautious.
A person,
upon climbing high will gaze afar,
facing depth will peer down.
It's not human nature to peer and gaze,
but the situation compels it.
Affairs may pursue wickedness,
circumstances may summon disaster.
Lǎo Dān said:
"Act before it exists,
govern before it is chaotic."
Guǎn Zhòng said:
"Prepare against calamity before it takes form,
that is the best."
A saying goes: "A tiny spark unquenched,
how to deal with the raging fire?
If the sprout is not cut,
it will break the axe handle."
To wisely prevent at the subtle stage,
is the next best.
Affairs heading toward chaos,
are like terrain that misleads people.
Gradually proceeding along,
suddenly east and west switch directions,
without one's awareness.
Hence, Mòzǐ wept at the crossroads,
grieving that one wrong step leads a thousand miles astray.
Formerly, the Marquis of Wèi came to pay court to Zhōu.
The Zhōu official asked his name,
and he replied:
"Wèi Hóu Pìjiāng."
The Zhōu official sent him back,
saying:
"To open territory and expand borders,
is the prerogative of the Son of Heaven;
feudal lords may not use it!"
The Marquis of Wèi changed his name to 𤎶,
and only then was he received.
Thus, those skilled in maintaining the hierarchy between superior and subordinate,
do not allow even empty names to overstep.
In ancient times according to the Zhōu rituals,
the Son of Heaven was buried with a sloping passage,
while feudal lords were lowered directly.
When King Xiāng of Zhōu fled from Bó Dòu,
Duke Wén of Jìn led troops to eliminate the rebels,
quelled the turmoil in the Zhōu kingdom,
and restored King Xiāng to his throne.
Thereupon, King Xiāng offered him the lands of Nányáng as reward,
but Duke Wén declined Nányáng,
requesting instead the privilege of a sloping passage upon his death.
King Xiāng would not consent,
saying:
"Though the Zhōu kingdom is diminished,
none have replaced it.
If the Son of Heaven uses the sloping passage,
and you, my uncle, also use it,
that would mean two Sons of Heaven.
If you consider the land insufficient,
I beg to increase it."
Duke Wén then withdrew.
According to ritual, the Son of Heaven's music had bells hung on all four walls,
feudal lords had them on three walls,
high ministers had them on one wall,
and scholars had only lutes and zithers.
Shūsūn Yúxī was a high minister of Wèi,
the three-walled bell arrangement was the musical system of the ruler of Wèi,
and the ornate trappings adorned the ruler's carriage.
When the Qí people attacked Wèi,
Shūsūn Yúxī led troops to confront them,
decisively defeating the Qí army.
Wèi then rewarded him with Wēn,
but Shūsūn Yúxī declined Wēn,
instead requesting the three-walled bells and ornate trappings for his court appearances.
The ruler of Wèi granted this.
When Confucius heard of it, he said:
"What a pity!
It would have been better to give him more cities.
For music carries the state,
and the state carries the ruler.
When that music is lost, ritual follows,
when ritual is lost, governance follows,
when governance is lost, the state follows,
when the state is lost, the ruler follows.
What a pity!
It would have been better to give him more cities."
When Mìzǐ governed Dǎnfù,
the Qí people attacked Lǔ,
passing through Dǎnfù.
Initially,
the elders requested:
"The wheat is ripe,
and now with the Qí invaders pressing,
if the people go out to harvest near the outer walls and return,
it can increase our food supply,
and not benefit the invaders."
After three requests,
Mìzǐ did not heed them.
Soon, all the wheat was taken by the Qí invaders.
When Jìsūn heard of this,
he was angered,
sending someone to reproach Mìzǐ:
"Is it not lamentable!
The people!
Toiling in cold and heat,
yet unable to eat what they've grown.
Not knowing would be one thing,
but having heard and reported it,
yet you, Master, did not listen."
Mìzǐ responded gravely:
"If there's no wheat this year,
we can plant it next year.
But allowing those who don't farm to reap
encourages welcoming invaders.
Moreover, one year's wheat
does not strengthen Lǔ if kept,
nor weaken it if lost.
But allowing the people thoughts of taking for themselves
will cause wounds that won't heal for years."
When Jìsūn heard this,
he felt ashamed,
saying:
"If a hole were to crawl into,
how could I bear to face Mìzǐ!"
Thus, the perceptive detect treachery early,
and eliminate rebellious plots from afar,
so evil does not advance.
《On Hierarchy》
The ruler's dignity is like a hall's difference from steps:
with nine levels of steps,
the hall is elevated about six feet;
if the hall had no steps,
its height would barely exceed a foot.
The Son of Heaven is like the hall,
ministers like the steps,
the masses like the ground—
such is the analogy.
Thus, with nine-step stairs,
the edge far from the ground,
the hall is high;
with no steps,
the edge near the ground,
the hall is low.
The high is hard to climb,
the low easily overrun—
such is natural order.
Therefore, ancient sage kings established ranks:
within, dukes, ministers, high officials, and scholars;
without, dukes, marquises, earls, viscounts, and barons;
then officials, minor functionaries,
extending to commoners.
With clear hierarchy,
the Son of Heaven towers above,
so his dignity is unattainable.
A proverb says:
"Wanting to throw at a rat but fearing the vase."
This is a good metaphor.
The rat near the vase
makes one hesitate to throw,
fearing to damage the vase—
how much more so for high ministers close to the sovereign!
Propriety, shame, and ritual govern gentlemen,
hence they may be ordered to die but not humiliated.
Thus, binding, flogging, shaving, amputating, tattooing, and nose-cutting punishments do not reach scholar-officials,
as they are not far from the ruler.
By ritual, one dare not count the teeth of the ruler's carriage horses;
kicking their fodder is a crime;
seeing the ruler's stool or staff, one rises;
encountering the ruler's carriage, one descends;
entering the main gate, one hastens.
Even if the ruler's favored ministers err,
corporal punishment is not inflicted on them—
this honors the ruler's majesty.
This is how the ruler prevents disrespect from afar,
and how he treats ministers with dignity to strengthen their integrity.
Now, the esteemed among kings, marquises, and the three highest ranks,
all whom the Son of Heaven treats with altered countenance and ritual respect,
whom ancient Son of Heaven called uncles or maternal uncles,
are subjected to the same tattooing, nose-cutting, shaving, amputating, flogging, humiliation, and public execution as commoners and slaves—
then is it not as if the hall has lost its steps?
Are the humiliated not too pressured?
When integrity and shame are not practiced,
might not high ministers holding heavy authority, great officers, harbor the shameless hearts of slaves?
The incident at Wàngyí,
where the Second Emperor was condemned under severe law,
exemplifies throwing at a rat without fearing the vase.
I have heard it said,
shoes, though new, are not placed on a pillow;
a hat, though worn, is not used to pad shoes.
Those who once held honored, favored positions,
whom the Son of Heaven treated with altered countenance and dignity,
whom officials and people bowed to in awe—
if they now err,
dismissing them is acceptable,
demoting them is acceptable,
ordering their death is acceptable,
executing them is acceptable;
but binding them,
tying them up,
sending them to the Minister of Works,
enrolling them among convict laborers,
under jailers and wardens,
overseers and petty officers,
cursing and flogging them—
this is hardly fit for the masses to see.
For the lowly to become accustomed to seeing the high treated so,
thinking "someday I too can do this to them,"
is not the way to accustom the world,
nor the transformation that honors the honorable.
Those whom the Son of Heaven once respected,
whom the masses once revered,
should die if they must die,
but how should base people be allowed to thus abuse and humiliate them!
Yù Ràng served the lord of Zhōngháng,
but when Zhì Bó attacked and destroyed Zhōngháng,
Yù Ràng transferred his service to Zhì Bó.
After Zhào annihilated Zhì Bó,
Yù Ràng disfigured his face and altered his appearance,
swallowed charcoal to change his voice,
determined to take revenge on Xiāngzǐ,
yet five attempts all missed their mark.
Xiāngzǐ changed his sleeping place five times in one night.
When people questioned Yù Ràng,
he replied:
"Zhōngháng treated me as one of the crowd,
so I served him as one of the crowd;
Zhì Bó treated me as a scholar of the state,
so I repay him as a scholar of the state."
Thus, this same Yù Ràng,
who turned against his lord to serve his enemy,
acting like a dog or pig,
later reformed himself to show utmost loyalty,
behaving like a heroic martyr—
this was shaped by his rulers.
Therefore, if a ruler treats his ministers like dogs or horses,
they will act like dogs or horses;
if treated like convict laborers,
they will behave as such.
Stubborn and shameless,
vile and without restraint,
lacking integrity and shame,
they will not self-respect,
but settle for whatever suffices,
so they flee at the sight of profit,
and seize at the sight of advantage.
If the ruler fails,
they will push him down;
if the ruler faces calamity,
they will merely seek to save themselves,
standing by to watch;
if something benefits them personally,
they will deceive and betray for gain.
What advantage does the ruler gain from this?
The subordinates are many,
while the ruler is but one;
the wealth, tools, and duties entrusted are mostly with the subordinates.
If they are shameless,
and only seek temporary safety,
then the ruler suffers most.
Thus, in ancient times, rites did not extend to commoners,
punishments did not reach gentlemen,
to encourage integrity among favored ministers.
When ancient ministers were dismissed for lack of integrity,
it was not called lack of integrity,
but "improper adornment of ritual vessels";
if dismissed for promiscuity with aunts, sisters, or mothers, without distinction between men and women,
it was not called promiscuity,
but "neglect of curtain maintenance";
if dismissed for weakness and incompetence,
it was not called weakness,
but "failure in official duties."
Thus, even when high ministers were clearly guilty,
they were not bluntly accused,
but were given委婉 treatment with euphemisms.
Those facing major reprimand or inquiry
would, upon hearing it, don a white hat with yak-tail tassels,
carry a tray of water with a sword on it,
go to the petition room to confess their crimes,
without the ruler having them bound and dragged.
Those with moderate offenses
would, upon command, discipline themselves,
without the ruler sending others to shackle and punish them.
Those with grave crimes
would, upon order, bow twice facing north,
kneel, and take their own lives,
without the ruler having them seized and executed,
saying:
"You, great officer, have erred yourself!
I have treated you with courtesy."
Treated with courtesy,
the ministers thus take pride in themselves;
encouraged with integrity and shame,
they strive for moral conduct.
If the ruler applies integrity, shame, rites, and righteousness to treat his ministers,
and they do not repay him with moral conduct,
then they are not human.
Thus, when transformation is complete and customs settled,
as ministers, they forget themselves for their lord's shame,
forget their families for the state's shame,
forget personal interests for public shame,
not hastily pursuing profit,
not hastily avoiding harm,
but only following righteousness.
Under the ruler's influence,
ministers related by blood sincerely die for the ancestral temple,
legal ministers sincerely die for the state,
assisting ministers sincerely die for the ruler,
defensive ministers sincerely die for the city walls and borders.
Thus, it is said that sages have a "metal wall,"
meaning this very principle.
If they are willing to die for me,
then I can live with them;
if they are willing to perish for me,
then I can exist with them;
if they are willing to face danger for me,
then I can be safe with them.
They consider conduct and forget profit,
uphold integrity and abide by righteousness,
thus they can be entrusted with unrestricted power,
or the care of a young orphan.
This results from encouraging integrity and shame, and practicing rites and righteousness—
what has the ruler lost?
Not doing this,
but persisting in the old ways,
is why it is said this is something to deeply sigh over.
"The Prevailing Apathy"
The current trend among high officials
is to treat unanswered documents,
or minor unmet deadlines,
as major issues.
Considering these major issues is wrong,
for the greater direction of the world,
if agitated,
leads to eroding customs,
and societal decay.
Yet, they remain complacent and unalarmed,
which is the true major issue.
With clerks and scribes
focused only on paperwork in boxes,
ignorant of the greater principles,
and Your Majesty not concerned personally,
this is how it has come to be!
As corrupt customs grow daily,
people habitually indulge without integrity or shame,
and righteous conduct is not followed.
How can a son not betray his father,
or a minister remain loyal to his lord?
How can a younger brother not deceive his elder,
or a subordinate trust his superior?
Even if Your Majesty holds authority and undertakings,
on whom can they be entrusted?
Guǎnzǐ said:
"The four bonds,
first are rites,
second righteousness,
third integrity,
fourth shame.
If the four bonds are not upheld,
the state will perish."
If Guǎnzǐ were a foolish, ignorant man, it would be excusable,
but if he had some understanding of governance,
then how can this not be chilling?
Nowadays, extravagance and luxury compete,
with no system from above,
discarding rites and righteousness,
abandoning integrity and shame,
worsening daily,
changing monthly and yearly.
Pursuing profit without regard,
considering thoughts but not conduct,
now the extreme cases include killing grandfathers,
harming grandmothers,
assaulting elderly women, stabbing brothers;
thieves plot to steal gold under pillars,
cut curtains at bedroom doors,
seize vessels from ancestral temples,
and in broad daylight in large cities, rob officials and take their gold.
Fraudsters embezzle hundreds of thousands of dan of grain,
extort over six million coins,
travel through provinces and feudal states with official passes—
these are the worst cases of decadence without righteous conduct.
Others recklessly follow,
driven like pigs and sheep,
is this not what Guǎnzǐ meant by the four bonds not being upheld?
I secretly lament this for Your Majesty;
in my opinion,
officials do not stir their senses,
thinking it all natural.
To change prevailing winds and customs,
making the world shift hearts toward the Way,
is not something ordinary officials can achieve.
If Your Majesty does not personally concern yourself,
I secretly lament for Your Majesty.
The establishment of sovereign and subject relationships,
the stratification of superior and inferior,
causing fathers and sons to possess ritual propriety,
and the six kinship relations to have order—
these are not acts of Heaven,
but institutions created by humans.
What humans have instituted,
if not practiced will not stand,
if not upheld will collapse,
if not maintained will decay.
The Qin abolished the four ethical pillars without extending them,
hence sovereign and subject became estranged and contended with each other,
superiors and inferiors fell into chaos without distinction between noble and base,
fathers, sons, and the six kinship relations suffered calamity and lost their proper order,
treacherous individuals rose together,
the myriad people turned rebellious,
lasting only thirteen years,
until the altars of state became ruins.
Now the four ethical pillars remain incomplete,
hence treacherous men harbor hopes of fortune,
and the masses below are filled with doubt.
How could this compare to establishing constant regulations now,
making sovereigns truly sovereigns and ministers truly ministers,
superiors and inferiors clearly distinguished,
fathers, sons, and the six kinship relations each finding their proper place,
treacherous men having no hopes of fortune,
and the multitude trusting their superiors without doubt?
Once this foundation is settled,
generations will enjoy enduring peace,
and thereafter have something to uphold and follow.
If constant regulations remain unsettled,
it is like crossing rivers without ropes or oars,
encountering wind and waves midstream—
the boat is certain to capsize.
How lamentable!
To not prepare in advance,
can we fail to examine this?
"On Changing Times"
The state of Qín lost its principles,
and the world fell into great ruin;
the many oppressed the few,
the clever deceived the foolish,
the brave coerced the timid,
the strong bullied the weak,
those who achieved through aggression were esteemed as worthy and noble,
those skilled in assault and theft joyfully became feudal lords,
those who devised flattery and mutual obstruction
and engaged in elaborate deception while appearing connected were considered wise—
the world had descended into utter chaos.
Therefore, a great worthy arose,
his might shaking the four seas,
his virtue uniting the world.
Those who once served Qín
now turned to serve Hàn.
What is the present situation?
The era for aggressive advancement has passed,
the momentum for annexation is over,
why still practice filial piety, fraternal duty, obedience, and conformity?
Just be skilled in writing to become an official!
Why practice righteousness, ritual, and moral restraint?
Just be wealthy at home and secure an official position!
The arrogant and shameless improperly become sacrificial elders,
the tattooed and noseless brandish their arms as sacrificial administrators,
behaving like dogs and swine.
If a family is rich and resources ample,
one may lean on a desk, gaze arrogantly, and become the Son of Heaven!
Only accuse one's brothers of crimes,
cheat and assault uncles,
defy one's parents!
Yet with abundant wealth and money,
and fine clothing in order,
why should I hesitate to become the world's foundation lord?
Only cherish the young aunts and fathers-in-law's connecting daughters?
With imposing carriages and horses,
and excellent hunting dogs,
falsify and deceive to beautify the household,
steal and rob to amass wealth—
what harm is there?
If wishing to socialize,
I select the noble and favored to befriend;
if desiring influence,
choose officials with power to employ;
in taking a wife or marrying a daughter,
unless they possess power and influence,
I will not form marriage alliances;
unless noble and with connections,
I will not treat as brothers;
unless rich and from great families,
I will not associate with—
for what reason?
Current customs are extravagant and wasteful,
using outward display to boast,
surpassing peers and exceeding ranks,
competing through wealth beyond one's station.
The present age values empty titles and despises the virtuous,
customs are decadent and honor the treacherous,
the rich who avoid treachery become poor,
and are vilified in the village;
honest officials resign and return home,
laughed at in the town;
those in office who dare practice deceit and grow rich
are considered worthy officials;
commoners who violate laws for profit
are deemed talented men.
Thus elder brothers exhort their younger brothers,
fathers exhort their sons,
and the depravity of customs has reached this point.
Lord Shāng abandoned ritual and righteousness,
discarded moral principles,
and focused wholeheartedly on aggressive advancement.
After practicing this for two years,
Qín's customs daily deteriorated.
Among the Qín people, when a son
from a wealthy family came of age, he would separate and divide the household;
if from a poor family, he would marry uxorilocally.
A borrowed father might wield hoe, plow, or bamboo broom—
yet expect a grateful demeanor!
If a mother took a gourd bowl, winnowing basket, or broom,
she would face immediate reproach;
while nursing her child in arms,
she would sit sprawled alongside her father-in-law;
if mother-in-law and daughter-in-law were displeased with each other,
they would curl their lips and glare.
Such indulgence of children and craving for profit
made them disregard and neglect their parents.
Reflecting on these faults reveals an absence of ethical principles,
differing from beasts only slightly!
Yet they still focused their hearts and seized the times,
saying achievement required abandoning righteousness!
They overthrew the six states,
and unified the world.
Achievement was complete and gains obtained!
Yet ultimately they failed to return to the integrity of shame,
and the substance of humaneness and righteousness.
Trusting in methods of annexation,
they pursued enterprises of aggression,
until after merely thirteen years the altars of state became ruins,
never understanding the methods of preserving achievements,
or the arts of maintaining gains.
How lamentable!
The emperor nourished scholars for advancement while discarding ritual.
"On the Magnificent and Extraordinary"
There exists a bizarre governance in the world where,
granting provisions to the people only makes them poorer,
clothing the people only makes them colder,
bringing joy to the people only makes them more miserable,
enlightening the people only makes them less able to avoid the law's net,
truly a marvel indeed.
Now there is an extraordinary method here:
taking from the people actually enriches them,
not clothing them makes them warmer,
causing them hardship makes them happier,
making them more ignorant makes them less likely to fall into the law's net.
Would Your Majesty not consider listening briefly to its principles?
For the carving of patterns and engraving of designs,
the variety of utensils in daily use multiplies,
delicate but poorly made vessels,
emerge daily with constant changes,
the people abandon sturdy and durable goods for intricately carved and delicate ones,
competing to outdo each other in elegance,
items that should take one day to make,
now cannot be completed easily in ten days,
items meant to last a year,
now wear out in half a year,
their production wastes time and multiplies labor,
their use leads to quick deterioration,
thus many eat the farmers' food without farming themselves,
this is why the world suffers poverty and insufficiency.
Hence, giving people trivial goods,
makes them extremely poor;
giving people fundamental resources,
makes them greatly wealthy.
Elaborate embroidery and ornate weaving harm women's work,
moreover, a hundred people laboring,
cannot clothe one person,
even mobilizing the entire world's strength cannot easily supply all,
how can this not lead to cold?
The worldly custom of extravagance encourages mutual display,
people admire what they cannot match,
driven by social pressure,
they crave what they have not attained,
competing to outdo each other,
while those above lack regulatory systems.
Now even convicts, concubines, and lowly persons,
wear clothing surpassing that of nobles,
imitating the Son of Heaven,
this allows the world to openly presume upon their superiors,
and everyone pursues extravagance.
Presuming upon superiors and pursuing extravagance,
then the world grows cold and clothing becomes insufficient.
Thus, clothing the people with ornate embroidery,
makes them colder,
whereas stripping them of such,
will surely make them warm with abundant cloth and silk.
Those engaged in clever crafts, petty skills, trade, and idle living,
are physically at leisure but mentally anxious about crimes,
their ambitions fixated on gain and their conduct indulgent and wasteful,
then resources become insufficient and savings dwindle.
If they encounter severe drought,
they will inevitably face dire poverty and personal hardship,
and suffer extreme hunger!
Now if the people are driven back to farming,
all rooted in fundamental production,
then everyone in the world will live by their labor,
those engaged in petty skills and idle living will turn to farming the fields,
then the people will settle into their nature and be encouraged in their work,
without anxiety about crimes,
without ambitions for undeserved gain,
practicing respect, frugality, and savings,
and they will find joy in their place,
hence it is said: causing hardship to the people makes them happier.
The world is steeped in extravagance,
those who adorn themselves with cleverness to deceive for profit are considered wise,
those who dare violate laws and commit great evils are seen as understanding principles,
thus wicked people thrive and multiply daily,
deceit and fraud proliferate uncontrollably,
criminals accumulate in great numbers without end.
Rulers and ministers presume upon each other,
superiors and inferiors lack distinction,
this arises from the absence of regulations.
Now if we eliminate extravagant customs,
practice methods of frugality,
set standards for carriages and vehicles,
establish regulations for clothing, tools, and equipment,
once regulations are fixed,
then rulers and ministers will cease excesses,
and superiors and inferiors will be clearly distinguished.
Those who overstep their retreat will be reprimanded,
those who presume above their station will be punished,
thus extravagance cannot arise,
cleverness and deceitful schemes have no reason to emerge,
treachery, evil, theft, and banditry will cease on their own,
then the people will stay far from crime.
With cleverness and deceitful schemes not arising,
this is called ignorance,
hence it is said: making them ignorant makes the people less likely to fall into the law's net.
These four points
cause rulers and ministers to presume upon each other,
superiors and inferiors to lack distinction,
the world to suffer poverty,
deceit, fraud, theft, and banditry to arise together,
and criminals to accumulate endlessly,
thus it is imperative to remedy this swiftly.
"On Base-born Children"
The people sell their own children,
yet can afford embroidered clothes, silk-trimmed sandals,
and decorative edges,
placing them in secluded chambers,
these are the garments of ancient emperors and empresses,
worn by empresses in temples but not in private,
yet now commoners can clothe their base-born concubines with them.
Outer garments of white gauze,
lined with thin silk,
trimmed with decorative borders,
the finest adorned with imperial embroidery,
these were the robes of ancient emperors,
now wealthy merchants and great traders squander resources as if on brothers,
and use them to cover walls at banquets to entertain guests.
In ancient times, heaven provided for one emperor and one empress with moderation and appropriateness,
now nobles and great traders have walls adorned with imperial robes,
merchants' wives, entertainers, and low-born women wear empress's ornaments,
yet if the world does not bend under this,
it is nearly impossible.
Moreover, the emperor himself wears plain black silk,
while extravagant merchants and nobles,
have walls and rooms draped in embroidered finery;
the emperor clothes his lowly empress with it,
trimming her collars,
while commoners' base-born concubines trim their sandals with it:
