this is what I call perversion.
And consider the logic of the matter,
a hundred people laboring cannot clothe one person,
how can we hope for a world without cold?
How is it possible?
One person farms,
ten gather to eat from it,
hoping the world escapes hunger,
is impossible.
When hunger and cold pierce the people's flesh,
expecting them to refrain from treachery, evil, theft, and banditry,
is impossible.
The state is already impoverished,
treachery, evil, theft, and banditry only await their moment,
if the year turns unfavorable,
they will rise like clouds,
and if nothing is done,
seeing the houses full,
how can they all be pacified?
To face this and still have a stable rule,
is nearly impossible.
Now in ordinary times, there is no preparation,
no respect and habitual leniency,
ensuring trouble when crises arise,
yet those offering advice mostly say "inaction is supreme."
But how can inaction
revive a world in decline?
They say:
"Governing as a great official is acceptable."
But if great chaos comes,
how can it be compared to small troubles?
Alas!
Customs have reached great disrespect,
extreme lack of hierarchy,
utmost presumption upon superiors,
yet those presenting plans still say "do nothing,"
this is what merits deep sighs.
"On Copper and Cloth"
When copper is distributed among the populace,
it becomes a calamity for the empire.
How can this be explained?
With copper spread among the people,
those who mint coins
will largely mix in stones, lead, and iron.
The crime of tattooing (as punishment) increases daily—
this is the first disaster.
With copper distributed among the people,
counterfeit coins proliferate endlessly,
currency becomes unreliable,
and the people grow increasingly suspicious of each other—
this is the second disaster.
With copper spread among the populace,
copper miners abandon their fields,
and household coin-casters neglect their farming duties.
If grain is not produced, famine approaches—
this is the third disaster.
Thus, if coin minting is not prohibited,
currency will remain chaotic,
tattoo-punishment crimes will accumulate daily,
creating a pitfall.
Moreover, with farming neglected,
doubts arise about disasters.
Therefore, private coin minting must be banned.
If the state prohibits coin minting
under penalty of death,
and minting is suppressed,
then currency will become scarcer and heavier,
leading to clandestine minting,
causing death sentences to accumulate again—
all due to copper's influence.
Hence, distributing copper among the people
brings widespread calamity.
Now, this broad disaster can be eliminated,
and seven blessings can be attained.
What are these seven blessings?
The state should confiscate copper and prevent its circulation among the people,
so they cannot mint coins,
and tattoo-punishment crimes do not accumulate—
first.
Without copper circulating among the people,
counterfeit coins will not proliferate,
and the people will not distrust each other—
second.
Without copper in circulation,
people cannot mine copper
or mint coins,
so they return to farming—
third.
Without copper among the people,
it all reverts to the state,
which can hoard copper reserves to control currency weight:
when coins are light, use methods to withdraw them;
when heavy, use methods to distribute them—
goods will stabilize in price,
and currency will be well-managed—
fourth.
Using accumulated copper to cast weapons,
loaned to noble officials,
with sizes and quantities
each regulated by system,
to distinguish nobility from commoners,
and differentiate ranks—
thus clarifying hierarchies—
fifth.
Using copper reserves to oversee all goods,
balancing surplus and shortage,
collecting excess profits—
then the government will grow wealthy while merchants suffer—
sixth.
Using copper reserves to control wasted resources,
competing with the Xiōngnú for their people's allegiance,
then the enemy will submit—
this is called the seventh blessing.
Therefore, those skilled in governing the empire
turn calamity into blessing,
and reverse defeat into victory.
Yet now we retreat from seven blessings to pursue widespread disaster—
truly lamentable,
and this is the first point.
"Unified Access"
Establishing passes like Wǔguān, Hángǔ, and Línjìn
was largely to guard against the eastern feudal lords.
The empire's governance lies with Your Majesty,
but now major lords have grown powerful,
necessitating passes for defense,
akin to the Qín dynasty's precautions against the six states.
Would it not be better to stabilize territorial control to eliminate the need for defense,
practicing impartial love and selfless principles,
abolishing passes for free movement,
so the lower ranks do not exclusively control Guānzhōng?
Restrictions on officials serving feudal lords
and bans on leaving passes
surely imply that lords gaining influence increase their power,
and more chariots in their states boost their strength.
Thus, clear laws are established
to prevent empowering the lords.
In my strategy,
alienating the eastern troublesome lords
to prevent unity
is precisely this approach.
Would it not be better to fix a land system
where even if the lords' people
each had two horses, it wouldn't pose a threat,
or adding ten thousand men wouldn't cause harm?
Now, without establishing grand principles,
frequently issuing bans,
failing to win hearts,
harming the ideal of universal care—
is unwise.
The Son of Heaven resides in Cháng'ān,
yet treats Huáinán's southeastern border as tribute land,
with routes spanning thousands of lǐ,
making transport difficult.
Some commanderies跨越 lords to have tax-exempt lands,
levying taxes from distant regions,
yet demanding uniformity,
with large states enclosing small ones territorially,
and small states nestled within large ones as capitals.
Sizes are mixed and overlapping,
distances uneven,
showing the disorder in imperial and feudal boundaries—
utterly chaotic.
Using fiefdoms to strengthen enemies,
offering marquisates as bait to usurpers—
most unwise.
Why has Your Majesty long not corrected this?
"Distant Territories"
In ancient times, the Son of Heaven's domain spanned a thousand lǐ,
with the capital centrally located,
so transport and labor services
reached even the farthest within five hundred lǐ.
Dukes and marquises had domains of a hundred lǐ,
centrally located capitals,
with transport and labor
covering the farthest within fifty lǐ.
Transporters did not suffer hardship,
laborers bore no excessive costs,
so distant people lived peacefully,
and all subjects delighted in their lands—
this is how the empire endured.
After Qín's fall, it reversed;
Qín would not cede an inch of land,
wanting all for itself.
Transport started from coastal areas,
where one coin in tax
cost ten coins in expense,
hardly easy to deliver.
The state gained little,
yet the people suffered deeply,
so when Chén Shèng rebelled, the empire collapsed.
Now Hàn spans between two lords,
yet uses Lújiāng as tribute land—
even Qín's remote borders
were scarcely farther.
If this land neither transports nor serves the ruler,
it violates tribute land principles.
Why long keep it anxiously attached?
If enforced as tribute land,
it repeats Qín's errors.
I deem this unwise.
Huáinán is a poor, barren region;
those sent to Cháng'ān for labor
exhaust themselves to compensate,
traveling mid-route in worn-out clothes,
already emaciated and destitute.
Forcing them in rags to arrive,
likely without borrowing or volunteering—
not what I've heard should be.
Sandals seldom replaced, insufficient for the journey; coin costs match this— how bitter!
I've heard of county magistrates and chancellors retiring,
likely not very strong,
seen without attendants.
Traveling thousands of lǐ across lords' lands,
yet nominally under Hàn,
such a situation cannot last.
Hàn families weep seeing them off,
and lament when laborers depart—
neither side desires it.
Some under Hàn seek kingship,
a common extreme,
while those fleeing back to lords
are numerous.
Your Majesty should act early,
not aiding treacherous men.
"Intimacy and Estrangement Lead to Danger and Chaos"
Your Majesty has refrained from certain actions,
so I dare not fail to fully present the matters and regulations.
Suppose the empire were as it was before,
with Huáiyīn Hóu still ruling Chǔ,
Qíng Bù ruling Huáinán,
Péng Yuè ruling Liáng,
Hán Xìn ruling Hán,
Zhāng Áo ruling Zhào,
Guàn Gāo serving as chancellor,
Lú Wǎn ruling Yān,
and Chén Xī in Dài—
if these six or seven lords were all unharmed,
maintaining their states and residing there,
at that time, were Your Majesty to ascend the throne as Son of Heaven,
could you feel secure?
I have reason to know that Your Majesty could not.
When the empire was in turmoil,
Emperor Gāo arose alongside these lords,
without the advantage of collateral lineage to rely upon.
The luckiest among them
only became palace attendants,
while the next best merely became household retainers.
When Emperor Gāo faced south and proclaimed himself emperor,
they all became his subjects,
their abilities falling far short.
In the fifth year of Emperor Gāo,
he ascended as Son of Heaven with brilliant sageliness and martial prowess,
dividing fertile lands
to enfeoff meritorious ministers as kings,
some receiving over a hundred cities,
others as few as thirty or forty counties—
such was the depth of his virtue.
Yet within ten years thereafter,
rebellions arose nine times,
nearly endangering the empire on five or six occasions.
As for Your Majesty and these lords,
you neither personally competed with them in ability to subdue them,
nor personally enfeoffed them as kings.
Since even Emperor Gāo could not remain secure for a year under such circumstances,
how could Your Majesty alone feel secure because of this?
Yet there is still an excuse to be made,
namely that they were distant relatives.
Allow me to speak of the close ones.
Suppose Qí Dàohuì Wáng ruled Qí,
Yuán Wáng ruled Chǔ,
Zhōngshān Wáng ruled Zhào,
Yōu Wáng ruled Huáiyáng,
Gòng Wáng ruled Liáng,
Líng Wáng ruled Yān,
Lì Wáng ruled Huáinán—
if these six or seven nobles were all unharmed,
each maintaining their state and residing there,
at that time,
were Your Majesty to ascend the throne as Son of Heaven,
could you govern effectively?
I privately know that Your Majesty could not.
Although the feudal lords are nominally subjects,
they all truly have the mindset of commoner brothers,
invariably considering how to adopt imperial institutions and act as sovereigns themselves.
They arbitrarily confer titles,
pardon capital crimes,
and some even go so far as to use the yellow canopy carriage.
Hàn laws are not established,
Hàn decrees are not implemented.
Even one as rebellious as the King of Huáinán—
if ordered, would he willingly obey?
If summoned, how could he be made to come?
If by chance he did arrive,
how could the law be applied to him?
Move against one relative,
and the whole empire would rise up looking on.
How then could the empire be controlled?
Though Your Majesty has ministers as brave as Féng Jìng,
as soon as he opens his mouth,
a dagger would already be plunged into his chest.
However worthy Your Majesty may be,
with whom will you lead the feudal lords?
This is what is meant by "close relatives."
Thus, the distant ones inevitably pose danger,
the close ones inevitably cause chaos.
If Your Majesty relies on the present situation for stability,
how can you know it will certainly become dangerous and chaotic?
Yet you persist and firmly control it—
what kind of governance is this?
With the situation hanging by a thread,
I can make it understood that chaos is as profitable as a hundred pieces of gold now.
"Worrying About the People"
The way of a true king
ensures that after three years of farming, the people have a surplus of one year's food;
after nine years, a surplus of three years' food;
after thirty years, the people have a ten-year reserve.
Thus, when Yǔ faced floods for eight years,
and Tāng drought for seven years,
so severe that the fields had no green grass,
yet the people showed no signs of hunger,
and there were no beggars on the roads.
Even after the years of recovery,
they still prohibited excessive plowing—
the ancients in governing the empire
truly had their methods.
The way of a true king
holds that a state without a nine-year reserve
is called insufficient;
without a six-year reserve,
it is called critical;
without a three-year reserve,
it is said the state is no longer a state.
Now, it has been thirty years since Hàn was established,
yet the empire grows increasingly strained,
food is extremely scarce—
does Your Majesty not reflect on this?
It is because the harvest has not been reaped.
The wealthy do not lend,
the poor face hunger,
if the season is missed, there will be no harvest,
they plead to sell titles and children—
this has already been heard.
Recently, when there was no rain,
it made people fearful;
once it rained,
they felt as if reborn.
The empire's lack of reserves is extremely dire!
What would this be called under the kingly laws?
To only worry when hardship arrives,
to plan only when destitution comes—
is it not too late?
I privately ponder this and find it sorrowful.
Then, what is meant by
"the state has no people"?
To possess the empire and desire its stability—
does it not rest with Your Majesty?
If the ruler does not worry himself,
on whom will he rely for complacency?
Five years of moderate prosperity,
ten years bring one disaster,
thirty years bring one great prosperity—
this is called the great cycle.
From the time of cannibalism until now,
how many years has it been?
If unfortunately, a drought of two or three thousand lǐ square occurs,
how will the empire rescue itself?
Suddenly, if the border faces emergency,
and millions of troops gather,
how will the empire supply them?
With war and drought compounding,
the people will fill the ditches and gullies,
banditry and attacks will arise successively,
the central states failing to rescue, foreign enemies will surely be alarmed,
it could happen in a single day—
this is inevitable.
Moreover, those in power
may not necessarily realize this,
and the ruler, not worrying himself,
when affairs become dire,
will panic and rebuke his subordinates:
"This is Heaven's doing,
what can be done?
Since things are as they are, what use is worrying?"
Now, as autumn begins,
it is a good time to act.
If Your Majesty has a moment,
you could have me discuss and follow the plans of the Chancellor and Yùshǐ.
I, Jiǎ Yì, propose that those with a rank of two thousand dàn or above
be allowed to participate in planning—
without favoring the close or distant—
it would likely do no harm,
and the timing is right.
"Resolving the County Issue"
The situation of the world is currently upside down,
I humbly wish Your Majesty would reflect upon it.
The Son of Heaven,
is the head of the world,
why is that?
Because he is superior.
The barbarians,
are the feet of the world,
why is that?
Because they are inferior.
Issuing commands to the barbarians,
is the authority of the sovereign;
offering tribute to the Son of Heaven,
is the ritual of subjects.
Now the feet are positioned above,
while the head is placed below,
this is an inverted situation.
With the world so upside down,
and no one able to resolve it,
can the state be said to have capable people?
It is not merely an inversion,
but also resembles lameness,
and moreover, paralysis.
Lameness affects one side,
paralysis causes pain in one region.
Now the west is the upper stream,
the east is the lower stream,
thus Lǒngxī is considered superior,
while Dōnghǎi is inferior,
so the northern border is entirely inverted.
In the western and northern commanderies,
even those with high ranks cannot easily be exempted,
those over five chǐ tall cannot easily rest,
their suffering is extreme!
The central lands and left garrisons,
extend for thousands of lǐ,
supplying provisions is extremely difficult!
Sentinels watch beacon fires and dare not sleep,
guarding officers and soldiers sometimes sleep in armor,
while the Xiōngnú bully, insult, and plunder,
with no end in sight.
Hoping to expand trust, authority, and virtue is difficult,
thus I say:
one region is afflicted.
Physicians can cure it,
yet the sovereign refuses to employ them,
the world's inversion is deeply distressing!
I privately lament this for Your Majesty,
advisors generally consider this predicament insoluble,
showing great lack of capability.
If Your Majesty would deign to heed my strategy,
I request You mobilize the resources of the Central Kingdom to pursue the Xiōngnú,
the Central Kingdom will grow prosperous and strong by leveraging its resources,
while the Xiōngnú will succumb to their crimes and be destroyed,
capture the Chányú by the neck and control his fate,
seize Zhōngháng Yuè and whip his back,
command the Xiōngnú masses entirely at Your discretion.
Execute them!
Or spare them!
It is secondary.
Your Majesty's authority inspires awe with great credibility,
Your virtue and righteousness are vast and far-reaching,
holding the world firmly and securely,
truly deserving of exalted titles,
looking down upon the Central Kingdom,
gazing up at the four barbarians,
all would align with Your will.
Then retreat to fast for three days,
to report to the ancestral temple,
so all people, wise or foolish, men or women, would say:
"The Emperor is indeed profoundly sage."
How can we bear that with Your Majesty's brilliance,
and the resources of the world,
You long endure such bullying and arrogance from the barbarians?
This can be said to show the state lacks capable people.
"Wei Bù Xìn"
The ancient righteous principle,
east, west, south, north,
wherever boats and carts can reach,
where human traces can go,
none fail to submit,
only then is one called Son of Heaven,
when virtue is profound,
when kindness is deep,
then one is called Emperor,
with added excellence,
then one is called Sovereign.
Now Your titles are most glorious,
yet Your actual influence does not extend beyond the Great Wall,
they not only do not submit,
but are greatly disrespectful,
the borders are long unsettled,
the interior long unpeaceful,
like a crouching tiger,
it will surely strike when opportunity arises,
when will this end?
Formerly Emperor Gāo rose from commoner status and subdued the nine provinces,
now Your Majesty rules the nine provinces yet cannot act against the Xiōngnú,
I privately feel this is unworthy of Your Majesty,
moreover, the situation has particularly adverse aspects,
its significance is especially critical.
The Son of Heaven,
is the head of the world,
why is that?
Because he is superior.
The barbarians,
are the feet of the world,
why is that?
Because they are inferior.
Issuing commands to the barbarians,
is the authority of the sovereign.
Offering tribute to the Son of Heaven,
is the ritual of subjects.
Now the feet are positioned above,
while the head is placed below,
this is an inverted situation.
The world's situation is inverted,
and no one can set it right,
can the state be said to have capable people?
Virtue can be extended afar.
Authority can be imposed distantly,
wherever boats and carts reach,
can be made to follow one's will,
yet specifically within a few hundred lǐ,
authority and commands lack credibility,
this is what merits weeping.
"Xiōngnú"
I surmise that the Xiongnu can field roughly sixty thousand cavalry in total.
With one soldier conscripted from every five individuals,
five times six makes thirty,
this amounts to a population of only three hundred thousand,
not even equivalent to a large Han county yielding a thousand shi of grain.
Yet they dare to speak of annual invasions and raids,
repeatedly seek to assert equal status,
obstruct the emperor's righteousness,
which is highly unprincipled.
Why does Your Majesty not appoint a capable person to manage this matter once and for all?
I propose to use the method of shaking the cicada's tree to startle them for Your Majesty,
establishing an official position for this purpose,
appointing an officer,
to take charge of the Xiongnu.
If truly capable,
even granting a salary of a thousand shi would be appropriate.
If Your Majesty is willing to heed this proposal,
the plan would ensure the Central Plains grows increasingly stable,
while the Xiongnu face daily peril,
the great state becomes immensely wealthy,
and the Xiongnu head toward extinction.
Commanding them like dogs and horses,
is the natural course of circumstances.
It is certain that the Xiongnu masses
will become subjects and people of the Han.
Organize them into states of a thousand households each,
stationing them beyond the frontier,
stretching from Lǒngxī to Liáodōng,
each allocated territory to guard the borders,
preparing against the turmoil of the Yuèzhī and other tribes,
all placed under the jurisdiction of established commanderies.
Thereafter, cease military campaigns and rest the border,
disarm the populace under heaven,
the emperor's majestic virtue,
practiced internally and trusted externally,
will please and subdue the four wilds,
then this humble minister's aspiration would be gratified.
Otherwise,
the emperor's authority will not prevail,
hearts will remain silent and discontented.
I have heard that the Xiongnu are currently growing weak,
this is the time they display martial prowess while blinded by greed,
and states like Jiànlóng and Yìqú in the eastern Hu regions
have somewhat come to surrender.
In my foolish opinion,
the Xiongnu are about to act,
likely deploying a cunning strategy with surprise,
presenting lavish gifts to make demands on the Han,
not ceasing until they launch a major offensive,
mobilizing hundreds of thousands in urgent haste,
amassing in the north.
How can the empire feed and supply them?
Faced with such events and severe hardship,
it would be difficult to achieve success.
Why does Your Majesty not plan early?
The founder of the state said:
"The Xiongnu show no respect,
their words are improper,
relying on their multitude,
they frequently commit banditry,
harass the borders,
disturb the Central Plains,
repeatedly act unjustly,
behaving deceitfully toward us.
What should be done about this?"
The response was:
"I have heard that strong states fight with wisdom,
kings fight with righteousness,
emperors fight with virtue.
Thus, Tāng prayed over the net and the Hànyīn surrendered;
Shùn danced with shields and feathers and the Sānmiáo submitted.
Now the Han emperor rules the Central Plains,
he should use abundant virtue to win over the four barbarians,
promoting bright righteousness to show it widely to distant lands.
Then wherever chariots and boats can reach,
wherever human footprints can go,
all will be as domesticated animals,
and who would dare defiantly not accept the emperor's will?
I propose for Your Majesty three demonstrations,
and five baits,
to use these to contend for the people with the Chányú,
then subduing the Xiongnu will be like shaking withered leaves.
Those without principle,
how could they resist this for long?
If Your Majesty is willing to employ my strategy,
I will use the situation to convey the emperor's words:
making the Xiongnu masses trust in Your Majesty,
through communication of words,
that must be carried out without change.
Even if one promises in a dream,
upon waking, one should not break that trust.
Once Your Majesty has made a promise,
it should be as bright as the rising sun.
Thus, hearing the ruler's word,
even from afar,
their resolve will not waver.
Even enemies,
their hearts will not be hostile.
Thus, trust is demonstrated—
nothing promised is left unfulfilled.
This is the first demonstration.
I will also use the situation to convey Your Majesty's compassion:
Let the Xiongnu see themselves,
that any with a Hu face but our demeanor
will feel beloved by the Son of Heaven,
like a child meeting a kind mother.
Thus, compassion is demonstrated—
the first demonstration.
I will further convey Your Majesty's appreciation:
Let the Hu people see that,
if they have any skilled expertise,
or craftsmanship,
it can align with the Son of Heaven's favor.
Thus, appreciation is demonstrated—
the first demonstration.
The appearance of loving others,
appreciating others' skills,
is the way of benevolence.
Trust is the great integrity,
the emperor's righteousness.
With genuine love and appreciation,
promises that can be relied upon,
even at the risk of ten deaths for one life,
they will surely come.
These are called the three demonstrations.
As for rewards in the state,
they must not be equal for all.
Equal rewards impoverish the state,
and meager rewards cannot move people.
Thus, skilled rewarders leap over norms,
break conventions,
and occasionally bestow generously,
making it visible enough to see,
talked about enough to discuss,
then they can sway the heart of a whole nation.
If Your Majesty graciously heeds my plan,
I will have surplus resources.
When Xiongnu come,
the heads of households and above will surely wear embroidered silk,
the younger ones will wear patterned brocade.
Prepare five silver carriages,
grandly carved and painted,
drawn by four horses,
bearing green canopies,
followed by several riders,
with charioteers and escorts.
Even the Chányú's own processions
may not surpass this.
Let surrendered Xiongnu
occasionally receive such gifts.
Those in the nation who hear or see this
will eagerly tell each other,
everyone hoping luckily,
thinking they too can gain this upon arrival.
This will dazzle their eyes—
the first bait.
When Xiongnu envoys arrive,
especially those of high rank,
gathered in large numbers,
the emperor should summon them to feast.
Serve four or five vessels of food,
with fine sliced and roasted meats,
complete with sauces and pickles,
spread over several feet before them.
Seat one person there,
with Hu observers
surely numbering in the hundreds nearby.
The joy of the rewarded,
laughing and eating,
tasting all their favorite yet previously unobtainable flavors.
Let newcomers occasionally enjoy such feasts.
Those in the nation who hear or see this
will drool and tell each other,
each anxious about their own lot,
hoping they too will receive this.
This will tempt their mouths—
the first bait.
For the elite among the surrendered,
or when envoys come,
the emperor should have them invited as guests,
allowing them to bring acquaintances.
Do not forbid Hu people who wish to watch.
Have women with powdered faces and dark eyebrows,
twenty or thirty in embroidered robes serving in the hall,
some lightly veiled or covered,
performing Hu plays to entertain.
Have the Music Bureau kindly provide entertainment,
playing flutes and drums,
with acrobats tumbling forward in turn,
dancers and performers appearing intermittently.
After a short while, drums beat,
puppets dance,
occasionally playing Róng music.
Hand in hand, they urge the honored guests onward,
with over ten women steadily assisting before and after.
Let envoys and surrendered ones occasionally enjoy such pleasures.
Those in the nation who hear or see this
will wide-eyed tell each other,
everyone eager, fearing to miss out by arriving late.
This will captivate their ears—
One bait.
All those who surrender are summoned and favored by Your Majesty,
which is the means to attract them,
Your Majesty must occasionally enrich them,
ensuring they have lofty halls and deep chambers,
fine kitchens and quarters,
large granaries,
stables filled with horses,
storehouses with chariots arrayed,
servants, various children, and livestock fully provided,
and on such occasions, grandly summon the Hú and guests to feast Hú envoys,
with Your Majesty ordering officials to assist in preparations and lend music,
so that their dwellings are joyful and their granaries and livestock abundant,
all surpassing what their former kings had,
considering that their chanyú might be drawn out,
and from time to time bestowing these upon them to establish their homes.
The entire state of the Xiōngnú will wholeheartedly hope,
each person eagerly fearing they might arrive too late,
this will be used to corrupt their bellies,
one bait.
As for those who come to surrender,
Your Majesty must occasionally summon and favor them,
comforting them before they can enter official service,
for the Hú chieftains are difficult to befriend,
but if Your Majesty deals with Hú children,
and the beloved sons of nobles,
Your Majesty must summon and favor several dozen of them,
dressing them in embroidered garments and fine leisure attire,
and when going out, they follow,
when residing, they take turns serving,
when Your Majesty feasts the Hú people,
holds grand wrestling matches,
or entertains Hú envoys,
warriors and martial guards steadfastly attend nearby,
Hú children are allowed to serve closely at hand,
Hú nobles take turns coming forward to assist with wine,
Your Majesty then personally attends to these gatherings,
having wine payments made,
occasionally pairing people appropriately,
and during intervals, presenting embroidered garments,
complete with belts and fine guest attire,
bestowing them from time to time,
Your Majesty then favors by patting the Hú children,
teasing them playfully,
jesting with them,
and even offering roasted meat to eat personally,
bringing out fine leisure clothes and personally gifting them,
Your Majesty rises, and the Hú children gather before and after,
the Hú nobles, having served wine,
when going out, wear robes and adorn sashes,
standing as nobles among the Hú,
letting a few obtain such status and dwell thus,
those in the state who hear or see this,
will gaze with longing and desire,
each person eagerly fearing they might arrive too late,
this will be used to corrupt their hearts,
one bait.
Thus, tug at their ears,
tug at their eyes,
tug at their mouths,
tug at their bellies,
once these four are tugged,
and their hearts are drawn in,
how can they not come?
Subduing the Hú and suppressing their resistance,
this is called the five baits.
As for responding to major changes,
generally decide and control with authority,
acting according to what is appropriate,
without predetermined forms,
honor the princess,
esteem the chancellor,
increase the number of senior officials,
and numerous gate ministers,
all of whom are strategists,
ensure sufficient wealth for use,
and our people will utilize their honor,
observing their limits,
spying on their plans,
with internal and external tallies and seals appropriately restrained,
how can others remain defiant for long like this?
Thus, with the three declarations already explained,
and the five baits made clear,
then within the Xiōngnú, discord and mutual suspicion will arise.
Causing the chanyú to lie restless without sleep,
losing appetite for food,
grasping his sword and bow,
crouching in the corner of his yurt,
looking left and right,
seeing all as enemies,
his ministers,
though wishing not to flee,
feel as if a tiger is behind them,
the masses, though wishing not to come,
fear they might be hindered,
this is called the inevitable trend,
when the nobles see the chanyú,
it is like confronting tigers and wolves,
their turning south to submit to Hàn,
is like a weak child yearning for a loving mother,
when the masses see our generals and officials,
it is like facing bitter enemies,
their desire to flee south to Hàn,
is like water flowing downward,
with the general and chanyú having no subjects to command,
no people to guard,
how can they avoid bowing their necks and knocking their heads,
begging to submit to Your Majesty's righteousness?
This is called victorious virtue.
When the Xiōngnú see they are being outmaneuvered,
they will lead their people far away,
and this can be achieved repeatedly,
as for border markets,
they are indeed what the Xiōngnú covet and deeply seek,
I hope Your Majesty will send envoys to make generous peace with them,
and reluctantly permit large markets,
when the envoys return,
at strategic and dangerous points,
carve out many openings,
extending them widely,
with border officials and soldiers sufficient to defend themselves,
and at each major pass, have butchers, wine sellers, food vendors, and those selling soups, stews, and roasts,
each type with one to two hundred people,
then the Hú people will gather at the foot of the Great Wall,
and thus the king will strengthen the north and inevitably attack their ruler.
With the Xiōngnú in hunger,
eating rice, soup, and roasted meats,
drinking much wine,
their exhaustion and depletion can be awaited immediately.
The more gifts given, the hungrier they become,
the more wealth exhausted, the more distressed they grow,
what the Hàn people aspire to and admire,
then becomes prized by the Xiōngnú,
for those who come in thousands,
honor two or three among them,
for those who come in tens of thousands,
honor over ten among them.
Honor and glory,
are the means to attract the people,
thus in the long term within five years,
or short term within three years,
the Xiōngnú will perish,
this is called victory through virtue.

clarifying the five baits,
abundantly supporting the princess,

with criminals and bandits,
accumulating endlessly,

to bring calamity upon the Xiōngnú,

The Xiōngnú invade most outrageously and insult most grievously,
treating the Son of Heaven with extreme disrespect,
becoming an affliction to the world without end.
For Hàn to annually send gold, silk, and embroidered fabrics,
this is paying tribute to the barbarians,
indeed making the Róng people into feudal lords.
Our position being so debased and humiliating,
and calamity still unceasing,
how can this continue endlessly?
How can Your Majesty bear to maintain the imperial title while residing in such a position?
I privately estimate the multitude of the Xiōngnú
does not exceed that of a large county of one thousand shí in Hàn.
With the vastness of the empire,
to be troubled by the multitude of a single county—
I am deeply ashamed for those in charge.
If Your Majesty has the intention,
why not let me try to manage this?
The Hú people in ancient times were subdued by small feudal lords with minimal authority,
how should they dare to be so fierce now?
If I were appointed as an official of the dependent state to oversee the Xiōngnú,
and by fortune my strategies were implemented,
within half a year,
the Xiūtú would lose their sustenance.
Given a little more time,
the Xiūtú would have ropes around their necks,
crawling on their knees and knocking their foreheads,
begging to submit to Your Majesty's righteousness.
Only if Your Majesty graciously considers,
and afterwards I am dismissed from the office of the dependent state,
granted to return and live in my rural cottage,
no longer defiling the imperial court,
then the loyal minister's aspiration would be satisfied.
Now, instead of hunting fierce enemies, we hunt field boars;
instead of fighting rebel bandits, we chase captive rabbits.
Are not the hunts too trivial?
Are not the fights too unimportant?
To attend to minor worries without planning for great calamities
is not the way to security.

One.

has not thoroughly deliberated with such as myself.

Your Majesty bowed and knocked your head in apology before the Empress Dowager,
yet the King of Huáinán showed no remorse or restraint,
and no blame was attached to him.
His retainers forcibly controlled the gates of the chambers,
Your Majesty pursued and pardoned them,
yet the officials were unable to arrest them.
The king's men roamed the Son of Heaven's state committing injustices without reprimand,
and he was bestowed with beauties and laden with gold upon returning.
The marquises' estates within his kingdom
were all moved to other places.
Your Majesty towards the King of Huáinán
cannot be said to have been stingy.
Yet the King of Huáinán
trampled upon and disregarded the Son of Heaven's laws.
The emperor's commands
were distorted and not implemented.
Who in the world does not know this?
The Son of Heaven selected meritorious officials with duties to serve as his ministers,
but the king merely trampled and expelled them;
there were none who did not claim illness and flee.
Who in the world does not know this?
Daily he harbored resentful words to slander Your Majesty's actions,
rejected and refused the Empress Dowager's gifts,
the Son of Heaven's envoys bearing decrees could not see him,
lying prostrate to receive the imperial edict.
Who in the world does not know this?
He gathered criminals, cunning youths,
allies like Tōng Zhànqí,
Qǐ Zhāng and others,
and plotted to become the Eastern Emperor.
Who in the world does not know this?
The King of Huáinán's crimes were already clear,
Your Majesty fortunately pardoned him from the death penalty,
releasing him on the path of gold, treating him as divine.
The man died of illness himself;
how has Your Majesty failed the great purpose of the world?
Who can say the king's death was inappropriate?
Your Majesty has no fault!
Thus,
the King of Huáinán was a criminal himself,
the sons of Huáinán are the sons of a criminal.
To honor the sons of a criminal
only invites slander from the world!
There is no resolution from the past affairs,
and if people do not have flesh for hearts, so be it,
but if they have flesh for hearts,
human hearts can be known.
Now the sons of Huáinán are young and vigorous,
hearing of their father's humiliating situation,
they stand weeping, tears soaking their collars,
lie weeping, tears crossing their necks,
their intestines twisted like ropes to their waists and elbows!
How could they momentarily forget their father?
Not to be so under these circumstances
is inhuman.
Your Majesty controls the fate of the world,
and the King of Huáinán reached such extremes.
To whom else would his sons direct their resentment but Your Majesty?
They only say the situation is not yet opportune,
the matter has not yet erupted,
suppressing turmoil and not daring to speak.
If they truly have such hearts,
how could they forget Your Majesty?
What Bái Gōng Shèng did to avenge his father
was to take revenge on his grandfather and uncles.
Lìngyǐn Zǐxī and Sīmǎ Zǐqí,
all close paternal uncles,
were all injured without exception.
In the past, when Bái Gōng stirred rebellion,
it was not to seize the state or replace the ruler,
but to vent his indignation and satisfy his will!
Thus, he wished to stab his hand into the enemy's chest,
indeed seeking mutual destruction only!
He certainly did not hope to live.
Now the territory of Huáinán, though small,
was once used by Qíng Bù!
Hàn's survival was merely fortunate!
To hand over resources to enemies sufficient to endanger Hàn—
how is this strategy safe or convenient?
Even if divided into four,
the four sons are of one heart, no different.
Yù Ràng avenged Zhì Bó against Zhào Xiāngzǐ,
attempting five times without success,
for no other reason
than lacking sufficient resources and strength.
When Wǔ Zǐxū took revenge on Chǔ,
he had the multitude of Wú.
When Bái Gōng accomplished his rebellion,
he had Bái Gōng's multitude.
Hé Lǘ was wealthy,
thus he could have Zhuān Zhū assassinate King Liáo of Wú.
Prince Dān of Yān was wealthy,
thus he could have Jīng Kē kill King Zhèng of Qín.
Now Your Majesty is about to honor untrustworthy people,
giving them multitudes,
accumulating wealth for them.
If this does not lead to revenge like Bái Gōng or Wǔ Zǐxū arising in the capital,
then perhaps assassins like Zhuān Zhū or Jīng Kē will emerge between the pillars.
How is this strategy safe or convenient?
This is what is called lending weapons to a robber and wings to a tiger.
I wish Your Majesty would spare a little thought to consider this.
"Lack of Storage"
Yǔ had ten years' worth of reserves,
thus he avoided the calamity of nine years of floods.
Tāng had ten years' worth of accumulation,
thus he overcame seven years of drought.
Now, the accumulation of reserves
is the great lifeline of the nation.
If grain is abundant and wealth plentiful,
what undertaking could not be accomplished?
In attack, one can conquer;
in defense, one can hold firm;
in battle, one can be victorious;
in winning over and pacifying distant lands,
who would not answer the call?
Guǎnzǐ said:
"When granaries are full,
people know礼节.
When food and clothing are sufficient,
people understand honor and shame."
That people could be governed without being well-provided for,
from ancient times to the present,
I have never heard of such a thing.
The ancients said:
"If one man does not plow,
some may go hungry because of it;
if one woman does not weave,
some may suffer cold because of it."
Production has its seasons,
yet consumption knows no limits—
then material resources must become exhausted.
Those who governed the world in ancient times
were extremely meticulous and thorough,
hence their accumulated reserves were reliable.
Now, turning away from the fundamentals to pursue the trivial,
with consumers being very numerous,
this is a great harm to the nation.
The sources of harm to life are rampant,
this is a great scourge to the nation.
The customs of extravagance, indulgence, and luxury
grow day by day,
this is a great curse upon the nation.
Harm and scourge prevail openly,
with no one to stop them;
the great lifeline is about to collapse,
with no one to save it.
What plan is there? Where can solutions be found? With producers being few and wasters numerous,
how can the situation of the nation not be perilous?
The Hàn dynasty has existed for nearly forty years,
yet the accumulations of both public and private sectors remain pitiable.
Thus, if the season passes without rain,
the people will be anxious;
in a bad harvest year with no income,
they will request to sell titles and children—
such reports have already reached our ears!
How can the ruler of the nation remain unalarmed when faced with such danger!
Famines in the world
are a common occurrence;
Yǔ and Tāng experienced them.
If unfortunately there is a drought covering two or three thousand lǐ,
how will the state provide relief?
Should an emergency suddenly arise at the border,
with hundreds of thousands of troops gathered,
how will the state supply them?
When war and drought occur together,
the nation faces great scarcity,
the brave and strong will gather followers and strike recklessly,
and the weak
will exchange children to eat their bones.
Political laws may not reach everywhere,
and those in distant regions who harbor doubts will rise together and contend.
If the ruler then tries to plan for it,
will there still be time?
It is possible to achieve wealth and security for the nation,
yet we merely face this precarious situation?
I secretly grieve for Your Majesty!
The Wángzhì says:
"A state without nine years' reserves
is called insufficient.
Without six years' reserves,
it is called urgent.
Without three years' reserves,
the state is no longer a state."
The Wángzhì is so pressing,
why does Your Majesty not order officials to calculate what should be done?
This is a matter for tears,
and it is indeed so.
"On Coin Casting"
Recently, I have privately heard that officials are again casting coins,
and people are being punished,
with up to a hundred per county in severe cases,
dozens in moderate ones.
Family members, acquaintances,
and even officials under suspicion,
those imprisoned, flogged, or fleeing—
the numbers are quite significant.
I have not verified this,
but the punishments are inevitable,
and those facing penalties are only the beginning;
this will not cease,
and the issues are numerous,
greatly inconveniencing the throne.
I hope Your Majesty will not neglect this.
The law allows the public to rent and cast copper and tin into coins,
but those who dare adulterate with lead or iron for deceit
face the punishment of tattooing.
However, in the reality of coin casting,
unless one mixes lead, iron, or stones with copper deceitfully,
profit cannot be made;
and mixing them slightly
is easy to do,
no harder than adding salt to soup,
yet the profits are substantial.
Though the law openly permits casting with rented metal,
casters are bound to engage in fraud,
nominally it's rented casting under the law,
but in reality, all deserve tattooing.
With such a law,
what can the throne rely on?
Affairs can invite disaster, and laws can give rise to deceit.
Now, allowing common people to engage in counterfeiting,
each hiding in their homes to cast coins,
while trying to prohibit their substantial profits and minor frauds—
even if tattooing punishments are daily reported,
the trend will not stop;
it's the nature of the people.
To openly request it,
then officials follow and cover it up,
setting traps for the people—
who is accumulating guilt here!
If the throne does not plan early,
the people's situation will be ruined.
Previously, banning coin casting
led to accumulated death penalties;
now, public casting
leads to accumulated tattooing penalties.
Though slightly different,
it's not much better.
The people are drowning,
and will the throne not save them?
Moreover, the people's use of coins
varies by county and commandery;
some use light coins,
adding a hundred or so,
with slight differences in circulation;
some use heavy coins,
not accepted at standard weight.
Without established standard coins,
should officials urgently enforce uniformity across the land?
Then officials become oppressive and the people cannot bear it, and it's neither feasible nor enforceable;
or to be lenient and not strict?
Then commanderies and counties differ, and markets vary.
Small and large coins used differently,
coin inscriptions greatly confused.
If the method is wrong,
what can be done to achieve it!
Farming is abandoned and not done,
while copper miners increase daily;
they lay down their plows and hoes,
to smelt in furnaces with charcoal,
counterfeit coins proliferate daily,
legitimate coins diminish daily,
good people are tempted into deceit,
honest folk fall into punishments,
tattooing penalties accumulate,
officials and people will increasingly conflict.
If it slightly worsens now,
punishments and executions will be most inauspicious—
how can this be neglected!
If the state recognizes this problem,
officials will surely propose to ban it.
But if the ban is not properly implemented,
the damage will be great;
how to prevent it?
If coin casting is banned,
coins will surely become heavier;
for four coins' worth of grain,
it will revert to two coins.
Heavier coins mean greater profits,
and illegal casting will rise like clouds;
then the penalty of execution in the market will not suffice to stop it.
Deceits become uncontrollable, and legal prohibitions repeatedly fail—
it's hard to speak of,
a major issue.
Long-standing chaos without early remedy
may not reflect well on Your Majesty's wisdom.
Whenever governance fails to align with heaven and earth,
stars and planets show movements—
no small matter,
possibly affecting the royal virtue.
Your Majesty must not be negligent;
now at the beginning,
I hope for a well-planned approach.
"On Official Duties"
Some teach the Spring and Autumn Annals,
to exalt goodness and suppress evil,
thereby reforming and guiding their hearts.
They teach rites,
to make them understand the norms of hierarchy and their proper application.
Some recite the Odes for them,
broadening the Way and manifesting virtue,
to gently illuminate their aspirations.
They teach music,
to cleanse their impurities and stabilize their frivolous spirits.
They teach historical narratives,
enabling them to understand ancient times,
and know that the former kings' task was to illuminate virtue among the people.
They teach ancient records,
so they learn the reasons for rise and fall, and become cautious and vigilant.
They teach the methods of governance,
enabling them to oversee the duties of all officials,
and understand the principles of orderly rule and transformation.
They teach the instructive classics,
so they comprehend the distinctions between clan relations and intimacy,
and subtly align themselves accordingly,
this is what is called instructing the crown prince with the virtue of the sages.
Some clarify generous giving to guide them toward loyalty,
clarify enduring reciprocity to guide them toward trustworthiness,
clarify standards and measures to guide them toward righteousness,
clarify hierarchical ranks to guide them toward propriety,
clarify reverence and frugality to guide them toward filial piety,
clarify respect and caution to guide them in service,
clarify kindness and affection to guide them toward benevolence,
clarify dignity and elegance to guide them toward refinement,
clarify eliminating harm to guide them toward martial prowess,
clarify purity and integrity to guide them in judgment,
clarify correct virtue to guide them in rewards,
clarify solemnity and reverence to guide them in education,
this is what is called teaching the crown prince.
To his left and right, before and behind,
there are none but worthy men to assist and support him,
with dignified demeanor to precede and follow him,
maintaining physical decorum to guide him left and right,
establishing righteous conduct to openly support him,
manifesting respect and reverence to oversee his actions,
encouraging him through diligent effort,
nurturing filial devotion within him,
strengthening him with sincerity and steadfastness,
inspiring him with loyalty and trustworthiness,
promoting him with virtuous words,
this is what is called proper guidance.
This is the way of the tutors,
which none but the worthy can practice.
If the Son of Heaven is not conversant with the virtue of the former sages,
does not know the way to rule the state and nurture the people,
does not see the correctness of ritual and righteousness,
does not discern the principles of responding to affairs,
is not learned in the ancient classics and traditions,
is not practiced in the norms of dignified demeanor,
has not mastered the Odes, Documents, Rites, and Music,
if the Son of Heaven's studies lack proper models,
all these matters fall under the responsibility of the Grand Tutor.
In ancient times, Tài Gōng of Qí held this duty.
If the Son of Heaven shows no kindness to relatives,
no benevolence to the common people,
no courtesy to great ministers,
improper handling of punishments and lawsuits,
no proper management of the hundred officials,
no grief in mourning,
no reverence in sacrifices,
no rectitude in military affairs,
no trustworthiness with the feudal lords,
no sincerity in rewards and punishments,
no richness in virtue,
no strength in conduct,
is lavish in gifts to close attendants,
but withholding to the distant and lowly,
cannot restrain anger and control desires,
in major conduct and great rituals,
in great righteousness and the great Way,
does not follow the Grand Tutor's teachings,
all these matters fall under the responsibility of the Grand Mentor.
In ancient times, Zhōu Gōng of Lǔ held this duty.
If the Son of Heaven's posture is not upright,
his reception of instruction not respectful,
his recitation and study of the Odes, Documents, Rites, and Music not according to the classics, models, or antiquity,
his speech not orderly,
his tones and sounds not in accord with pitch,
in learning walking, yielding, advancing, and retreating,
taking his seat not according to ritual,
ascending, descending, bowing, and yielding without proper demeanor,
in looking, gazing, lowering, and raising,
moving about without rhythm,
coughing and spitting arbitrarily, frequently looking around,
unable to walk properly,
facial expression not harmonious and compliant,
careless with zithers and lutes,
all these matters fall under the responsibility of the Grand Guardian.
In ancient times, Shào Gōng of Yān held this duty.
If the Son of Heaven, in his leisure studies, reverses his learning,
those around him practice deceit against their teachers,
in replying to distant feudal lords,
or meeting noble personages,
does not know the language of the Great Odes,
in answering close attendants,
does not know the proper response to requests and promises,
in casual questions and minor recitations, is neither broad nor practiced,
all these matters fall under the responsibility of the Junior Tutor.
In ancient times, Shǐ Yì held this duty.
If the Son of Heaven's dwelling, resting, going out, and entering are not according to ritual,
his clothing, hats, and belts not according to regulation,
the vessels at his side not according to measure,
mixed colors and following beauty not serving to manifest virtue,
anger and joy not according to righteousness,
giving and criticizing not according to moderation,
in minor conduct and small rituals,
minor righteousness and small ways,
all these matters fall under the responsibility of the Junior Mentor.
If the Son of Heaven, in his private quarters and leisure,
is at ease in inappropriate places,
excessively indulgent in pleasure,
at night dismissing people to count the water clock,
drinking wine to drunkenness,
eating meat to satiety,
forcing himself to eat when full,
going hungry when starved,
suffering heatstroke in summer,
shivering with cold in winter,
sleeping without assistance,
sitting unattended,
walking without proper precedence or following,
personally opening doors and windows,
personally taking playthings,
personally holding utensils,
frequently turning his head to look back,
vessels and equipment not properly arranged or stored,
broken, destroyed, lost, or damaged,
all these matters fall under the responsibility of the Junior Guardian.
If the dances with shield-axe, dagger-axe, and feathers,
the harmonies of pipes, flutes, zithers, and lutes,
the cries, calls, songs, and ballads are not in accord with pitch,
the banquet music and court hymns,
violate the proper sequence of music,
all these matters fall under the responsibility of the Music Master.
Not knowing the untimeliness of sun and moon,
not knowing the taboos of the former kings and the great prohibitions of the state,
not knowing the portents of wind, rain, thunder, and lightning,
all these matters fall under the responsibility of the Grand Historian.
"Bǎo Fù"
The Yīn held the Son of Heaven
for over thirty generations before the Zhōu received it;
the Zhōu held the Son of Heaven
for over thirty generations before the Qín received it;
the Qín held the Son of Heaven
for only two generations before perishing.
Human nature is not vastly different,
so why did the rulers of Yīn and Zhōu possess the Way and endure long,
while Qín was without the Way and violently short-lived?
The reason can be known.
In ancient times, when the king's
heir was first born,
he was invariably raised with ritual propriety,
having scholars carry him.
Officials, solemn and dignified in ceremonial caps,
presented him at the southern suburb,
to be introduced to Heaven.
Passing through palace gates, he would descend;
passing by ancestral temples, he would quicken his steps—
such is the way of a filial son.
Thus, from infancy,
he was already taught through action.
Long ago, when King Chéng of the Zhōu dynasty was still in swaddling clothes,
Duke Shào served as Grand Guardian,
Duke of Zhōu as Grand Mentor,
and Grand Duke as Grand Preceptor.
The Guardian safeguarded his physical well-being,
the Mentor instilled moral righteousness,
the Preceptor guided him with teachings—
these were the duties of the Three Dukes.
Thereupon, three junior positions were established,
all held by high-ranking ministers:
namely,
Junior Guardian, Junior Mentor, and Junior Preceptor,
who accompanied the crown prince in his daily life.
Thus, from the age of understanding,
the Three Dukes and Three Juniors diligently instructed him in filial piety, benevolence, ritual, and righteousness through guidance and practice,
driving away corrupt individuals
to prevent him from witnessing evil deeds.
They selected upright scholars from across the land,
those filial, fraternal, erudite, and possessing moral principles,
to support and protect him,
ensuring they accompanied the prince in all his activities and movements.
Hence, from birth, the prince witnessed proper affairs,
heard proper speech,
and walked the proper path,
surrounded on all sides by righteous people.
For when one habitually dwells among the upright,
one cannot but become upright—
just as growing up in Qí,
one cannot but speak the Qí dialect;
and when one habitually dwells among the unrighteous,
one cannot but become unrighteous—
just as growing up in Chǔ,
one cannot but speak the Chǔ dialect.
Therefore, in selecting his preferences,
he must first receive instruction
before partaking in them;
in choosing his pleasures,
he must first practice them
before engaging in them.
Confucius said:
"What is formed in youth becomes like innate nature;
what is habitual becomes like second nature."
This is why the Yīn and Zhōu dynasties long remained virtuous.
When the prince grew older,
and became aware of desires,
he entered the academy.
The academy is the place of learning.
The "Rites of Learning" state:
"The emperor enters the Eastern Academy,
where reverence for kinship and honor for benevolence are emphasized,
so that distinctions between close and distant relations are ordered, and kindness extends accordingly;
the emperor enters the Southern Academy,
where respect for age and honor for trust are emphasized,
so that distinctions between elder and younger are clear, and the people do not deceive;
the emperor enters the Western Academy,
where esteem for worthiness and honor for virtue are emphasized,
so that the wise and sagacious hold office, and no merit is overlooked;
the emperor enters the Northern Academy,
where honor for nobility and respect for rank are emphasized,
so that distinctions between high and low are maintained, and subordinates do not overstep;
the emperor enters the Great Academy,
where he receives teachings from mentors and inquires about the Way,
retires to practice, and is examined by the Grand Mentor,
who penalizes his transgressions and corrects his shortcomings,
so his virtue and wisdom grow, and he masters the art of governance."
When these five studies are accomplished by the ruler above,
the common people are transformed and harmonized below.
With learning complete and governance achieved,
this is why the Yīn and Zhōu dynasties long remained virtuous.
When the prince reached capping age,
and adulthood,
free from the strict oversight of guardians and mentors,
there were historians to record his integrity,
and stewards to withdraw his meals.
If the prince erred,
the historian must record it—
for it is the historian's duty to record faults;
failing to do so meant death.
Once the fault was recorded, the steward would withhold his meal.
It was the steward's duty
to withdraw the meal;
failing to do so meant death.
Thus, there were banners for presenting good advice,
posts for posting criticisms,
and drums for daring remonstrance;
blind historians recited poetry,
artisans recited admonitions,
ministers offered counsel,
and scholars conveyed the people's words.
As habit and wisdom grew together,
he felt no shame in self-reflection;
as transformation and heart matured as one,
he followed the Middle Way as if by nature.
This is why the Yīn and Zhōu dynasties long remained virtuous.
The rites of the Three Dynasties decreed:
The Son of Heaven welcomed the sun at dawn in spring,
and bid farewell to the moon at dusk in autumn,
to demonstrate reverence;
in spring and autumn, he entered the academy,
seated the elderly of the state,
and personally served them with sauce,
to demonstrate filial piety;
his carriage moved with harmonious bells,
his walking pace matched the "Cǎi Jì,"
his hastened steps matched the "Sì Xià,"
to demonstrate measure;
toward birds and beasts,
he could not bear to see them killed after seeing them alive,
nor taste their meat after hearing their cries,
so he kept away from the kitchen,
to nurture compassion
and demonstrate benevolence.
He ate with ritual decorum,
rested with musical harmony,
and if he strayed from measure, the historian recorded it,
the artisans recited it,
the Three Dukes presented and read it,
the steward reduced his meals—
thus, the Son of Heaven was prevented from wrongdoing.
The "Positions in the Ming Hall" state:
"One who is deeply benevolent and fond of learning,
erudite and compliant with the Way—
when the Son of Heaven has doubts, he inquires of him,
and he responds without exhaustion—
is called a Guide.
The Guide guides the Son of Heaven with the Way.
He always stands before him—
this was the Duke of Zhōu.
One who is steadfast and decisive,
supporting goodness and assisting righteousness—
is called a Supporter.
The Supporter aids the Son of Heaven's intentions.
He always stands to the left—
this was the Grand Duke.
One who is pure, incorruptible, and straightforward,
rectifying errors and remonstrating against evil—
is called a Corrector.
The Corrector corrects the Son of Heaven's faults.
He always stands to the right—
this was Duke Shào.
One who is widely learned and strong in memory,
quick and adept in response—
is called a Remembrancer.
The Remembrancer recalls what the Son of Heaven has forgotten.
He always stands behind—
this was Historian Yì."
Thus, with King Chéng standing centrally to hold court,
the four sages supported him,
ensuring no plan was ill-considered
and no action mistaken.
The reason the Yīn and Zhōu endured long
was their comprehensive system of assisting the crown prince.
By the time of the Qín dynasty, this was no longer so.
Its customs did not value humility and deference;
what it promoted was accusation and exposure.
It did not value ritual and righteousness;
what it promoted was punishment and penalty.
Zhào Gāo was assigned to teach Hú Hài about law,
and what he learned was nothing but beheading, mutilation,
or extermination of three clans.
Thus, the day after ascending the throne, he was shooting people;
loyal admonishers were accused of slander,
and deep strategists were called spreaders of evil tales.
He regarded killing people as mowing grass.
Was it Hú Hài's nature that was evil?
No, it was the way he was taught and guided—
not the proper method of governance.
A common saying goes:
"If untrained in office,
look to accomplished affairs."
Another says:
"When the front carriage overturns,
the rear carriage should take warning."
The reason why the Yin and Zhou dynasties endured for so long
can be understood from their past affairs;
yet if one fails to follow them,
it is because they do not emulate the wisdom of the sages.
The reason why the Qin dynasty quickly collapsed
can be seen from its tracks;
yet if one does not avoid it,
it is like the carriage ahead overturning and the one behind about to overturn again.
The reversal of survival and demise,
the pivot of order and chaos,
their essence lies herein.
The fate of the world
hangs on the crown prince;
the goodness of the crown prince
lies in early education and the selection of attendants.
If education is imparted before the mind becomes corrupted,
then transformation is easily achieved.
To be enlightened in the ways and arts,
to understand the principles of righteousness,
is the achievement of education.
As for habituation through accumulated practice,
that depends solely on the attendants.
The people of the Hú and Yuè,
born with the same cries,
their desires no different,
yet when they grow up and form customs,
even after multiple translations they cannot understand each other,
and there are actions for which they would die rather than perform for one another—
this is due to education and habituation.
Therefore, I say that selecting attendants and early education are most urgent.
If education is proper and the attendants are upright,
then the crown prince becomes upright,
and with the crown prince upright, the world is stabilized.
The "Shū" says:
"When one man has blessings,
the myriad people rely on him."
This is the task at hand.
"Lián Yǔ"
Zhòu,
being the son of the Son of Heaven,
rightfully possessed the world,
but if he turned his back on the Way and abandoned righteousness,
discarding reverence and caution to act arrogantly and wantonly,
then the people of the world
would scatter from him like a collapse,
and turn against him unsummoned as if by appointment.
For a ruler,
how can one not be cautious?
When Zhòu was about to battle King Wǔ of Zhōu,
Zhòu arrayed his troops,
left and right flanks,
but when drums beat, they did not advance;
instead, they turned their blades
to face Zhòu.
Zhòu fled back to his ancestral temple,
fought to his death,
with none of his attendants willing to aid him.
Zhòu's palace guards and his corpse
were abandoned outside the Jade Gate,
and the observing people rushed forward to kick it,
trampling his belly,
stomping his kidneys,
crushing his lungs,
stepping on his liver.
King Wǔ of Zhōu then had someone set up a curtain to guard it,
but the observing people lifted the curtain and entered,
those carrying stones still unwilling to stop—
how lamentable!
To be in a position as the people's master
yet directly make enemies of the people,
bringing calamity and resentment to this extent,
that the people would even trample his corpse,
let alone follow his governance and teachings! How shameful!
I have privately heard it said:
"Goodness cannot be called small and without benefit,
nor badness small and without harm."
When an ox is in the womb,
it is as tiny as a shrew mouse;
Zhòu's ruin of the world began with ivory chopsticks.
Thus, minor evils and major evils are of the same kind.
Faults and failures, though small,
are all Zhòu's crimes.
A Zhōu proverb says:
"The carriage ahead overturns, warning the one behind."
Now the carriage ahead has overturned,
yet the one behind does not know to take warning—
this cannot be overlooked.
Liáng once had a doubtful legal case,
with half the ministers deeming it deserving of punishment,
and half deeming it not,
so even the King of Liáng was uncertain.
The King of Liáng said:
"Old Man Táo Zhū Gōng, though a commoner, amassed wealth rivaling a state;
he must possess extraordinary wisdom."
So he summoned Lord Zhū and asked him:
"Liáng has a doubtful case;
half the officials deem it punishable,
half not;
even I am uncertain.
Decide this for me—
what should be done?"
Lord Zhū said:
"I am a humble man,
unfamiliar with legal cases.
However,
my household has two white jades,
identical in color,
