Thus, fearing the leech would be discovered,
I swallowed it."
The Prime Minister left his mat, bowed twice, and congratulated him:
"I have heard that Heaven is not partial,
but supports only virtue.
Your Majesty possesses humane virtue,
which Heaven upholds.
This illness will not harm you."
That night,
after the king relieved himself, the leech came out,
and his chronic illness of abdominal accumulation was cured.
Thus, the sight and hearing of Heaven
cannot be said to be unperceptive.
Duke Yì of Wèi was fond of cranes;
some cranes were adorned with embroidery and rode in carriages.
He imposed heavy taxes without regard for his people,
valued entertainers over important ministers,
and if any minister remonstrated, he would rebuke them to their faces.
When the Dí tribe attacked Wèi,
and the enemy reached the city walls,
the Duke of Wèi wept and bowed to his officials and people:
"The enemy is upon us;
gentlemen and people, exert yourselves!"
The people said:
"Let Your Majesty send his valued entertainers
and lead his beloved cranes
to fight for you!
We are but discarded men—
how can we defend and fight?"
Then they broke through the gates and fled.
The Dí invaders entered,
the Duke of Wèi fled to his death,
and thus his state was lost.
Therefore, a worthy ruler
does not allow plants, trees, birds, or beasts
to harm the people.
He advances the loyal and upright and keeps away the wicked and false,
so the people submit and his ministers serve him.
To neglect the people and love birds and beasts,
to distance oneself from loyal ways and value entertainers and jesters—
this is perversion indeed!
The reason a ruler remains a ruler,
acting without failure,
is that he relies on the worthy.
Now, to betray his charge and abandon his support—
his collapse
is only fitting!
As the saying goes:
"Harm given out returns as harm;
those who hate others will be hated in turn."
Guǎnzǐ said:
"If you do not travel the wilds,
do not neglect your horse."
This is neglecting one's horse.
Duke Mù of Zōu had an order:
those feeding ducks and geese must use chaff,
daring not to use grain.
Thus, when the granary had no chaff and sought to exchange with the people,
two shí of grain for one shí of chaff,
an official petitioned:
"Feeding geese chaff
is to avoid waste,
but now seeking chaff from the people,
exchanging two shí of grain for one shí of chaff,
then feeding the geese chaff
is very wasteful.
I request to feed them grain."
The duke said:
"Away!
This is beyond your understanding!
The people feed oxen to plow,
expose their backs to weed,
laboring diligently without daring to slack—
is it for the sake of birds and beasts?
Grain is the finest food for humans;
how can we use it to feed birds?
Moreover, you know petty accounts but not the greater reckoning.
A Zhōu proverb says:
'What leaks from the bag remains in the storage.'
Have you not heard it?
The ruler is the parent of the people;
taking grain from the granary
and transferring it to the people—
is this not my grain?
If the birds eat Zōu's chaff,
it does not harm Zōu's grain.
Whether the grain is in the granary
or among the people,
what difference does it make to me?"
When the people of Zōu heard this,
they all understood that their private stores and the public stores were one and the same.
The King of Chǔ intended to corrupt the Lord of Zōu,
so he sent him four skilled musicians and beautiful women.
Lord Mù inspected them in the morning and disposed of them by evening,
giving them as wives to orphans of the deceased in service.
Thus, women whose age was inappropriate were not kept,
and he restrained himself without keeping a crowd.
The royal carriage was not covered with furs or silk,
and the imperial horses were not fed grains or beans.
There were no licentious or depraved affairs,
no arrogant or indulgent behavior.
His meals did not include a variety of flavors,
his clothes were not of mixed colors.
He disciplined himself to benefit the people,
drew close to the worthy to stabilize the state,
and treated the people as his own children.
Under the governance of Zōu,
lost items on the road were not picked up,
ministers and subordinates were obedient,
like the hand responding to the heart.
Therefore, despite Zōu's small size,
neither Lǔ nor Wèi dared to slight it,
and neither Qí nor Chǔ could intimidate it.
When Lord Mù of Zōu died,
the people of Zōu
felt as if they had lost a loving father.
They mourned for three months,
and neighbors from all borders adjacent to Zōu,
scholars and commoners faced the direction and wept on the roads,
holding hands and walking in sorrow.
Wine sellers did not sell their wine,
butchers closed their stalls and returned home,
playful children did not sing,
those pounding rice or building did not chant with their pestles.
Women removed their pearl earrings,
men set aside their jade pendants and archery gear.
Lutes and zithers made no sound.
It took a full year before things began to return to normal.
Thus, love given out returns as love,
blessings sent forth come back as blessings.
The *Yì Jīng* says:
"The calling crane is in the shade,
its young ones respond to it."
Is this not what it means?
Therefore, it is said:
"When the Son of Heaven possesses the Way,
his defense lies with the four barbarian tribes.
When the feudal lords possess the Way,
their defense lies with their neighboring states."
During the time of King Kāng of Sòng,
a sparrow gave birth to a sparrowhawk in a corner of the city wall.
He had his historian divine it,
who said:
"The small giving birth to the large
surely means you will become hegemon over the world."
King Kāng was greatly pleased.
Thereupon, he destroyed Téng, attacked the feudal lords,
and seized lands north of the Huái River.
He grew even more self-confident,
desiring swift achievement of hegemony.
Thus, he shot at the sky and whipped the earth,
attacked the altars of soil and grain and burned them,
saying:
"My majesty subdues heaven, earth, and the spirits."
He insulted the elderly ministers who remonstrated,
made caps without tops,
to display his courage.
He split the backs of hunchbacks,
cut off the shins of those who waded in the morning.
The people of the state were terrified.
The King of Qí heard of this and attacked him.
The people scattered,
and the city could not be defended.
The king then fled to the residence of the Earl of Ní,
where he fell ill and died.
Thus, seeing an auspicious omen but acting improperly,
the omen turns into disaster.
When Duke Wén of Jìn went out hunting,
his vanguard returned and reported,
"Ahead lies a great serpent,
as tall as a dike,
lying across the road."
Duke Wén said:
"Turn the chariots around and return."
His charioteer said:
"I have heard that one welcomes auspicious signs
and confronts ominous ones.
Now there is an omen ahead;
please let our followers attack it."
Duke Wén said:
"No.
I have heard it said:
If the Son of Heaven has a bad dream, he cultivates the Way;
if a feudal lord has a bad dream, he reforms his governance;
if a high minister has a bad dream, he rectifies his office;
if a commoner has a bad dream, he cultivates his person.
If this is done,
then disaster will not come.
Now I have committed faults,
and Heaven is warning me with this omen;
if I attack it,
I would be defying Heaven's mandate."
So he returned.
After fasting, he prayed in the temple, saying:
"I am indeed unworthy,
failing to honor the Way—
this is my first crime;
my administration is not virtuous,
my attendants are not good—
this is my second crime;
my governance is not diligent,
the people do not trust me—
this is my third crime;
fundamental duties are neglected,
bringing blame upon the people—
this is my fourth crime;
my fasting and reverence are not solemn,
the sacrificial grains are not pure—
this is my fifth crime.
I ask to promote the worthy and employ the capable,
to highlight virtue and practice goodness,
to guide the people,
and not repeat past errors."
Then he withdrew and reformed his governance.
After three days,
he dreamed that Heaven punished the great serpent,
saying:
"How dare you block the path of an enlightened ruler!"
Duke Wén awoke,
sent someone to check,
and the serpent had already rotted like fish.
Duke Wén was greatly pleased,
trusted in the Way and practiced it unceasingly.
Thus, he achieved hegemony.
Therefore, it is said:
Confront an omen with virtue,
and the omen turns into a blessing.
King Huái of Chǔ was arrogant and fond of loftiness,
lacking the Way yet desiring the title of hegemon and king.
He cast bronze figures in the likeness of the feudal lords and rulers,
ordering the kings of major states
to be lined up as outriders for his horse,
with the King of Liáng as his charioteer,
the King of Sòng as his attendant,
and the rulers of Zhōu, Shào, Bì, Chén, Téng, Xuē, Wèi, and Zhōngshān
all depicted as following and hastening behind.
The feudal lords heard of this
and deemed it improper,
so they raised armies to attack him.
Seeing that his soldiers and people were not diligent in service,
King Chǔ then conscripted ten thousand laborers
and even dug up the graves of the state's people.
The people heard this and were shaken,
forming groups by day and rioting by night.
The people of Qí attacked them,
and the Chǔ army collapsed.
King Huái fled to Qín,
where the magistrate of Kè killed him at Xīhé.
He became a laughingstock of the world.
This was the crime of being fond of arrogance and lacking humility.
Is it not shameful?
When Duke Huán of Qí began his hegemony,
the Dí people attacked Yān.
Duke Huán campaigned north against the Dí for Yān's sake,
reaching as far as Gūzhú.
On his return, he had the Lord of Yān restore the duties of the Duke of Shào.
As Duke Huán was returning,
the Lord of Yān escorted him,
entering Qí territory for 166 lǐ.
Duke Huán asked Guǎn Zhòng:
"According to ritual,
when feudal lords escort each other,
should they go beyond the borders?"
Guǎn Zhòng replied:
"Unless it is the Son of Heaven, one does not go beyond the borders."
Duke Huán said:
"Then the Lord of Yān, out of fear, has breached ritual.
I fear that later generations will think I preserved Yān and made it pay court to me."
So he dismounted and ordered the Lord of Yān to turn his chariot back,
then ceded the land the Lord of Yān had reached to him,
dug a ditch to mark the border, and only then departed.
The feudal lords heard of Duke Huán's righteousness,
and though they did not speak of it, in their hearts they all submitted.
Thus, when he nine times assembled the feudal lords,
none failed to delight in his virtue.
In supporting and elevating the Son of Heaven,
none failed to urge compliance.
Truly, with humility and deference,
who would not uphold him?
When Hú Hài, the Second Emperor, was still a prince,
he had several brothers.
An imperial decree set a feast for all the ministers,
summoning the princes to dine first before dismissing them.
Hú Hài descended the steps,
noticed the well-arranged shoes of the ministers,
and trampled them as he passed, leaving them ruined.
The feudal lords heard of this,
and none failed to sigh deeply.
When the Second Emperor ascended the throne,
all knew that the world had abandoned him.
When Sūn Shū Áo was an infant,
he returned from an outing,
troubled and refusing to eat.
His mother asked the reason,
and he replied tearfully:
"Today I saw a two-headed snake,
and I fear my death is imminent."
His mother said:
"Where is the snake now?"
He answered:
"I heard that whoever sees a two-headed snake dies,
but I feared others might see it too,
so I killed it and buried it."
His mother said:
"Do not worry,
you will not die.
I have heard that
those who perform hidden virtues
are rewarded with blessings by heaven."
People who heard of this
all recognized his capacity for benevolence.
When he grew up,
he became the Prime Minister of Chǔ,
and even before governing, the people trusted him.
"First Awakening"
King Huái asked Master Jiǎ:
"Why are those who understand the Way called 'Xiānshēng' (first-born)?"
Master Jiǎ replied:
"This is a broad term.
At the highest level, it refers to rulers;
at the middle, to ministers and high officials;
at the lowest, to common scholars.
But its true meaning
is not 'first-born',
but 'first awakened'.
Those rulers who do not study principles
remain silently confused about gains and losses,
unaware of the causes of order and chaos, survival and ruin,
dazed as if drunk.
But worthy rulers tirelessly pursue learning,
never weary of the Way,
and serenely take the lead in studying principles.
Thus, before governing, they know how to govern;
before chaos, they know what causes chaos;
before stability, they know how to achieve it;
before danger, they know what brings peril.
So they awaken clearly to the reasons for survival and ruin,
hence called 'first awakened',
like being the first to sober up among drunkards.
Therefore, among rulers, some are first awakened,
some later awakened,
and some never awaken.
In the past, when King Zhuāng of Chǔ ascended the throne,
he remained quiet for three years,
reflecting on gains and losses,
then dismissed the corrupt and promoted the loyal and upright,
appointing the capable to office and only later elevating them to high rank.
Internally, he governed the state, clearing obstacles to implement education,
enriching the people,
uniting them in constancy,
so that lost items were not picked up on roads,
and there were no lawsuits in the state.
At that time,
the Zhōu court was decaying and weak,
and the Son of Heaven had lost control.
Sòng and Zhèng acted without principle,
deceiving the feudal lords.
King Zhuāng besieged Sòng and attacked Zhèng.
The Earl of Zhèng bared his shoulder and led a sheep,
offering hairpins and surrendering his state.
King Zhuāng said:
'In ancient campaigns,
if there was disorder, it was rectified;
if they submitted, they were spared,
not for profit.'
Thus, he did not accept,
then fought the Jìn at Liǎngtáng,
greatly defeating them,
and assembled the feudal lords at Hànyáng,
reiterating the Son of Heaven's prohibitions,
and the feudal lords were pleased and submitted.
"In the past, when King Zhuāng of Chǔ fought the Jìn,
he achieved a great victory.
On his return, he passed through the domain of Lord Shēn,
who offered him a meal.
By midday, the king had not eaten.
Lord Shēn asked for punishment, saying:
'I fasted and prepared a very clean meal,
yet by midday you have not eaten;
I dare ask for my fault.'
King Zhuāng sighed deeply and said:
'It is not your fault.
I have heard it said:
"A ruler who is worthy and has teachers will become king;
a middling ruler with teachers will become hegemon;
a inferior ruler whose ministers are no better than he will perish."
Now I am an inferior ruler,
and my ministers are no better than I,
so I fear we are doomed to perish.
I have heard:
the world never lacks sages,
a state never lacks worthies,
yet all under heaven has worthies, and I alone cannot obtain them.
How can I eat, being as I am!'
Thus, King Zhuāng, having militarily subdued great states
and righteously led the feudal lords,
remained deeply worried and fearful,
feeling that sage wisdom was not in him,
regretting his own inadequacy,
and longing for worthy aides,
forgetting to eat by midday.
He can be called a wise ruler.
This is what it means to first awaken to the reasons for survival and ruin,
the 'first awakened'.
"In the past, Duke Zhāo of Sòng fled into exile and reached the border,
where he sighed deeply and said:
'Alas!
Now I understand the reasons for survival and ruin.
When I stood robed in finery,
attended by hundreds of servants,
none failed to say, "Our lord is magnificent."
When I spoke and acted,
with hundreds of court ministers,
none failed to call me sage.
I heard no faults of mine, inside or out,
and thus I have come to this.
My plight is fitting.'
Thereupon, he reformed his heart and changed his conduct,
wore coarse cloth,
ate simple food,
studied the Way by day and discussed it by night.
Within two years, his virtue was renowned in Sòng,
and the people of Sòng brought chariots to welcome him back to the throne.
He ended as a worthy ruler,
posthumously titled Duke Zhāo.
Having been ruined,
he then awakened
to the reasons for survival and ruin.
This is the 'later awakened'."
"In the past, the Lord of Guó was arrogant and self-aggrandizing,
flatterers and sycophants were held dear and honored,
ministers who remonstrated were interrogated and exiled,
governance was chaotic and disordered,
the people of the state were discontent,
the army of Jìn attacked it,
the people of Guó did not defend,
the Lord of Guó fled,
reaching the marshes,
and said:
'I am thirsty and wish to drink.'
His charioteer then offered clear wine,
and he said:
'I am hungry and wish to eat.'
The charioteer presented dried meat and millet provisions,
the Lord of Guó joyfully said:
'How is it so provided?'
The charioteer said:
'I have stored it for a long time.'
He said:
'For what reason did you store it?'
In reply, he said:
'For the time when you, my lord, would flee and suffer hunger and thirst on the road.'
The lord said:
'You knew I would flee?'
He replied:
'I knew.'
He said:
'Since you knew,
why did you not remonstrate?'
In reply, he said:
'You, my lord, favored flattery and detested forthright words;
I wished to remonstrate,
but feared I would perish before Guó fell.'
The Lord of Guó changed countenance and grew angry,
the charioteer apologized, saying:
'My words were mistaken.'
After a while,
the lord said:
'The reason for my downfall,
what truly was it?'
His charioteer said:
'Do you not know, my lord?
The reason for your downfall
is because of your great worthiness.'
The Lord of Guó said:
'Worthiness is what ensures survival;
yet I perished—
why is that?'
In reply, he said:
'All the lords under heaven are unworthy;
they resented that you alone were worthy,
hence you fell.'
The Lord of Guó was pleased,
leaning on the chariot rail, he laughed and said:
'Alas!
Is worthiness truly so bitter?'
Then he went on foot and dwelt in the mountains,
hungry and weary,
he lay down with his head on the charioteer's knee,
the charioteer used a clod of earth to substitute and slipped away,
the lord then starved to death,
and was eaten by birds and beasts.
This one had already perished,
yet still did not realize the causes of survival and downfall,
this is one who never awakens.
Thus, those who awaken early
become hegemons in their time;
those who awaken later
recover after three years;
those who never awaken
die with their head on the soil,
devoured by tigers and wolves.
Alas!
Take warning from this!"
"Ěr Bì"
I have heard it said:
To see what is right but speak falsely brings harm,
To proclaim good fortune for the people of Cuò yet bring calamity leads to ruin;
To betray the Way brings death,
To obstruct light ensures failure in darkness;
To act without divine sanction and defy humanity,
Then Heaven will surely ruin such endeavors.
Thus, in the past, King Píng of Chǔ had a minister named Wǔ Zǐxū,
The king killed his father unjustly,
So he fled to Wú,
Saying:
"If my father dies and I do not die,
Then I am no true son of my father;
But to die without achieving anything,
Would be a miscalculation;
Rather than die with him without making things clear,
It is better to achieve fame throughout heaven and earth."
Thereupon, he restrained himself and did not act rashly,
Going to Hé Lǘ,
He cooked flavors to gain closeness,
Hé Lǘ saw him and was put at ease,
Delighted by his strategies,
Supported his actions,
Admired his virtue,
Employed him to administer the governance of Wú,
The people preserved their lives without loss,
Harvests were abundant without calamity,
The five officials were just and not selfish,
Upper and lower ranks were harmonious without grievance,
All under heaven submitted and were governed,
The four borders were tranquil and without trouble.
Then, with a heart full of wrath, he unleashed his anger,
Uttering fierce words,
Secretly resolved to lead the state to attack Chǔ,
Five battles and five victories,
Corpses lay piled by the hundreds of thousands,
Breached the gates of Yǐng,
Seized high weapons,
Injured the vital organs of the state,
Smashed the ten-dragon bells,
Whipped the tomb of King Píng.
King Zhāo lost his state and fled,
His wife was captured alive and taken to Wú,
Thus, King Píng of Chǔ, harboring hidden malice,
Killing the innocent,
Brought calamity to this extent.
Zǐxū, venting his pent-up rage,
Assisted Hé Lǘ in carrying out great cruelty,
After fifteen years,
Hé Lǘ died and Fūchāi ascended the throne,
Who then fought the Yuè people by the river,
Forcing them to take refuge on Kuàijī Mountain,
The King of Yuè in dire straits,
To the point of eating mountain grass,
Drinking putrid water,
Exchanging children to eat,
Thereupon, treading on tiles and wearing jade discs,
Crying out, proclaiming his innocence,
Calling upon the August Heaven,
Sent his minister Wén Zhǒng to seek peace with the King of Wú,
The King of Wú was about to agree,
But Zǐxū said:
"It cannot be.
The customs of Yuè,
They toil without resentment,
Favor chaos and victory over propriety,
Cunning and quick to betray,
Prone to curses and breaking alliances,
Those of this kind,
Are like the companions of birds and beasts,
The vile sort of foxes.
To let them live is to invite trouble,
To kill them incurs no blame,
I beg you not to make peace."
Minister Zhǒng beat his chest and wailed,
Washing his face with tears, he spoke of sincerity,
Sacrificed a white horse as offering,
Pointed to the nine heavens as witness,
Offered women as concubines,
Men as servants,
Precious treasures for generations,
Storing them in official warehouses,
Himself becoming a vassal within the passes,
Loyal for generations.
The King of Wú could not bear it,
Withdrew his troops and made peace,
Then turned his plans to attack Qí,
Zǐxū remonstrated but was not heeded,
His loyal words went unused.
Once Yuè achieved peace,
They praised goodness and accumulated virtue,
To win the people's hearts,
Thereupon, Heaven sent down disaster,
Ending Wú's fate at the Zhí River,
Ruler and minister turned discordant and uncoordinated,
The altars of state were shattered and divided,
Ceremonial towers and pavilions lay in ruins,
Dogs howled in packs and plunged into the abyss,
Pigs carried offerings to the inner chambers,
Swallows and sparrows were cut open, and venomous snakes were born,
They ate pickles and leeches appeared,
Bathing in clear water, they encountered scorpions,
Wǔ Zǐxū, seeing that nothing could be done,
Tied a weight and threw himself into the water,
His eyes gouged out, gazing toward the east gate,
His body placed in a leather sack and floated down the river,
Harboring malice, acting cruelly,
Seeking deep revenge and harming the innocent,
Disaster reached him personally.
Yuè then indeed plotted treachery and broke the treaty,
Attacking and defeating Fūchāi,
Annexing Wú and taking control,
Their task accomplished, their achievement complete,
Fàn Lǐ carried a stone and leaped into the Five Lakes,
Minister Zhǒng hung himself in his chamber of apology,
Qú Rú was torn apart by chariots at Huí Quán.
After this,
Gōu Jiàn found no joy,
Sorrow and grief repeatedly came,
He collapsed internally and died,
Thus, the punishments of Heaven cannot be withstood,
In vast emptiness and secluded spaces,
Remote and devoid of people,
Even if hidden deep within stone,
Heaven will surely know.
If punishments follow the principle and guilt is just,
Killing three armies incurs no blame,
But punishing and killing the innocent,
Slaying a single common man,
His crime will be heard by the August Heaven,
Hence it is said:
Heaven resides on high,
Yet its hearing is low,
Its governance is subtle,
Its vision is keen,
Therefore, in all actions, one must be cautious.
"On Sincerity"
Tāng saw a net-setter spreading his net on all four sides,
Who prayed:
"From the heavens descending,
From the earth emerging,
From the four directions arriving,
All fall into my net."
Tāng said:
"Alas!
That is exhaustive indeed,
Who but a Jié could be like this?"
He ordered three sides removed, leaving one,
And taught him to pray:
"The spider spins its web,
Now men follow its example,
Those wishing to go left, go left,
Those wishing to go right, go right,
Those wishing to rise high, rise high,
Those wishing to descend low, descend low,
I only take those who defy fate."
The scholars and people heard this,
Saying:
"Tāng's virtue extends even to birds and beasts,
How much more to us?"
Thereupon, the people cherished their ruler.
King Zhāo of Chǔ stood in his chamber,
Looking sorrowful with a chill expression,
Saying:
"In this morning of famine,
I have two vessels of wine,
Stand in heavy furs,
Yet still feel a biting cold,
What then of my countless common people?"
That very day,
He distributed furs from the treasury to clothe the cold,
And grain from the granaries to relieve the hungry.
Two years later,
When Hé Lǘ attacked Yǐng,
King Zhāo fled to Suí,
Those who had received the chamber-bestowed gifts,
Requested to return and fight the invaders to the death,
Hé Lǘ had to change his sleeping place five times in one night,
Unable to secure Chǔ,
He withdrew his army and left,
King Zhāo thus returned,
All due to the virtue of the chamber gifts.
Long ago, King Zhāo of Chǔ battled the men of Wú.
The Chǔ army was defeated,
and King Zhāo fled.
His shoe strap broke, and he lost it while walking.
After walking thirty paces,
he turned back to retrieve the shoe.
When he reached Suí,
his attendants asked him:
"Why did Your Majesty bother to spare a single broken shoe?"
King Zhāo replied:
"Although Chǔ is poor,
how could I possibly begrudge just one broken shoe?
I thought of returning together with it."
From this time onward,
it became a custom in Chǔ
that no one would abandon another.
King Wén was lying down by day
when he dreamed of a man climbing the city wall and calling to him:
"I am the dried bones from the northeastern corner.
Bury me quickly with royal rites."
King Wén said:
"So be it."
Upon awakening,
he summoned his officials to investigate,
and indeed it was so.
King Wén said:
"Bury him quickly with the rites due a ruler."
The officials said:
"These bones have no master.
We request to use the rites for a senior official."
King Wén said:
"I have already promised him in my dream.
How can I go back on my word?"
When the officers and people heard this, they said:
"Our lord does not break his promise to dried bones because it was only a dream,
how much more so towards living people?"
Thus, those below trusted their superiors.
Yǜ Ràng served the lord of Zhōngháng.
When Earl Zhì destroyed the Zhōngháng clan,
Yǜ Ràng went to serve Earl Zhì.
After Lord Xiāngzǐ of Zhào defeated Earl Zhì,
Yǜ Ràng slashed his face to alter his appearance,
swallowed charcoal to make himself hoarse.
He begged at his wife's place, yet his wife did not recognize him.
Then he lay in ambush to assassinate Xiāngzǐ,
making five attempts but failing each time.
Xiāngzǐ grew troubled by this,
could not savor his food,
changed his sleeping place three times in one night,
and felt he could not preserve his life.
Someone said to Yǜ Ràng:
"You did not die for Zhōngháng but instead served his enemy.
How utterly shameless!
Now you insist on crushing your body and grinding your bones for Earl Zhì.
Why is this so different from before?"
Yǜ Ràng replied:
"When I served the lord of Zhōngháng,
he gave me curtains for clothing,
and a gate bar for a pillow.
Since he treated me as an ordinary man,
I therefore served him as an ordinary man would.
But with Earl Zhì,
he shared his garments with me,
fed me from the tripod's contents,
and raised his quilt in courtesy.
Thus, he treated me as a state scholar,
and I therefore repay him as a state scholar would.
Hence the saying:
'A man will die for one who knows his worth,
a woman will adorn herself for one who delights in her.'
This is no idle talk.
It all lies in how the master treats one."
"Yielding and Concession"
There was a senior official of Liáng named Jiǜ Sòng
who served as a county magistrate on the border,
neighboring Chǔ.
The border stations of both Liáng and Chǔ grew melons,
each having a certain number.
The Liáng border station worked diligently and frequently watered their melons,
so the melons were fine.
The Chǔ people were lazy and seldom watered their melons,
so the melons were poor.
The Chǔ magistrate, because of the fineness of Liáng's melons,
was angered by the poor state of his station's melons.
The Chǔ station people resented that Liáng's station outdid them,
so they went at night to secretly trample Liáng's melons,
leaving many withered and dead.
The Liáng station discovered this
and requested their captain,
wishing also to sneak over and retaliate by trampling Chǔ's melons.
The captain reported this to Jiǜ Sòng,
who said:
"Alas,
how can this be?
This is the way to foster enmity and invite disaster.
If others do wrong, and we do wrong too,
how narrow-minded that would be!
If I may advise you,
have men go every night without fail,
secretly watering the Chǔ station's melons well at night,
and do not let it be known."
Thereupon,
the Liáng station each night secretly watered the Chǔ station's melons.
When the Chǔ station people went to tend their melons in the morning,
they found them all already watered.
Their melons grew finer day by day.
The Chǔ station found it strange and investigated,
discovering it was the Liáng station.
The Chǔ magistrate heard of this and was greatly pleased,
reporting it fully to the King of Chǔ.
The King of Chǔ, upon hearing it,
felt deeply ashamed and reproached himself in his heart.
He told his officials:
"Apart from the melon-trampling, do they have any other offenses?"
Praising Liáng's covert concession,
he sent apologies with generous gifts
and sought friendship with the King of Liáng.
The King of Chǔ often spoke of the King of Liáng as trustworthy,
so the amity between Liáng and Chǔ began with Jiǜ Sòng.
As the saying goes:
"Turn defeat into achievement,
and misfortune into blessing."
Lǎozǐ said:
"Requite enmity with virtue."
This is what it means.
If others act unkindly,
why should one imitate them?
The King of Dí sent an envoy to Chǔ.
The King of Chǔ wanted to boast to the envoy about the Zhānghuā Tower,
which was exceedingly high,
requiring three rests to reach its top.
The King of Chǔ said:
"Does the state of Dí also have such a tower?"
The envoy replied:
"No.
Dí is a humble state;
how could it have such a tower?
When the King of Dí built his own palace,
the hall was only three chǐ high,
the earthen steps three layers,
the thatch left untrimmed,
the wooden rafters unplaned.
Moreover, the King of Dí still thought that building it was too toilsome,
and living in it too indulgent.
How could the state of Dí have such a tower?"
The King of Chǔ felt ashamed.
"The Way of the Ruler"
King Zhòu made thousands of shackles,
glaring at feudal lords who did not flatter him,
he caned and shackled them.
King Wén was imprisoned in Yǒulǐ with fetters,
and was only released after seven years.
When King Wǔ conquered the Yīn dynasty,
after establishing order,
he ordered the people of Yīn to cast off their shackles into the river.
Those delivering the shackles
removed them with their hands,
not daring to drop them,
knelt to place them in the water,
not daring to throw them.
They said:
"Long ago, King Wén often bore these."
Thus, out of love and remembrance for King Wén,
they still revered his shackles,
how much more so his laws and teachings?
The Book of Songs says:
"With many accomplished scholars,
King Wén found peace."
This means that with the support of worthy and upright men,
one's person is sure to be secure.
It also says:
"Unknowing, unperceiving,
they follow the rules of God."
This means that when the officers and people delight in his virtue and righteousness,
they emulate and imitate him.
Where King Wén's will was directed,
and his intentions desired,
the common people did not begrudge their lives,
nor fear their toil,
following him like a gathering crowd.
The Book of Songs says:
"When he planned the Spirit Tower,
the common people worked on it.
In no time they completed it.
When he planned, he did not rush them,
the common people came like sons."
King Wén had the will to build a tower,
and ordered its nearby planning.
When the people heard of it, they came in crowds,
asking for tasks and working on it,
growing more numerous each day.
Thus, without urging, they hastened;
without a set deadline, they completed it.
They named the tower "Spirit Tower,"
named the garden "Spirit Garden,"
called the pond "Spirit Pond,"
such was the extremity of their love and reverence.
The Book of Songs says:
"The king was in the Spirit Garden,
the doe deer lay about.
The doe deer were sleek,
the white birds glistening.
The king was at the Spirit Pond,
how the fish leapt!"
King Wén's beneficence
extended down to the birds and beasts,
reaching the fish and turtles.
Thus, birds, beasts, fish, and turtles all found joy,
how much more so the officers and people?
The Book of Songs says:
"A joyous and courteous gentleman,
is the parent of the people."
This speaks of the virtue of a sage king.
The Book of Changes says:
"A calling crane in the shade,
its young ones answer it."
This speaks of the response of the officers and people.
The Book of Documents says:
"The great Way is profound,
it is not far from oneself."
All people possess it,
but Shǔn alone used it.
He who shoots and misses
does not blame the target,
but instead cultivates himself.
He who rules a state and cares for the people,
turning to seek within himself,
then the way of rulership is complete.
"On Appointing Officials"
A king appoints officials in six grades:
first, the Teacher;
second, the Friend;
third, the High Minister;
fourth, the Attendants;
fifth, the Servants;
sixth, the Menials.
One whose wisdom is sufficient to be a fountainhead,
whose conduct is sufficient to be a model,
who responds when asked,
and provides when sought,
entering a man's house,
can dignify that house;
entering a man's state,
can dignify that state—
such a one is called a Teacher.
One whose wisdom is sufficient for refinement,
whose conduct is sufficient for support,
whose benevolence is sufficient for consultation,
who is clear-sighted in advancing the worthy,
and bold in dismissing the unworthy,
internally rectifying and correcting,
externally promoting and praising—
such a one is called a Friend.
One whose wisdom is sufficient to plan state affairs,
whose conduct is sufficient to lead the people,
whose benevolence is sufficient to harmonize the joy of high and low,
who upholds the state's laws when retired,
and advances to die for the ruler in difficulty,
guarding his duties,
not used by the ruler for selfish favors—
such a one is a High Minister.
One who cultivates his person and corrects his conduct,
not ashamed in the local villages,
whose speech and discourse,
are not ashamed in the court,
whose wisdom and ability are not hindered in affairs,
who, sent as a single envoy,
can bring joy to two rulers,
holding a halberd before the ruler,
can point out the ruler's faults and errors,
not hesitating to uphold this even unto death—
such a one is an Attendant.
One who is not greedy for wealth,
not lustful for beauty,
serves the ruler without a second thought,
stays by the ruler's side without leaking his plans,
and when the ruler has faults or errors,
though unable to remonstrate directly, upholds with his life,
looking haggard and worried,
yet not urging compliance—
such a one is a Servant.
One with a soft countenance and stooped posture,
engaging only in flattery,
listening only to words,
serving the ruler for trivial reasons—
such a one is a Menial.
Thus, he who rules the state with Teachers becomes an Emperor;
he who rules with Friends becomes a King;
he who rules with High Ministers becomes a Hegemon;
he who rules with Attendants becomes strong;
he who rules with Servants may survive or perish;
he who rules with Menials—
his ruin can be expected immediately.
The ritual for obtaining a Teacher:
abdicate one's position and court him;
for obtaining a Friend:
personally take the lead;
for obtaining a High Minister:
offer skins and silk first;
for obtaining Attendants:
send messengers first;
for obtaining Servants:
issue an order for their arrival;
for obtaining Menials:
issue a summons.
When a Teacher arrives, clear the court at dawn and attend him,
not bringing forth minor matters;
when a Friend arrives, clear the hall and attend him,
not allowing performers of music and skills to appear together;
when High Ministers present affairs,
then actors and dwarfs withdraw and hide,
performers of music and skills do not perform together;
when Attendants are at the side,
music is not seen;
when Servants are at the side,
sons and daughters do not mingle;
thus, if the ruler enjoys elegant music,
then Friends and High Ministers may attend;
if the ruler enjoys banquet music,
then Attendants and Servants may attend.
If the ruler opens the north room for the music of fragrant garments,
then Menials follow, hearing governance from early morning,
discussing after court is dismissed,
leisurely enjoying moistening feasts,
and in the evening, opening the north room for the music of fragrant garments.
Thus, in hearing governance and discussions,
leisurely moistening feasts,
dignity and solemnity are all differently ordered,
after which the enterprise of emperor and king can be carried out.
"Exhortation to Learning"
He said to his disciples and learners:
"What kind of person was Shùn?
What kind of person am I?"
Now in opening ears and eyes,
carrying thoughts and intentions,
standing upright and moving about,
we share the same nature,
yet Shùn alone possessed the reputation of worthiness and sageliness,
manifesting the substance of a noble gentleman,
while I have not even gained the recognition of my neighbors or the wisdom of broad understanding -
why is this so?
It must be that Shùn exerted himself diligently with focused will,
while I have been negligent and unreflective!
If even the beautiful Xī Shī were covered in filth,
passersby would all avert their gaze and cover their noses.
But if she were adorned with powder and mascara,
wearing elegant hairpins and slanted combs,
adorned with fragrant zhǐ and ruò herbs,
with eyes like those viewing tiny insects,
enhancing her smiling lips,
displaying charming postures and graceful demeanor,
composed in her conversation,
then even kings and nobles
would all feel delighted and captivated in their hearts,
eager to catch a glimpse of her.
Now with your abilities,
if you remain clouded by foolish and confused wisdom,
I fear passersby will show the expression of covering their noses.
In ancient times, Nánróng Zhū,
ashamed of forgetting the sagely way within himself,
traveled across mountains and rivers,
braving thorns and brambles,
journeying over a thousand lǐ with calloused feet, not daring to rest long,
until he met Lǎo Dān.
Trembling as before a compassionate father,
he walked like geese in formation avoiding shadows,
standing cautiously like the kuí and advancing like a snake,
only then daring to ask his questions.
When he received one profound teaching,
it was like obtaining a grand feast after ten days of hunger,
so illuminating as heaven and earth,
inspiring later generations.
Now my master's enlightenment
surpasses even Lǎo Dān,
while your talents
do not exceed Nánróng Zhū's,
yet you suffer no thousand-lǐ journey nor hardship of calloused feet,
personally sitting alongside a great sage on connected mats,
facing each other knee to knee,
conversing comfortably,
with no question unanswered -
this is heaven sending great destiny to enlighten our virtue.
I have heard it said:
Opportunity is hard to gain but easy to lose.
Let learners strive diligently!
Heaven's favor does not come twice.
The "Art of the Dào"
says:
"I have frequently heard the name of the Dào,
but do not yet know its reality.
May I ask what is meant by the Dào?"
The reply was:
"The Dào is that by which one connects with things.
Its root is called emptiness,
its branches are called methods.
Emptiness refers to its subtle essence,
plain and without artificial contrivance;
methods
are what follow to regulate things,
the principles of movement and stillness -
all these constitute the Dào."
The question:
"May I ask how emptiness connects with things?"
The reply:
"Like a mirror properly positioned,
holding nothing yet concealing nothing,
beauty and ugliness all arrive,
each finding its proper place.
Like a balanced scale without bias,
calmly situated,
light and heavy all suspended,
each finding its appropriate position.
The enlightened ruler,
facing south and rectifying,
clear and empty while tranquil,
lets names define themselves,
things settle themselves,
responding like a mirror,
weighing like a scale.
Where there are gaps, harmonize them;
where there are beginnings, follow them.
Things reach their extremes,
and one applies what is appropriate.
This is how emptiness connects with things."
The question:
"May I ask how methods connect with things?"
The reply:
"When the ruler is benevolent, the realm becomes harmonious,
therefore his officers and people all feel affection;
when the ruler is righteous, the realm becomes orderly,
therefore his officers and people all feel compliant;
when the ruler is courteous, the realm becomes respectful,
therefore his officers and people all feel reverent;
when the ruler is trustworthy, the realm becomes upright,
therefore his officers and people all feel faithful;
when the ruler is impartial, the realm becomes submissive,
therefore his officers and people all feel supportive;
when the ruler follows laws, the realm becomes regulated,
therefore his officers and people all feel assisting.
Promoting the worthy transforms people toward goodness,
employing the capable ensures official positions are well-managed,
having talented people in office makes the ruler respected,
having competent assistants makes the people distinguished,
maintaining virtue steadfastly establishes authority,
teaching obedience consistently ensures orders are followed,
listening comprehensively prevents being misled,
verifying evidence prevents confusion,
clarifying preferences and aversions transforms people's hearts,
keeping matters confidential makes the ruler divine.
Methods are the pathways for connecting with things.
Generally, those with weighty authority must be careful in affairs,
those whose orders are followed must be careful in speech,
then errors and failures will be few.
This is the way methods connect with things.
Their source never exhausts,
their adaptation to change has no limit,
therefore the sages honor them.
The details of the Dào
cannot be fully recounted."
