"Liù Shù"
Virtue has six principles:
What are these six principles?
Dào, dé, xìng, shén, míng, mìng.
These six
are the principles of virtue.
Without the six principles,
nothing is born;
once born, the six principles exist within that which is born.
Therefore, yīn and yáng, heaven and earth,
and humans all take the six principles as their internal measure.
The internal measure accomplishes tasks,
hence they are called the six standards.
The six standards are stored within,
transform and flow outward to achieve expression,
and this outward expression through six methods
is called the six practices.
Thus, yīn and yáng each have six-month cycles,
heaven and earth have the affairs of the six directions,
and humans have the practices of rén, yì, lǐ, zhì, shèng.
When practices are harmonious, there is music;
correlating with music makes six,
this is what is meant by the six practices.
The movements of yīn, yáng, heaven, and earth
do not lose the six practices,
thus they can accord with the six standards.
If humans carefully cultivate the six practices,
then they too can accord with the six standards.
However, although humans possess the six practices,
they are subtle and difficult to recognize.
Only the former kings were able to discern them,
ordinary people cannot know them by themselves,
therefore they must await the instruction of the former kings
to know what to engage in.
Thus, the former kings established teachings for the world,
based on what people possess,
using it as instruction,
guiding human emotions,
using it as truth.
Therefore, internally rooted in the six standards,
externally embodying the six practices,
together with the six arts of the Shū, Shī, Yì, Chūnqiū, Lǐ, and Yuè,
they form the great meaning,
called the six arts.
They cause people to follow them for self-cultivation;
when cultivation is accomplished, one attains the six practices.
If the six practices are not correct,
they conversely accord with the six standards.
The reason the arts are six
is because they emulate the six standards and embody the six practices.
Hence it is said: with six, completeness is achieved.
These six are not solely the basis for the six arts;
other affairs also use six as the measure.
The way of sound takes six as primary,
using the cycles of yīn and yáng as the measure.
Therefore, one year has twelve months,
divided into yīn and yáng,
each having six months.
Thus, there are twelve bells for sound instruments,
each bell corresponding to one month,
six bells for yīn sounds,
six bells for yáng sounds.
The method of sound and pitch arises from this,
hence it is called the six pitch standards.
The six pitch standards harmonize with the tuning of the five notes,
to emit the clear sounds of yīn, yáng, heaven, earth, and humans,
and internally accord with the way of the six practices and six standards.
Therefore, the five notes gōng, shāng, jué, zhǐ, yǔ,
when sung in harmony respond to each other and become tuned.
When tuned and forming principle, it is called music.
The notes are five,
but must be completed with six,
hence it is said that notes and music make six.
That which standardizes them
is like measuring them;
what is measured is six,
hence called the six pitch standards.
Human kinship
uses six as the model.
Humans have six relations,
the first of the six relations is called father;
a father has two sons,
the two sons are brothers;
brothers again have sons,
the sons follow the father and are brothers,
hence called paternal cousins;
paternal cousins again have sons,
the sons follow the grandfather and are brothers,
hence called grandpaternal cousins;
grandpaternal cousins again have sons,
the sons follow the great-grandfather and are brothers,
hence called great-grandpaternal cousins;
great-grandpaternal cousins again have sons,
the sons are clan brothers,
completing the six,
this is what is meant by the six relations.
Kinship begins with one person,
generations separate,
dividing into six relations.
If kinship relations are not six,
then the measure of root and branch is lost,
therefore it stops at the system of six.
The six relations have an order,
they cannot overstep each other.
If they overstep, the clan becomes disordered,
unable to be close.
Therefore, the former kings established the three temples of zhāo, mù,
to prevent such disorder.
What are the three temples?
The upper chamber is zhāo,
the middle chamber is mù,
the lower chamber is for grandsons and heirs.
Each has its order,
upper and lower alternate positions.
The three temples distinguish,
closeness and distance have regulations.
Mourning garments correspond to closeness and distance to determine heaviness and lightness.
For close relations, heavy;
for distant relations, light.
Thus, there are again cūshuāi, zīshuāi, dàhóng, xìhóng, sīmá,
completing six,
each wearing what is appropriate.
The garments differ,
this is how the former kings prevent disorder.
The way of numerical measures
uses six as the standard.
Numbers increase from the small, and measures emerge from the minute.
The beginning of numerical measures
starts from the tiny.
Among tangible things,
nothing is finer than a hair,
therefore a single hair is established as the start of measure.
Ten hairs make a fà,
ten fà make a lí,
ten lí make a fēn,
ten fēn make a cùn,
ten cùn make a chǐ,
completing with six,
hence the former kings used it for all affairs under heaven.
Affairs that use six as the standard
are innumerable.
What is discussed here as six
demonstrates that affairs entirely use six as the measure, called the six principles.
It can be called the six nodes of yīn and yáng,
can be called the six standards of heaven and earth,
can be called the six practices of humans.
"Explanation of Dào and Dé"
Virtue encompasses six principles.
What are these six principles?
They are: Dào, Dé, Xìng, Shén, Míng, and Mìng.
These six
are the principles of Dé.
All living things
are born from what Dé generates,
yet only jade can symbolize human virtue.
Observing the substance of Dé's six principles,
they are fully manifested in jade, each having its own form. Therefore, jade is used to emulate the six principles of Dé.
That which is lustrous and reflective is called Dào;
that which is glossy like stealthily applied fat is called Dé;
deep, moist, thick, and adhesive is called Xìng;
tranquil like flowing water is called Shén;
brilliant and radiant is called Míng;
firm and solid is called Mìng.
These are what are called the six principles.
Reflectiveness generates hollow apertures,
and connects them through Dào.
Dé generates principles,
and connects them through the complete, distinct manifestations of the six virtues.
The six attainments
refer to Dé having six principles,
principles with distinct manifestations.
Xìng generates Qì and connects it through understanding;
Shén generates change and connects it through transformation;
Míng generates perception and connects it through knowledge;
Mìng generates form and connects it through stability.
Dé possesses six excellences.
What are the six excellences?
They are: possessing Dào, possessing Rén, possessing Yì, possessing Zhōng, possessing Xìn, and possessing Mì.
These six
are the excellences of Dé.
Dào is the foundation of Dé;
Rén is the expression of Dé;
Yì is the order of Dé;
Zhōng is the substantiality of Dé;
Xìn is the steadfastness of Dé;
Mì is the loftiness of Dé.
The six principles and six excellences
are how Dé generates Yīn-Yáng, heaven and earth, humanity, and the myriad things.
Thus, they serve as the model for all that is generated.
Therefore it is said:
To embody this is called Dào,
to possess this is called Dé,
to practice this is called conduct.
What is called practicing this
is Dé.
Therefore, inscribing this on bamboo and silk is called the Shū;
the Shū is that which records this;
the Shī is that which expresses the intent of this;
the Yì is that which divines this;
the Chūnqiū is that which chronicles this;
the Lǐ is that which embodies this;
the Yuè is that which brings joy through this.
Sacrificing to the ghosts and spirits
is done to seek blessings from this.
Broad learning and skilled debate
are the means of articulating this.
Dào is formless,
tranquil and spiritual.
Dào, as that which carries things,
causes all things to follow principle, harmony, and appropriate action.
Therefore, things possess clarity and luster.
Luster is reflectiveness;
reflectiveness relies on the spirituality of Dào.
It molds and penetrates the forms of things,
reaching through hollow apertures,
holding unity of inflow and outflow as primary.
Therefore it is called reflectiveness.
Reflectiveness is that which enables capability;
seeing belongs to the eye.
The Dào and Dé bestow upon things essence and subtlety, manifesting as the eye.
Therefore, when a thing first takes form,
the division forming the eye comes first.
Once the eye is formed, the body follows.
Thus, in humans and other beings existing through Qì,
nothing is more essential than the eye.
The eye, being clear and moistly lustrous as if soaked,
free from coarse impurities,
is thus able to see.
From this perspective,
the eye is sufficient to illuminate the moist luster of Dào and Dé.
Therefore it is said: Luster
is reflectiveness;
it generates hollow apertures,
connecting them through Dào.
Dé separates from non-being to enter being.
Thus, through moistening, it takes shape turbidly and firmly.
Hence, the six principles emerge.
The six principles are what bring about change and generation.
What is generated possesses principle,
and thus things receive moisture to live.
Therefore, it is called moistening Dé.
Dé is the source from which change and the principles of things emerge.
What is unchanged
is the manifestation of Dào.
Dao congeals to become Dé,
and Shén is carried within Dé.
Dé is the luster of Dào.
Although Dào is spiritual, it must be carried by Dé,
and its manifestation must have a basis
to initiate movement, transformation, and thus change.
Change and the principles of all living things
are all transformations of Dào.
Each has its own orderly principle, carried by Dé.
Dé receives the transformation of Dào
and manifests it in various distinct forms.
Dé moistens;
therefore it is said:
Like fat,
it is called Dé.
Dé generates principles,
connecting them through the complete, distinct manifestations of the six virtues.
Xìng is when Dào and Dé create things.
Things have form,
and the spiritual essence of Dào and Dé concentrates to become a unified Qì,
making its moistening and enriching effect even thicker.
Turbid and adhesive, interconnected,
residing within things,
it is what enables things to live.
Qì gathers there entirely.
Therefore, it is called Xìng.
Xìng is where Shén and Qì converge.
Once Xìng is established,
then Shén and Qì, bright and active, issue forth and circulate externally,
responding to stimuli from external things.
Therefore it is said:
Moist, thick, and adhesive is called Xìng.
Xìng generates Qì,
connecting it through understanding.
Shén is the Shén-Qì of Dào and Dé issuing forth from Xìng.
Tranquil like flowing music,
it cannot be fully represented by physical forms.
In transformation, there is nothing it does not do.
The principles of things and the arising of all changes
are all transformations of Shén.
Therefore it is said:
Tranquil like flowing music is called Shén.
Principle generates change,
connecting it through transformation.
Míng is when Shén-Qì is internal, there is no external radiance, yet there is awareness.
When it is Míng, then there is brilliance shining outwardly.
The external and internal communicate as one,
then distinctions of gain and loss,
the right and wrong of affairs and principles,
all fall under the purview of awareness.
Therefore it is said:
Brilliance and radiance are called Míng.
Míng generates consciousness,
connecting it through knowledge.
Mìng means that all things receive the bestowal of Dào and Dé to be born.
Then the luster, moisture, Xìng, Qì, Shén, Míng, and the positional arrangement, proportion, and measure of the physical form
each have their definite limits and assigned structures.
These are all received from its Dào and Dé,
not determined by personal cravings or choices.
Having received this endowment,
it is firmly set,
and cannot be refused.
Therefore, it is called Mìng.
Mìng means one cannot avoid being born.
Being born entails having form.
Once formed, the Dào, Dé, Xìng, and Shén of the thing are thereby carried within its physical form.
Therefore, firm and solid is called Mìng.
Mìng generates form,
connecting it through stability.
That from which things originate via the Dào is called Dào.
That which they obtain to live is called Dé.
The possession that is Dé
has Dào as its root.
Therefore it is said:
Dào is the root of Dé.
Dé generates things and also nurtures them.
Then things are peaceful and benefited.
That which brings peace and benefit to things
is the conduct of Rén.
The conduct of Rén issues from Dé.
Therefore it is said:
Rén is the expression of Dé.
Dé generates principles.
Once principles are established, there is appropriateness.
Conforming to this is called Yì.
Yì is principle.
Therefore it is said:
Yì is the principle of Dé.
Dé generates things
and further nurtures and raises them without abandoning them,
enabling them to attain peace and benefit.
Dé's encounter with things is marked by Zhōng and substantiality.
Therefore it is said:
Zhōng is the substantiality of Dé.
The loyalty and sincerity of virtue,
are steadfast and unchangeable,
this is the constancy of virtue,
hence it is said:
Steadfastness is the firmness of virtue.
Virtue is born from the Way and possesses principle,
upholding principle aligns with the Way,
intimately connected with the Way and principle without separation,
thus it can nurture and sustain all things,
all things rely upon virtue,
this is the loftiness of virtue,
hence it is said:
Intimacy is the loftiness of virtue.
Following the Way without losing it,
then one possesses the Way;
attaining and preserving it,
then one possesses virtue;
acting without ceasing,
then actions are accomplished;
therefore it is said:
This is what is called the Way,
this is what is called virtue,
this is what is called action.
All these statements,
exhaust the transformations of virtue,
transforming the world,
is principle.
The Shū records the principles of virtue on bamboo and silk,
displaying them for people to observe,
to clarify what should be practiced,
hence it is said:
The Shū is that which records this.
The Shī embodies the principles of virtue,
clarifying its intent,
enabling people to follow it for self-cultivation,
hence it is said:
The Shī is that which embodies this.
The Yì examines whether people follow the subtle principles of virtue,
and divines their fortune or misfortune,
hence it is said:
The Yì is that which divines this.
The Chūnqiū observes past events' alignment with the principles of virtue,
recording successes and failures accordingly,
to serve as guidance for future affairs,
hence it is said:
The Chūnqiū is that which records this.
The Lǐ embodies the principles of virtue through rituals and patterns,
accomplishing human affairs,
hence it is said:
The Lǐ is that which embodies this.
The Yuè,
when the ways of the Shū, Shī, Yì, Chūnqiū, and Lǐ are complete,
they harmonize with virtue,
and such harmony brings great joy,
hence it is said:
The Yuè is that which is called joy.
If one can cultivate the principles of virtue,
then safety and benefit are called blessings,
all desire blessings,
but cannot guarantee obtaining them,
so people believe spirits can influence gains and losses,
thus preparing sacrifices, vessels, and offerings,
purifying and fasting to worship spirits,
seeking to assist in attaining blessings,
hence it is said:
Sacrificing to spirits is for this blessing.
When the principles of virtue are fully extended to people,
within humans,
they are internal and hard to perceive,
thus ancient kings praised virtue's essence,
through words,
to illuminate its principles,
displaying them to the world,
for people to observe,
passing them to later generations,
debating and examining them,
spreading through mutual instruction,
so disciples learn by following teachers,
broadening knowledge to attain understanding,
clarifying words to establish sincerity,
hence it is said:
Broad learning and debate,
are for these words.
Virtue fully bestows upon things,
though things possess it,
it is subtle and hard to recognize,
jade is the true manifestation of virtue.
The six principles reside in jade,
clear and easily seen,
thus jade is used as metaphor,
for what things receive from virtue,
is one with jade.
Dà Zhèng Shàng
I have heard that in governance,
the people are the foundation of all things;
the state takes them as its foundation,
the ruler takes them as his foundation,
officials take them as their foundation.
Thus, the state relies on the people for its security or peril,
the ruler relies on the people for his authority or disgrace,
officials rely on the people for their honor or baseness.
This is what is meant by "the people are the foundation of all things."
I have heard that in governance,
the people are the lifeblood of all things;
the state takes them as its lifeblood,
the ruler takes them as his lifeblood,
officials take them as their lifeblood.
Thus, the state relies on the people for its survival or demise,
the ruler relies on the people for his clarity or blindness,
officials rely on the people for their worthiness or incompetence.
This is what is meant by "the people are the lifeblood of all things."
I have heard that in governance,
the people are the achievement of all things,
so the state takes them as its achievement,
the ruler takes them as his achievement,
officials take them as their achievement.
The state relies on the people for its prosperity or ruin,
the ruler relies on the people for his strength or weakness,
officials rely on the people for their capability or incapability.
This is what is meant by "the people are the achievement of all things."
I have heard that in governance,
the people are the strength of all things,
so the state takes them as its strength,
the ruler takes them as his strength,
officials take them as their strength.
Therefore, victory in battle
depends on the people's desire to win;
success in attack
depends on the people's desire to gain;
preservation in defense
depends on the people's desire to survive.
Thus, if you lead the people in defense,
but they do not wish to survive,
then none can achieve survival.
If you lead the people in attack,
but they do not wish to gain,
then none can achieve success.
If you lead the people in battle,
but they do not wish to win,
then none can achieve victory.
Therefore, when the people serve their superiors,
they joyfully engage the enemy,
advancing unstoppably,
and the enemy is sure to be terrified—
victory in battle arises from this.
But if the people, in serving their superiors,
are fearful upon engagement and flee,
defeat in battle arises from this.
Thus, calamity and blessing
are not solely determined by Heaven,
but also by the scholars and common people.
Alas!
Be cautious, be cautious!
The will of the scholars and common people
must not be disregarded.
Alas!
Be cautious, be cautious!
If one's actions are good,
it purely leads to blessings.
Alas! Be cautious, be cautious! If one's actions are evil,
it purely leads to calamity.
Therefore, those who receive Heaven's blessings
are not assailed by Heaven;
those afflicted by Heaven's calamities
should not blame Heaven,
for it is their own actions that bring it upon them.
To know what is good but not practice it
is called lack of clarity;
to know what is evil but not reform
will surely incur Heaven's punishment.
Heaven has constant blessings,
which it bestows upon the virtuous;
Heaven has constant calamities,
which it inflicts upon those who rob the people of their time.
Therefore, the people,
though most humble, must not be treated lightly;
though most ignorant, must not be deceived.
Thus, from ancient times to the present,
those who make enemies of the people,
whether sooner or later,
are inevitably overcome by them.
To know what is good but not practice it
is called recklessness;
to know what is evil but not reform
is called confusion.
Therefore, recklessness and confusion
are what the sage kings warned against,
and what the noble man feels ashamed of.
Alas!
Be cautious, be cautious!
How can one take recklessness and confusion as one's lot?
The enlightened ruler and the noble man,
upon hearing of goodness, pursue it as if in a race;
upon hearing of evil, reform it as if confronting an enemy.
Only then can calamities be avoided,
and blessings preserved.
Be cautious, be cautious!
Be prudent in punishment and reward.
Thus, rather than kill the innocent,
it is better to err by sparing the guilty.
Therefore, in cases of crime,
if there is doubt, let it be dismissed.
In cases of merit,
if there is doubt, let it be rewarded.
Then there will be no one innocent yet punished,
nor anyone meritorious yet unrewarded.
Be cautious!
Be cautious!
Be prudent in punishment and reward.
Thus, the ancients established penalties
to restrain the unworthy,
and to rouse the indolent people.
Therefore, if a crime is doubtful, do not carry out punishment,
so the unworthy may reform;
if a merit is doubtful, do not withhold reward,
so the ignorant people may be encouraged.
Thus, the ruler gains a reputation for benevolence,
and the subjects achieve order and renown.
To dismiss doubtful crimes
is benevolence;
to reward doubtful merits
is trustworthiness.
Be cautious!
Be cautious!
Be attentive to those below,
so that punishments are carried out without bias,
and rewards are given without distortion.
Do not add to the people's crimes and加重 them,
nor diminish the people's merits and discard them.
Thus, if the superior acts wrongly,
admonish and stop him,
guiding him with the Way;
if the inferior acts wrongly,
pity and forgive them,
guide and pardon them,
gently and tolerantly.
Therefore, even if there are unworthy people,
they can be transformed and regulated.
Thus, even the emperors of old,
in valuing their ministers,
did so in this manner.
The way of a minister
is to reflect on goodness and offer it to the superior,
hear of goodness and offer it to the superior,
know of goodness and offer it to the superior.
The people
belong solely to the ruler,
and the minister assists the ruler in governing them.
Therefore, the duty of a minister
is to achieve merit by enriching and delighting the people,
and to incur blame by impoverishing and afflicting them.
Thus, the ruler demonstrates wisdom by recognizing the worthy,
and officials demonstrate loyalty by loving the people.
Therefore, if ministers are loyal, the ruler is wise—
this is what is called a sage king.
Thus, office may be borrowed, but virtue cannot be borrowed;
position may be lowly, but righteousness is not lowly.
Therefore, one with a low position but high righteousness,
though humble,
is noble;
one with a high position but low righteousness,
though esteemed,
will surely meet adversity.
Alas!
Be cautious!
Be cautious!
If one fails to practice the Way,
poverty and hardship will follow.
That which, once uttered, cannot be taken back
is speech;
that which, once done, cannot be concealed
is action.
Therefore, speech and action
are the markers of wisdom and folly,
the distinction between worthiness and unworthiness.
Thus, the wise are cautious in speech and action,
considering them as personal blessings;
the foolish are careless in speech and action,
considering them as personal calamities.
Therefore, the noble man speaks only what can be put into practice,
and then speaks it;
acts only what can be spoken of,
and then acts it.
Alas!
Be cautious!
Be cautious!
The performance of actions lies with oneself,
but the decree of fate lies with others—
this is the root of blessing and calamity.
The Way is the root of blessing,
and auspiciousness is the bloom of blessing;
those without the Way
will surely lose the root of blessing.
Those who are inauspicious,
are bound to lose the glory of blessings;
hence, those who act without following the Way,
their words surely disregard righteousness.
Thus, Zhòu called himself the Celestial King,
and Jié called himself the Son of Heaven,
yet after their downfall,
the people curse them,
from this perspective,
position alone does not confer honor,
and titles alone do not bring glory.
Therefore, the nobility of a gentleman,
is esteemed by the scholars and people,
hence it is called nobility.
Thus, the wealth of a gentleman,
brings joy to the scholars and people,
hence it is called wealth.
So, the nobility of a gentleman,
shares blessings with the people,
therefore the scholars and people honor him.
And the wealth of a gentleman,
shares riches with the people,
thus the scholars and people rejoice in it.
If a gentleman's wealth and nobility
decline by the time of his descendants,
the scholars and people will all say:
"Why has the gentleman's Way declined so!"
Unworthy tyrants,
when calamity befalls them,
the scholars and people all say:
"Why is Heaven's punishment so slow?"
The people are the foundation for all generations,
and cannot be deceived.
Those in high positions,
who neglect scholars and oppress the people are called foolish,
while those who respect scholars and love the people are called wise,
for it is the scholars and people who determine foolishness or wisdom.
Thus, the people are a great multitude,
and one must stand in awe of them,
for the people are powerful and cannot be opposed.
Alas!
Be cautious of this!
Be cautious of this!
Those who make enemies of the people,
will surely be overcome by them.
If the ruler can do good,
then the officials will surely do good;
if the officials can do good,
then the people will surely do good.
Thus, if the people are not good,
it is the fault of the officials;
if the officials are not good,
it is the error of the ruler.
Alas!
Be cautious!
Be cautious!
Therefore, the scholars and people,
led by the Way,
will then follow the Way;
led by righteousness,
will then be righteous;
led by loyalty,
will then be loyal;
led by trustworthiness,
will then be trustworthy;
hence, when a ruler issues commands,
they are like a sound,
and the scholars and people learn from them like an echo,
bending to follow the ruler,
as shadows follow form.
Alas!
Be cautious of this!
Be cautious of this!
If the ruler inclines towards goodness here,
harmoniously and steadily,
the people will all incline towards goodness there,
just as a shadow resembles the shape.
If the ruler does evil here,
grumbling and discordantly,
the people will all do evil there,
like an echo responding to a sound.
Therefore, sage kings and gentlemen,
those who govern and face the people must be cautious daily,
then the scholars and people will also be cautious daily,
for they lead the people with the Way.
The Way is the conduct of sage kings,
culture is the words of sage kings;
reverence is the demeanor of sage kings,
loyalty and trustworthiness are the teachings of sage kings.
Sages are the teachers of the worthy and wise,
benevolence and righteousness are the nature of enlightened rulers;
thus, Yáo, Shùn, Yǔ, and Tāng in governing the world,
are called enlightened rulers,
the scholars and people rejoiced in them,
each reigned for a hundred years before passing,
yet the scholars and people still felt it was too brief.
Jié and Zhòu are called tyrannical and chaotic rulers,
the scholars and people suffered under them,
each reigned only decades before their fall,
yet the scholars and people still felt it was too long.
Therefore, if the feudal lords
are loved by all scholars and people,
the state will surely prosper;
if the scholars and people all suffer under them,
the state will surely perish;
for the scholars and people are what the state cultivates,
and the foundation of the feudal lords,
and cannot be taken lightly.
Alas!
To slight the foundation is inauspicious,
and truly brings calamity upon oneself,
be cautious of this!
Be cautious of this!
"Great Governance Part Two"
Those easily made happy and hard to anger are fit to be rulers;
those who recognize others' merits and forget their faults are fit to be honored;
hence it is said:
Punishments cannot nurture the people,
negligence and leakage cannot win scholars.
To try to nurture the people with punishments,
is like taming a dog with a whip,
even over time, it will not become close;
to try to win scholars with negligence,
is like scaring birds with a bow,
even over time, it will not succeed;
therefore, scholars,
if not respected, will not come;
and the people,
if not loved, will not adhere;
so to ensure scholars come and the people adhere,
only reverence and respect, loyalty and trustworthiness,
have never changed from ancient to modern times.
Marshes may have withered trees,
but a state should have no withered scholars;
thus, there may be rulers unable to attract scholars,
but there are no scholars who cannot be won;
there may be officials unable to govern the people,
but there are no people who cannot be governed;
hence, if the ruler is enlightened, the officials will be worthy,
and if the officials are worthy, the people will be well-governed;
thus, by observing the people, one knows the officials,
and by observing the officials, one knows the ruler;
so the ruler's achievement is seen in selecting officials,
and the officials' achievement is seen in governing the people;
thus, those encouraged from above,
are observed from below upward,
this is what is meant by the Way.
Therefore, those who govern the state,
by practicing the Way,
the state will surely be tranquil;
if they profess the Way but act falsely,
the state will surely be empty;
hence, governance must be handled with care,
and officials must be selected carefully,
and the Way must not be abandoned,
Alas!
Be cautious of this!
Abandoning the Way brings disaster.
There has never been an era without sages,
though some may remain unknown;
there has never been a state without scholars,
though some may not be obtained.
Thus, the world has never lacked sages,
but without a sage king, they do not arise;
a state has never lacked scholars,
but without a noble ruler, they do not assist.
When the ruler is enlightened, scholars discreetly refine themselves.
Therefore, when a sage king holds the highest position,
even if there is one worthy scholar per hundred miles,
it is as if there were none;
thus, when the king declines,
scholars vanish.
But when a tyrant or chaotic ruler is in power,
even if there is one worthy scholar per thousand miles,
it feels as if they stand shoulder to shoulder;
so, a state may be unfortunate to lack an enlightened ruler,
but if the ruler is enlightened,
the state will not be unfortunate to lack worthy scholars.
From ancient times to the present,
there may be marshes without water,
but no state has ever been without scholars.
Thus, scholars are easy to find but hard to seek,
easy to attract but hard to retain.
For if one seeks scholars without the right way,
even scouring the entire realm,
not a single one can be obtained;
but if one seeks scholars with the right way,
many will be found within the state.
This is what is meant by "scholars are easy to find but hard to seek."
If scholars are treated with respect,
they will surely stay;
if treated without the right way,
they will surely leave.
This is what is meant by "scholars are easy to attract but hard to retain."
A king may change policies but not the state,
may change officials but not the people.
Thus, he brings stability by relying on this state,
and order by relying on these people.
Hence, Tāng used the chaotic people of Jié to achieve order,
and King Wǔ used the northern troops of Zhòu to build strength.
Therefore, the order or chaos of the people lies with the officials,
and the safety or peril of the state lies with the policies.
Thus, an enlightened ruler is cautious in governance,
and selective in appointing officials,
after which the state prospers.
If the ruler can do good,
then officials will surely do good;
if officials can do good,
then the people will surely do good.
Thus, the people's failings
are the fault of the officials;
the people's goodness
is the achievement of the officials;
the officials' failings
are the fault of the ruler;
the officials' goodness
is the achievement of the ruler.
Therefore, if the ruler is enlightened and officials are worthy,
then the people will be well-governed.
For if those above favor something,
those below will inevitably be transformed by it—
this is the way of governance.
The term "mín" (people) implies obscurity,
and "méng" (masses) implies blindness; thus, depending on what the superiors support and guide,
the people are always transformed.
Hence it is said:
"The people are the masses."
The people as masses!
This directly expresses their nature and names them.
The people are the material for both the worthy and unworthy;
both are present among them.
Thus, the worthy find their place,
the unworthy submit,
skills are contributed,
and loyal ministers are refined.
Therefore, the people accumulate ignorance;
though the people may be ignorant,
an enlightened ruler selects officials
and must involve the people in the process.
So, if scholars and the people praise someone,
the enlightened ruler investigates and, seeing their allegiance, honors them;
if scholars and the people suffer under someone,
the enlightened ruler investigates and,
seeing their dissent, removes them.
Thus, when a king selects officials, he does not forget
to let the people lead in opinion,
and then follows them.
For the people are the measure of officials;
by observing officials through the people,
he then acts accordingly.
The people are the humblest,
yet when tasked to choose officials,
they will surely pick those they love.
Thus, if ten people love and support someone,
he is an official for ten people;
if a hundred love and support him,
he is an official for a hundred;
if a thousand love and support him,
he is an official for a thousand;
if ten thousand love and support him,
he is an official for ten thousand;
and such an official for ten thousand
may be selected as a minister or chancellor.
The people are the foundation of the feudal lords,
education is the foundation of governance,
and the Dào is the foundation of education.
With the Dào, there is education;
with education, governance is orderly;
with orderly governance, the people are encouraged;
with the people encouraged, the state becomes prosperous;
and with the state prosperous and wealthy,
the ruler finds joy.
Loyalty is the achievement of ministers;
ministers' loyalty
stems from the ruler's enlightenment.
With loyal ministers and an enlightened ruler,
this is called the essence of governance.
Thus, the state's framework of conduct,
when established, leads to its goodness.
Therefore, the ruler's trust depends on whom he trusts;
if those trusted are untrustworthy,
even if he wishes to speak of trust,
he will never achieve it in his lifetime.
Thus, he must be cautious in whom he trusts.
The way of serving a ruler
does not exceed that of serving a father;
thus, one who is unworthy in serving his father
cannot serve a ruler;
the way of serving elders
does not exceed that of serving an elder brother;
thus, one who is unworthy in serving his brother
cannot serve elders;
the way of commanding subordinates
does not exceed that of commanding a younger brother;
thus, one who is unworthy in commanding his brother
cannot command subordinates;
the way of social interactions
does not exceed that of conducting oneself;
thus, one who is unworthy in self-conduct
cannot make friends;
the way of caring for the people
does not exceed that of loving one's child;
thus, one who is unworthy in loving his child
cannot care for the people;
the way of holding office
does not exceed that of managing a household;
thus, one who is unworthy in household management
cannot hold office.
For the Dào, if practiced with one's father,
can be practiced with one's ruler;
if practiced with an elder brother,
can be practiced with elders;
if practiced with a younger brother,
can be practiced with subordinates;
if practiced in self-conduct,
can be practiced with friends;
if practiced with one's child,
can be practiced with the people;
if practiced in household management,
can be practiced in office.
Thus, a scholar can be tested before taking office;
when a sage king selects and promotes,
he uses this as a standard.
He inquires to understand their words,
consults to know their limits,
assigns tasks to observe their reliability,
and thus ascertains their trustworthiness.
Therefore, ancient sage kings and noble men did not arbitrarily reject people—
this was their way of discernment.
The governance of the state
lies with the feudal lords, ministers, and scholars;
the method of investigation
lies in their associates and followers.
The ruler must choose his ministers,
and ministers must choose their companions.
Thus, one with clear discernment excels in judging others' words;
without leaving the chamber,
nothing remains unseen.
One with clear discernment, employing others without leaving his post,
can penetrate everywhere.
Hence, a king residing in the central state,
without leaving his realm, understands the governance of the world.
How is this so?
It is through the words of worthy men.
Without leaving his position,
if those within the borders are close to him,
it is said that people act on his behalf.
Thus, the way of loving others—
in speech, it is called one's treasury;
the way of loving others—
in action, it is called one's propriety.
Therefore, to be loyal to feudal lords,
nothing surpasses respecting scholars;
to be loyal to noble men,
nothing surpasses loving the people.
If feudal lords do not obtain scholars,
they cannot prosper.
Thus, if a nobleman fails to win the people's support,
he cannot be esteemed.
Therefore, a scholar who can speak of the Way but cannot practice it is called a vessel;
one who can practice the Way but cannot speak of it is called a tool;
one who can both speak of and practice the Way is called genuine.
Hence, the nobleman examines the vessel,
employs the tool,
and relies on the genuine,
and thus order is achieved and prosperity arises.
Alas!
People, oh people!
When feudal lords ascend the throne and enjoy their states,
with sacrifices made to the altars of soil and grain,
yet governance is dictated by fate,
the state has no true ruler.
When officials hold administrative positions,
and the people have someone to belong to,
yet governance is dictated by fate,
the state has no true officials.
When a hundred chariots are driven for the court,
and a thousand people are fed,
yet governance is dictated by fate,
the state has no true men.
Why is this?
The term "ruler" (jūn) implies examination;
thus, the ruler is the source of the Way;
if the worthy are not promoted,
and the unworthy are not removed,
this shows the ruler lacks the Way,
so governance deems this state to have no ruler.
The term "official" (lì) implies management;
thus, the official is the source of order;
if superiors do wrong and they dare not remonstrate,
and inferiors do good and they do not encourage them,
this shows the official lacks order,
so governance deems this state to have no officials.
When a hundred chariots are driven for the court,
and a thousand people are fed,
yet those close at hand are insufficient for consultation and advice,
and the court's reach is inadequate for examination and measure,
so governance deems this state to have no men.
Alas!
How sorrowful!
The ruler is about gathering the masses;
without men, who is there to rely on?
Without reliance, collapse is inevitable,
so governance deems this state already lost.
"Xiū Zhèng Yǔ Shàng"
Huángdì said:
"The Way is like the water of rivers and valleys,
its source never ceasing,
its flow never stopping;
thus, it subdues people without making enemies,
distributes without being deemed presumptuous—
this is solely due to the Way;
hence, what is spread throughout the world and not forgotten
is solely the Way."
Therefore, the Way's height is compared to heaven,
its brightness to the sun,
its stability to mountains;
so those who speak of it are seen as wise,
those who learn it are seen as worthy,
those who uphold it are seen as trustworthy,
those who delight in it are seen as benevolent,
those who practice it are seen as sages.
Thus, only the Way cannot be stolen,
nor can it be made empty.
So Huángdì held fast to the Way and righteousness,
ordered heaven and earth,
regulated human relationships,
sequenced all things,
taking trustworthiness and benevolence as priorities for the world,
then crossed the Eastern Sea into the river,
internally obtained the green chart,
and crossed Jīshí Mountain,
traversed the Liúshā Desert,
ascended Kūnlún,
then returned to dwell in the Central Kingdom,
to pacify the world;
the world was at peace,
solely through embodying the Way.
Emperor Zhuānxū said:
"The ultimate Way cannot be surpassed,
the ultimate righteousness cannot be altered."
Therefore, later generations follow these traces;
thus, he followed Huángdì's Way and practiced it,
learned Huángdì's Way and esteemed it,
adding without reducing,
and the world was also pacified.
Zhuānxū said:
"No merit is greater than abandoning evil for good,
no crime is worse than abandoning good for evil."
Thus, it is not that I merely love the good, but that goodness follows goodness;
not that I merely hate evil,
but that evil follows evil;
I grow more cautious each day,
and that is all.
Emperor Kù said:
"Follow the words of those who embody the Way to join in the Way,
follow the deeds of the skillful to learn skill,
practice the conduct of the benevolent to join in benevolence."
Thus, he tempered the vessel of benevolence to cultivate himself,
and personally concentrated on its excellence.
So scholars followed Huángdì's Way and illuminated it,
learned Emperor Zhuānxū's Way and practiced it,
and the world was also pacified.
Emperor Kù said:
"No virtue is higher than broad love for people,
no governance is greater than broad benefit for people."
Thus, nothing in governance is greater than trustworthiness,
nothing in rule is greater than benevolence,
and I am cautious only of this.
Emperor Yáo said:
"I set my heart on antiquity,
focus my will on the impoverished,
grieve for the people's suffering from crime,
and worry that the multitude may not thrive."
So if even one person is hungry,
he would say:
"This is because I made him hungry."
If even one person is cold,
he would say:
"This is because I made him cold."
If even one person commits a crime,
he would say:
"This is because I led him into it."
Benevolence was practiced and righteousness established,
virtue was broad and transformation rich,
so without rewards, the people were encouraged;
without punishments, the people were orderly;
he first showed forgiveness and then acted,
thus his virtuous reputation spread far.
So Yáo's teachings reached the tattooed faces of Shǔ and Yuè,
pacified Jiāozhǐ,
personally crossed the Liúshā Desert,
bestowed lands at Dúshān,
went west to see the Queen Mother,
instructed as far as Dàxià and Qúsǒu,
north to central Yōudū,
and to the dog country and those with human bodies and bird faces,
and to Jiāoyáo;
he loved the worthy and concealed others' shortcomings,
was strong in action and careful in intent,
guided by benevolence and forgiveness,
and that was all.
Emperor Shùn said:
"I exhaust my reverence in serving my superiors,
so I am called loyal;
I exhaust my reverence in dealing with my peers,
so I am called trustworthy;
I exhaust my reverence in employing my subordinates,
so I am called benevolent."
Thus, he was loved and cherished by the people of the world,
and found joy and belonging among them,
and was esteemed and trusted by the rulers of the world;
so I carefully adopted this through reverence,
and I achieved it through reverence.
Therefore, to illuminate the Way and teach clearly,
only by being reverent can one ensure loyalty and submission.
When Dà Yǔ governed the world,
there were ten thousand feudal lords,
and Yǔ knew each one's substance entirely.
How could Dà Yǔ know them all at one glance?
Or recognize them all at one hearing?
When feudal lords came to court, Yǔ personally responded to them,
so thus Yǔ knew each state entirely;
when scholars attended monthly, Yǔ personally met them,
so thus Yǔ knew each one's substance entirely;
yet Dà Yǔ still greatly feared,
and at feudal lords' gatherings,
he would ask them:
"Do the feudal lords think I am arrogant?"
On the first day of the month, when scholars came to court,
he would ask them:
"Do the feudal lords and ministers think I am extravagant?
Have they heard of my extravagance?
If they do not tell me,
this teaches me the way of cruelty!
It destroys the teachings of the world!
So what I resent in people,
nothing is greater than this."
Great Yǔ said:
"If the people have no food,
then I cannot command them;
if achievements are made but do not benefit the people,
then I cannot encourage them."
Therefore, he channeled the river to guide it through the nine provinces,
dug the Yangtze to direct it through nine routes,
regulated the five lakes and stabilized the Eastern Sea.
The people indeed labored hard,
yet they did not complain or suffer,
because the achievements benefited them.
Yǔ once had no time to eat by day,
nor to sleep at night.
At that time,
he was preoccupied with urgent tasks,
thus Yǔ shared the same duties with his officers and people.
So without proclaiming his own trustworthiness,
trust was understood,
thus in governing the world,
he did so through trustworthiness.
Tāng said:
"Those who study the way of the sage kings
can be compared to the sun;
quietly thinking while living alone,
can be likened to a fire."
If one abandons studying the way of the sage kings,
and instead lives quietly thinking alone,
it is like leaving the bright sunlight in the courtyard,
and approaching the light of a fire indoors.
This may allow for small insights but not great understanding.
Therefore, enlightened rulers and noble persons
value learning the Way and disdain solitary thinking.
Thus, when lords find worthy individuals and promote them,
or associate with them,
it is like climbing a mountain;
when they find unworthy individuals and promote them,
or associate with them,
it is like descending into an abyss.
For climbing a mountain to look out,
what cannot be overseen and what cannot be seen?
But gradually entering the abyss,
who would not sink and drown?
Hence, enlightened rulers are cautious in their promotions,
and noble persons are careful in their associations.
Only then can blessings surely come,
and calamities surely be avoided.
Tāng said:
"Medicine and food are first tasted by the lowly,
then reach the noble;
medicinal advice is first offered to the noble,
then heard by the lowly."
Thus, medicine and food tasted by the lowly
before reaching the noble
is education;
medicinal advice offered to the noble
before being heard by the lowly
is the Way.
So, having others taste food
before eating it oneself,
one gains more flavor;
having others assess words
before hearing them oneself,
one gains less from the words.
Therefore, the enlightened ruler regarding words
must personally listen to them, personally select them, personally gather them, personally store them, and personally act on them.
Thus, the Way becomes clear when grasped through method,
becomes manifest when practiced through method,
becomes stored when applied to all things through method.
Hence, those seeking the Way use not their eyes but their hearts,
those acquiring the Way use not their hands but their ears,
those conveying the Way use words,
those entering the Way use loyalty,
those accumulating the Way use trustworthiness,
those establishing the Way use people.
Thus, if a ruler has the desire for orderly governance
but lacks the policies for it,
even if he wishes for manifest glory,
he will not attain it.
So, orderly governance cannot be achieved emptily,
nor can manifest glory be gained emptily.
Therefore, the enlightened ruler respects scholars, inspects officials, and loves the people to align with these principles.
Without this,
the four excellences will not adhere.
"Xiū Zhèng Yǔ Xià"
King Wén of Zhōu asked Yùzǐ:
"May I ask, when a noble person is about to assume office,
how should he be towards the people?"
Yùzǐ replied:
"Yes.
Hesitantly.
Allow me to inform Your Majesty with the governance of ancient times:
The governance says:
When a noble person is about to assume office,
he should be towards the people
brightly, like the sun just rising."
King Wén of Zhōu said:
"I accept this instruction."
He asked:
"When a noble person has assumed office,
how should he be towards the people?"
The reply was:
"When a noble person has assumed office,
he should be towards the people
brilliantly, like the sun at its zenith."
King Wén of Zhōu said:
"I accept this instruction."
He asked:
"When a noble person has left office,
how is he towards the people?"
The reply was:
"When a noble person has left office,
he is towards the people
dimly, like the sun after it has set.
Thus, the noble person about to assume office being bright
means righteousness is heard first;
having assumed office being brilliant
means the people preserve their blessings;
having left office being dim
means the people lose his guidance."
King Wén of Zhōu said:
"I accept this instruction."
King Wǔ of Zhōu asked Yùzǐ:
"I wish to defend and necessarily preserve,
attack and necessarily gain,
fight and necessarily win.
How should I achieve this?"
Yùzǐ replied:
"Indeed, attack and defense with victory share the same vessel,
and harmony with strictness are its preparations.
Therefore it is said:
Harmony can defend,
and strictness can defend,
but strictness is not as solid as harmony;
harmony can attack,
and strictness can attack,
but strictness lacks the virtue of harmony;
harmony can fight,
and strictness can fight,
but strictness cannot win like harmony.
Thus, only through harmony is it possible.
Therefore, when feudal lords issue decrees and implement policies,
if the governance is fair to the people,
it is called civil governance;
when feudal lords receive scholars and employ officials,
if the rites are respectful to people,
it is called civil rites;
when feudal lords hear cases and decide punishments,
if they are benevolent to people,
it is called civil punishment.
So when these three civilities are practiced in governance,
established in administration,
and displayed in action,
that from this one defends but does not preserve,
attacks but does not gain,
fights but does not win—
from ancient times until now,
since the opening of heaven and earth, such has never been heard.
Now,
if Your Majesty wishes to defend and necessarily preserve,
attack and necessarily gain,
fight and necessarily win,
then only by following this path is it possible."
King Wǔ of Zhōu said:
"I accept this instruction."
King Wǔ of Zhōu asked Prince Dàn:
"May I ask if governance can certainly achieve success and warfare can certainly secure victory?
Can attacks certainly capture and defense certainly preserve?"
Prince Dàn replied:
"Yes.
The governance principles state:
When feudal lords maintain internal stability and project external authority,
When gentlemen cultivate personal conduct and earn the people's trust,
Then the governed become orderly,
And reputation becomes honorable.
Therefore, those aspiring to govern
Must cultivate through the Way and act with reverence,
Only then can they achieve success.
Those aspiring to wage war
Must cultivate through governance and mobilize with righteousness,
Only then can they secure victory;
Those aspiring to attack
Must establish alliances through covenants and demonstrate credibility,
Only then can they capture;
Those aspiring to defend
Must strengthen through harmony and instruct with love,
Only then can they preserve."
King Wǔ of Zhōu said:
"I accept this instruction."
Shī Shàngfù said:
"I have heard about governance:
It is said:
The vast world,
Belongs to one person.
The multitudes of people,
Are governed by one person.
Thus the world
Does not belong to any single family,
But to those who possess the Way;
Therefore the world
Can only be governed by those with the Way,
Can only be regulated by those with the Way,
Can only be directed by those with the Way,
Can only be appropriately maintained long-term by those with the Way;
Thus the world is difficult to obtain but easy to lose,
Difficult to maintain constantly but easy to neglect;
Therefore, those who preserve the world
Cannot do so long without the Way;
Thus the Way is the treasure of ten thousand generations."
King Wǔ of Zhōu said:
"I accept this instruction."

Saying:

I too wish to be instructed,
May I ask how to pursue the way of building a state?"

When the ruler contemplates goodness, act upon it;
When the ruler hears goodness, act upon it;
When the ruler knows goodness, act upon it;
Maintain constant reverence in position,
Practice enduring faithfulness in conduct,

"I accept this instruction."

"May I ask about the essentials of the Way?"

I hesitate.
Allow me to instruct Your Majesty with ancient governance principles,

Those in subordinate positions should be respectful and solemn,
Those in superior positions should be reverent and benevolent,

"I accept this instruction."
King Chéng of Zhōu said:
"May I ask about the way to govern a state?"
Master Zhōu said:
"Yes.
I hesitate.
Allow me to instruct Your Majesty with ancient governance principles,
The principles state:
The way to govern a state:
Above, be loyal to the sovereign,
In the middle, respect the scholars,
And below, love the people;
Therefore, being loyal to the sovereign above
Without moral principles cannot constitute true loyalty;
Respecting scholars in the middle
Without ritual propriety cannot demonstrate true respect;
Loving the people below
Without loyalty and trust cannot express true love;
Thus when loyalty and trust prevail among the people,
Ritual propriety is understood by scholars,
And moral principles reach the superiors,
This is the way to govern a state.
Even those governing the entire world
Proceed from this alone."
King Chéng of Zhōu said:
"I accept this instruction."
King Chéng of Zhōu said:
"I have heard:
There are superior people,
There are inferior people,
There are worthy people,
There are unworthy people,
There are wise people,
There are foolish people.
May I ask how superior and inferior people differ?"
Master Zhōu replied:
"Yes.
I hesitate.
Allow me to instruct Your Majesty with ancient governance principles,
The principles state:
All people,
Whether humble or noble,
Whether young or old,
Who hear of the Way, remember it and preserve it,
Know the good of the Way and practice it,
Are superior people;
Those who hear of the Way but do not preserve it,
Know the Way but do not practice it,
Are called inferior people.
Therefore, those whose actions are good are called worthy people,
Those whose actions are evil are called unworthy;
Those whose words are good are called wise,
Those whose words are not good are called foolish.
Thus wise and foolish people are distinguished by their speech,
Worthy and unworthy people are differentiated by their actions,
Superior and inferior people are classified by their aspirations."
King Chéng of Zhōu said:
"I accept this instruction."
King Chéng of Zhōu said:
"I have heard:
When a sage king occupies the throne,
He makes the people wealthy and long-lived,
Wealth can be achieved,
But is longevity not in Heaven's hands?"
Master Zhōu said:
"Yes.

Allow me to instruct Your Majesty with ancient governance principles,
The principles state:
When a sage king occupies the throne,
The world is free from military conflicts,
Feudal lords do not attack each other privately,
People do not fight or quarrel privately,
Do not kill each other privately,
Thus when a sage king occupies the throne,
The people are spared from one death,
And gain one life;
When a sage king occupies the throne,
The ruler accumulates the Way,
Officials accumulate virtue,
And people accumulate productive labor,
Thus women produce clothing,
Men produce food,
And the people suffer no cold or hunger;
When a sage king is above,
The people are spared from two deaths,
And gain two lives;
When a sage king is above,
The ruler accumulates benevolence,
Officials accumulate love,
And people accumulate obedience,
Then punishments are abolished,
And people face no untimely executions,
Thus when a sage king is above,
The people are spared from three deaths,
And gain three lives;
When a sage king is above,
He employs people at proper times,
And uses resources with moderation,
Then people suffer no epidemics;
Thus when a sage king is above,
The people are spared from four deaths,
And gain four lives;
Therefore when a sage king is above,
He promotes the virtuous throughout the land to suppress evil,
Thus worthy people are employed and unworthy people do not arise,
Then the people attain their destined longevity.
Therefore wealth and longevity
Are achievements of the sage king."
King Chéng of Zhōu said:
"I accept this instruction."

presenting gifts to the senior officials and to Dān Jìnggōng.

frugal yet respectful.
The guest rituals and gifts were the same,
all conducted with propriety and compliance.
The feasts and entertainments were without personal bias,
and the send-off did not extend beyond the suburbs.

might Zhōu be revived?

'In action, nothing surpasses respect;
in dwelling, nothing surpasses frugality;
in virtue, nothing surpasses humility;
in affairs, nothing surpasses reliance on resources.'

in matters of ritual,
he embodies all these.

his vessels are without ornate carvings—
this is frugality;
his person is reverent and clean,
his household orderly and well-managed—
this is respect;
in feasts and gifts,
though joyful, he does not overstep ranks—
this is humility;
in guest rituals,
he matches the superior with appropriate distinctions— this is reliance on resources.

and further avoiding extravagance,
he can avoid resentment.

practicing ritual humility and relying on resources in affairs,

with such a man as a minister,
how can there not be revival?

which the two sovereigns received.

but day and night laid the foundation of the mandate with broad tranquility.'
'Mì' means peace and abundance;
'mìng' means decree and order;

'kāng' means ease;
'hòu' means king.

King Wǔ had great achievements but his governance was incomplete.
When King Chéng succeeded them,
he ruled the people with benevolence,
hence it is called 'Heaven';
he dared not be idle or at ease,
rising early and retiring late,
to continue King Wén's enterprise,
spreading culture and establishing norms,
regulating institutions,
setting up sacrifices,
so that within the four seas,
all cherished virtue beautifully,
each following their way,
hence it is said 'has a fixed mandate.'
He inherited and followed King Wǔ's achievements,
upholding and promoting King Wǔ's virtue.
The people of the nine provinces,
the states of the four frontiers,
sang of the glory of Wén and Wǔ,
coming through multiple translations to request audience,
presenting tributes for the sacrifices,
hence it is said 'the two sovereigns received it.'
At that time,
heaven and earth were in harmony,
spirits and people were compliant and abundant,
ghosts caused no harm or hauntings,
the people had no slander or complaints,
hence it is called 'broad tranquility.'
King Chéng, by nature benevolent and sagely,
could illuminate his ancestors,
could continue his kin,
daring not be lazy or negligent,
to secure the world,
and to respect the people.
Now Dānzǐ beautifully expounds his intent,
to assist the royal house;
therefore I say:
Might Zhōu be revived?"

and when Dānzǐ assisted in governance,
the Son of Heaven was more honored,
and the Zhōu house saw increased revival.

The "Book of Changes" says:
"Correct the root and all things are ordered,
miss by a hair's breadth,
err by a thousand miles."
Therefore, the gentleman is cautious at the start.
The beginning of the "Spring and Autumn Annals,"
the "Guān Jū" in the "Book of Songs," the "Capping" and "Marriage" in the "Rites," the "Qián" and "Kūn" in the "Book of Changes,"

Sincerity in simplicity leads to abundant achievement.
Carefully, when arranging marriages for sons and daughters,
one must choose those from families generation after generation filial, fraternal, and righteous.
Thus,
their descendants will be kind and filial,
dare not be debauched or violent,
with no faction being unvirtuous,
supported by the three clans.
Hence it is said:
The phoenix is born with a mind for benevolence and righteousness,
the tiger and wolf with a heart of greed and ferocity,
the two are unequal,
each having their own mother.
Alas!
Be warned of this!
Do not nurture a nursing tiger,
for it will injure the world.
Therefore, it is said achievement comes from simplicity.
The way of prenatal education
is written on jade tablets,
stored in golden cabinets,
placed in the ancestral temple,
to serve as a warning for later generations.
The Records of the Qīngshǐ Clan states:
In ancient times, the way of prenatal education dictated that
when the queen consort was with child for ten months,
she would move to a secluded chamber.
The Grand Master held bronze bells and stood guard to the left of the door,
the Grand Steward held a measuring vessel and stood guard to the right of the door,
and the Grand Diviner held yarrow stalks and tortoise shells, standing guard below the hall.
All officials attended within the gate according to their duties.
When the three months had passed,
if the sounds the queen consort requested were not proper music,
the Grand Master would stroke his instruments and claim unfamiliarity.
If the flavors she desired were not correct tastes,
the Grand Steward would bear the vessel and dare not cook or season,
saying:
"We dare not serve these to the crown prince."
When the crown prince was born and cried,
the Grand Master blew the bronze bells and said:
"His sound matches such-and-such pitch."
The Grand Steward said:
"His taste accords with such-and-such."
The Grand Diviner said:
"His destiny is such-and-such."
Only then was the ritual of hanging the bow for the crown prince performed.
The bow for the East was made of wú wood,
for wú is the plant of the East,
the wood of spring;
the sacrificial animal was a chicken,
for the chicken is the animal of the East.
The bow for the South was made of willow,
for willow is the plant of the South,
the wood of summer;
the sacrificial animal was a dog,
for the dog is the animal of the South.
The bow for the Center was made of mulberry,
for mulberry is the wood of the Center;
the sacrificial animal was an ox,
for the ox is the animal of the Center.
The bow for the West was made of jí thorn,
for jí is the plant of the West,
the wood of autumn;
the sacrificial animal was a sheep,
for the sheep is the animal of the West.
The bow for the North was made of jujube,
for jujube is the plant of the North,
the wood of winter;
the sacrificial animal was a pig,
for the pig is the animal of the North.
With five bows and five portions of arrows,
they shot to the East in the East,
to the South in the South,
to the Center in the Center,
to the West in the West,
to the North in the North,
each shooting three times.
Four bows were kept complete,
with the remaining arrows divided into two portions each,
hung to the left of the state's four thoroughfare gates;
the central bow was also kept complete,
with the remaining arrows divided into two portions,
hung to the left of the Altars of Soil and Grain gate.
Then they divined for the crown prince's name,
which should not be taken from above—the heavens,
nor from below—the earth,
nor from the famous mountains and accessible valleys in between,
nor contradict local customs.
Hence, a gentleman's name is hard to know but easy to avoid.
This is the way to nurture grace.
As for the correct ritual,
the crown prince had no subjects to be ashamed of,
being the son of leading ministers,
thus called the son of leading ministers.
The husband attends court to the king, the wife to the queen,
and their son to the crown prince;
this is called the son of a minister.
This is the correct ritual and prenatal education.
When King Wǔ of Zhōu's queen consort was pregnant with King Chéng,
she stood without leaning,
sat without imbalance,
stayed alone without arrogance,
and even when angry did not curse—
this is what is meant by prenatal education.
When King Chéng was born,
the benevolent nurtured him,
the filial swaddled him,
with four worthies by his side.
King Chéng, being wise,
selected Duke Tài as his tutor,
and Duke Zhōu as his mentor.
Thus, he had advisors for planning
and counselors for deliberation,
enabling him to fēngsacrifice on Mount Tài and shàn-sacrifice at Liángfù,
receive the feudal lords in court and unify the realm.
From this, it is evident
that the selection of left and right ministers must be discerning.
In the past, Yǔ ruled Xià and became king,
while Jié ruled Xià and perished;
Tāng ruled Yīn and became king,
while Zhòu ruled Yīn and perished;
Hélǘ of Wú was undefeated in battle,
yet Fūchāi was captured by Yuè because of it;
Duke Wén of Jìn became hegemon,
yet Duke Lì was killed in the palace of Jiànglì;
King Wēi of Qí made it powerful under heaven,
yet Duke Jiǎn was assassinated at the Tántái terrace;
Duke Mù of Qín gained fame and honor,
yet the Second Emperor was seized at the Wàngyí Palace;
the reason they all held kingship but achieved different outcomes
lies in whom they appointed.
Thus, King Chéng, while still in swaddling clothes, received feudal lords in court
because Duke Zhōu was in charge;
King Wǔlíng, at fifty, was killed at Shāqiū
because he appointed Lì Duì.
Duke Huán of Qí obtained Guǎn Zhòng,
convened the feudal lords nine times,
and rectified the realm,
being called a righteous ruler.
After losing Guǎn Zhòng,
he appointed Shù Diāo and Yì Yá,
and when he died, his body went unburied,
becoming a laughingstock of the world.
That one person can experience both glory and disgrace
depends on his appointments.
Thus, Wèi had Lord Wújì,
and regained lost territory;
Zhào appointed Lìn Xiàngrú,
and Qín's troops dared not advance;
Ānlíng appointed Zhōu Zhān,
and the state stood independently;
Chǔ had Shēn Bāoxū,
and King Zhāo was restored;
Qí had Tián Dān,
and King Xiāng regained his state.
From this, it is evident
that without wise assistants and outstanding men,
to achieve success, establish a name, secure safety, or restore a fallen line
has never been possible.
Therefore, a state should not aim for size but for winning the people's hearts;
assistants should not be numerous but worthy.
Win the people's hearts, and the people will come;
win the worthy, and the worthy will gather.
King Wén requested the removal of the páogé punishment, and the people of Yīn followed;
Tāng removed three sides of the net, and submissions came from two directions;
the King of Yuè did not linger long, and the people of Wú submitted—
because their actions complied with human feelings.
Thus, those of like voice respond though apart;
those in harmony feel close though unacquainted.
When the worthy stand in the court,
the heroes of the world lead one another to hasten there.
How do we know this is so?
Guǎn Zhòng was Duke Huán's enemy.
Bào Shū, considering him worthier than himself, recommended him to Duke Huán.
After seventy persuasions, his advice was heeded,
leading Duke Huán to set aside his enmity
and entrust him with state affairs.
Duke Huán ruled effortlessly and received feudal lords in court—
all due to Bào Shū's efforts.
The reason Guǎn Zhòng could go north to Duke Huán without fear for his safety
was his shared understanding with Bào Shū.
During the time of Duke Líng of Wèi,
Qú Bóyù was worthy but unused,
while Mí Zixiá was unworthy but employed.
Shǐ Qiú was troubled by this
and repeatedly spoke of Qú Bóyù's worth to no avail.
As he fell ill and neared death,
he said to his son:
"When I die,
hold the funeral in the north hall.
In life, I could not advance Qú Bóyù and dismiss Mí Zixiá,
meaning I failed to correct my lord.
One who in life cannot correct his lord
should not have a complete funeral in death.
To place my corpse in the north hall
is sufficient for me."
When Duke Líng came to mourn,
he asked the reason,
and the son reported his father's words.
Duke Líng, saddened and his expression changed, was awakened.
He immediately summoned Qú Bóyù and advanced him,
summoned Mí Zixiá and dismissed him,
moved the funeral to the main hall,
and left only after the rites were complete.
Thus, Wèi was well-governed,
thanks to Shǐ Qiú's efforts.
In life, he wished to advance the worthy and dismiss the unworthy;
in death, he did not cease,
but remonstrated with his corpse—
truly, he can be called loyal without decline.
King Zhòu killed Prince Bǐgān,
while Jīzǐ let down his hair and feigned madness.
Duke Líng of Chén killed Xiè Yě,
and Dèng Yuán left Chén with his entire clan.
From then on,
Yīn was annexed by Zhōu,
and Chén perished under Chǔ,
because they killed Bǐgān and Xiè Yě, thereby losing Jīzǐ and Dèng Yuán.
King Zhāo of Yān obtained Guō Wěi,
whereupon Zōu Yǎn and Yuè Yì came from Qí and Wèi,
and then raised troops to attack Qí,
driving King Mǐn to seek refuge in Jǔ.
Yān's territory and population were not equal to Qí's,
yet the reason they could achieve their will to this extent
was due to obtaining capable men.
Thus, there is no perpetually secure state,
nor people inherently suited to good governance.
Gaining the worthy leads to prosperity and prominence,
losing them brings danger and ruin.
From ancient times to the present,
this has never been otherwise.
A clear mirror is for reflecting one's form,
the past is for understanding the present.
If one knows to dislike the causes of ancient peril and downfall
but does not strive to follow the path of their security and survival,
it is no different from running backward while trying to catch up with those ahead.
Tàigōng understood this,
so he sought out the descendants of Wēizǐ
and built a tomb for Bǐgān.
If sages treat the death of other sages
with such generosity,
how much more should they treat living contemporaries!
They must not be lost.
"On the Principles of Establishing Successors"
When an ancient sage emperor was to establish the heir apparent,
he would don court robes and ascend the eastern steps,
facing west toward the consort;
the consort would carry the heir apparent out from the chamber,
facing east.
The Grand Historian, holding the document, would ascend the hall westward,
standing between the two steps,
facing north,
and announce:
"The heir apparent's name is so-and-so" three times.
The emperor would perform the rites and declare,
instructing the heir apparent:
"I entrust to you the Great Ancestor, the Great Forebear, and the altars of soil and grain" three times.
At his command,
the consort would say "I dare not" twice,
and upon the third command,
she would say:
"I humbly accept the mandate."
Then she would bow and withdraw.
The Grand Historian would inform the Grand Invocator,
who would then inform the Great Ancestor, the Great Forebear, and the altars of soil and grain.
The Grand Historian would go out
to inform the Grand Steward,
who would inform the regional chiefs,
and the regional chiefs would order it stored in the regional archives.
All nobles and below,
down to the common men and women,
dared not share the same name as the heir apparent.
Even with such precautions among the people,
some still contended to become ruler.
When clarity is maintained, the people are settled,
and all follows one principle,
thus everyone strives to become prime minister
but does not treacherously seek to be heir apparent.
It is not that the prime minister is esteemed and the heir apparent humble,
but that it cannot be sought through wisdom
nor contended for by force.
Now, if it is thought that no one knows a son like his father,
so when hastily appointing a successor upon death,
the father's wishes are followed arbitrarily,
this causes relatives not to be close,
and brothers not to love each other,
disrupting the order of the world,
and leading the customs of the world
to lose clarity, respect, and deference.
No method is more contrary to principle than this.
Upon hasty death, appoint the successor as the eldest son by the primary wife,
so that relatives love each other,
and brothers do not contend.
This is the ultimate righteousness in the world.
If the people do not contend,
it is also by learning from the royal palace and the houses of the lords.
Shāng Tāng exiled Jié,
and King Wǔ attacked Zhòu,
which is known throughout the world;
for a minister to exile his sovereign,
or a subordinate to assassinate his superior,
is the utmost rebellion in the world.
Yet the reason they long possessed the world
is that they opened benefits and removed harms for the world,
and continued it with righteousness.
Thus, their fame spread throughout the world
and was passed down to later generations,
because later generations concealed their faults and extolled their virtuous deeds,
establishing their meritorious achievements and transmitting them far and wide.
Therefore, the world all calls them sage emperors of perfect governance.
Their way was such that, amidst the world's chaos,
the strong bullied the weak,
the many oppressed the few,
the clever ruled the foolish,
soldiers were exhausted,
dying in warfare,
the old and weak were disturbed,
unable to manage their livelihoods,
all because the world lacked a Son of Heaven.
Emperor Gāo arose from common cloth and united the world,
subduing all feudal lords,
becoming the sovereign of the world.
He promoted benefits and removed harms,
putting the world's weapons to rest,
the highest virtue in the world.
Yet the world fails to clarify Emperor Gāo's virtuous deeds,
establish his meritorious achievements,
and extend them to later generations.
Thus, the world still practices the flawed virtues, achievements, and customs of a decayed age.
As for emperors and kings,
none fail to establish norms according to the times,
and handle affairs based on the circumstances,
to suit their era.
Those who wish to alter the ancient and change the constant
will die if not perish,
as the sages have decreed.
They disliked the people changing them,
so they recorded them in writing,
to bind it firmly,
and thereby be known to later generations.
